WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION. 1892. . TO THE RATEPAYERS OF WIDNES. LADIES AND GENTLEM&N.-
Having been nominated by the Widnes Educational Association to represent the Nonconformist and Independent portion of the community, we respectfully offer ourselves for election.

We come before you as the friends of the Public School System, intent, if elected, on doing our best to provide In your Board Schools the utmost educational facilities afforded by the Education Acts, and we may be depended upon to see that the e.dminietration of the Board is conducted with due regard to economy.

We are in sympathy with the course of religious instruction and observances which now obtain in the Board Schools. We would point out the inadequacy of your representation on the Board,leaving the control of your Board Schools largely tothose whose first care must be the interests of their own schools.

We trust, therefore, that the great body of Nonconformists and Independent voters will support us in this effort to alter this anomalous condition of things. This is the more necessary by reason of the regrettable retirement of Mr. T. S. Tirnmis, who is an ardent and thorough progressive educationalist.
This is the People's Question, and we appeal to all friends of education to support a Progressive Educational Policy by voting for
DENJAMIN BROWN. DAVID LEWIS, ROBERT SHAW, who have no interest in any other schools.

ON one occasion when Rowland Hill was preach In ,/ for a public charity, a note was handed him I inquiring if it would be right for a bankrupt to contribute. He noticed the matter in the course of his sermon, and pronounced that such a person could not do so in Christian honesty. "But, my fi iends," he said, "I would advise you who are not insolvent not to pass the plate this evening, or the people will be sure to say There goes the bank- rupt " TErE Laird of Garscadden and a friend happened one day, after a keen day's sport, to visit unex- pectedly the residence of a Water-of-Endrick farmer. The sportsmen were very cordially received by the family, and, among other apologies, the landlord regretted that dinner was over, as he bad just finished some excellent chickens. " Mak nae apologies, George," said Garscadden ; "I weel believe what you say, for I 13e3 the feathers (alluding to some spots of pease-brose) still on your breast."

--- The representative of a New York news agency, who interviewed Mr. Carnegie in London, was in- formed by that gentleman that he was about to visit various manufacturing centres on the contin- ent for the purpose of making a stuiy of industrial questions. After referring to his forthcoming book and to the labor riots at Homestead, Mr. Carnegie declared that the industrial outicok in Great Britain was very dark, and predicted that America will be able to undersell Britain in her own markets.

Miss Francis Power Cobbe, who has irritated Dr. Victor Horsley out—far out of the philosophic calm of the scientist by her book the " Nine Circles," is an extremely jolly old lady, very stout, with a round rubicund face, and her merry laugh is most infectious. She worships the animal creation, and looks upox it as a mission laid upon her to protest with all her might and main against vivisection. She is generally surrounded by an army of pet dogs. Miss Cobbe is Irish—daughter of the late Charles Cobbe, of Newbridge House, co. Dublin.

The Rev. Dr. Rainy, of whose views on the theatre Mr. Beerbohm Tree has been falling foul in Glasgow, is the recognised leader of the Scotch Free Church. Dr. Rainy is the principal of the Free Church College in Edinburgh, and even in vacation time spends most of his time in the Scots capital. There are only two other B.;zures—John Stuart Blackie and Professor Mason—who are as familiar in Edinburgh as Dr. Rainy. It is no exaggeration to say that Dr. Rainy is perhaps the ablest ecclesiastic in Scotland. If the phrase can be understood, he is the statesman as well as the professor and minister. Dr. Rainy has fought zealously for the disestablishment of the Church of Scotland.

It is not generally known that one of Mr. Wool- ner's sculptures produced very tragic results on the careers at Oxford of several young men. Mr. Woolner had executed in his early years a bust of Dr. Leland, a former dean of Christ Church. This bust was placed in the library of the college. In the summer term of 1870 some undergraduates in a mad freak, the results of a wine party, broke into the library, brought Dean Leland's bust and a Byzantine Venus into the quadrangle, and deliberately des- troyed both these works of art. This vandalism, which created a great sensation at the time. led to the public expulsion of three of the delinquents, and the banishment from Oxford for a few terms of several others.

The Princess of Wales is still in excellent health. Certain of the Court chroniclers recently stated that her Royal Highness was slightly indisposed. It was an unimportant matter, and was easily thrown off. The Princess has, as I wrote some time since, •mtirely recovered the bright spirits of which her great sorrow had deprived her. The people on the Deeside are loud in her praises, and laud her charity, her sweet temper, and her womanly sym- pathy. On the Deeside the country folk invariably issociate the Royal Family with deeds of sentiment and benevolence, and, though the Princess has been greatly occupied with the duties of hospitality, she has found time to visit the sick poor. She has on more than one occasion accompanied the Queen on her expeditions of charity.

Apropos of the adoption of the ivy-leaf as a badge by the Yemenite faction, Mr. Tim Healy has de- livered himself of a neat moral in verse. Thus runs "Tim's" artless lay : I Fit symbol of those parasitic minds • - • That cling, destructive, to the stately tree With grip that drags to earth whate'er it binds, Whether hoary oak or noble pile it be. The clingin,, ivy, emblem of decay Of ruindshrines, of leafless trunks, of ill ro all it grapples, sapping life away— l'hou art not Erin's badge; she wears her Shamrock
still. Mr. Healy thus proves that he csn be as sarcastic and hard-hitting in versa as in prose.

The first of the Irish County Conventions was held in Tipperary on Monday. In theresolutions passed it was recognised that the present Government had givr,n " satisfactory indications of a sincere desire and honest re'olution to keep faith with the people of Ireland." Mr. Dillon, in a speech following up rhe resolutions, dealt with the position of the evicted tenants now being inquired into by the Government Commission. What will be done with rhe tenants ? Mr. Dillon wants to see those who have been unjustly evicted during the past thirteen wears reinstated in their holdings,and on terms that will enable them to live and thrive in their homes."

On this settlement will depend the future relations between Irish tenants and landlords. Meantime, while the Government is settling what is to be done with the landless tenantry, an appeal is to be made to the Irish people for a relief fund in their aid.

Each Australian mail now brings us a fresh financial sensation. 83, Monday's we have news of the bankruptcy of Sir Benjamin Benjamin, who had the reputation of a colonial Rothschild, and was a director of a number of Australian financial institu- tions in which a considerable amount of British capital was invested. Most of these institutions have collapsed, and Sir Benjamin has been involved in their ruins. Finding it impossible to extricate nimself in any other way, he has filed his schedule, and resigned his seat in the Victorian Upper House as well as his position as a Melbourne alderman. Sir tienjamin is the President of the Melbourne Hebrew 'ongregation, and has always been actively associa- ted with the Jewish institutions of Melbourne. lie was born in London fifty-eight years ago, but has Tent nearly all his life in Melbourne. Be has been thrice mayor of that city and was knighted for his lavish civic hospitalities during the Exhibition year, 1888.

2 "Who will free us from the tyranny of the Chinese domestic ?" This cry of despair comes to us from Singapore, where, if we may trust the local papers, the difficulties to which it refers have now reached a climax. In particular the extortions of the Chinese cook (all domestic servants in the Straits Settlements appear to be Chinese) are re- presented as something appaling. His pilferings in collusion with the tradesmen are locally known as " squeezes." and it is affirmed that an offer to a Chinese servant of an increase of wages in lieu of these irregular imposts would be met with scorn and derision. " A Housewife and Mother " writes complaining piteously of the " rapacity and wickedness" of these "tyrants of the kitchen but it appears to be easier to complain than to find a remedy. One editor feebly suggests that some- body or other" should make an effort "—a course which, it will be remembered, was recommended to the first Mrs. Dombey with no very satisfactory result. Mr. Thomas7Tertius Paget, who has just passed away at his seat at Humberstone, at the ripe age of eighty-four, had clOne splendid service for the Liberal party in his native county. Thirty years ago he was chiefly instrumental in healing the breach between the Whigs and the Radicals in Lei- cester, and five years later he carried the popular cause to victory in the southern division of the .county, beating Mr. Albert Yell by thirty-nine votes. Apart from politics Leicester owes Mr. Paget a deep debt of gratitude. As the head of Paget's Bank he rendered such services to the mer- cantile and manufacturing community of Leicester as are not to be lightly estimated. On more than one occasion the chief partner in one of the largest and most flourishing manufactories in the town has testified that it was to the timely assistance of the bank that his firm owed its foundation and upward progress,and this is only one of many cases in which he contributed to the development of trade in the town.

early Christians whose preaching was " foolishness to the Greeks " who " sought after wisdom and , were indeed the wisest nation then existing." And again, as to their working the mines of ignor- ance—this is rather to their credit ; as no otherl Idenomination digs so deep—and, even if, by pass- ling through the fire of fanaticism, a small propor- tion only are induced to lead better and more temperate lives, society as well as the individuals so affected, are benelitted thereby. " Quite no" interjected mine host, " your men- tion of the denominations reminds me how he spoke of them. " Denominations are now mere names— names of things whose essence has changed almost to revolution. Where now is Calvinism? Dead asl its founder, surviving only in name as the pale shadow of its former self, as Calvinism mitigated , and ameliorated by modern influences. It would require a horde of Cal vins now to burn one Servetus.l Calvin could not exist in our modern religious atmosphere—his belief was too logical. We arel less logical, but more tolerant. Then there isl Wesleyanism ; the decadence here is not so marked, but is still very evident when the founder and hisl belief is compared with those who still denomin- ate themselves by his name. Jlhn Wesley be- lieved in witches, in possession of devils and that, the world and its inhabitants was specially created in 144 hours. Who, now, would go this length? Wesleyanism is gone, but left Methodism behind." Here I grew impatient with my prolix host and interrupted him by saying—" And better so. As: the old order giveth place to the new " so a too strict following of the mere opinions of a founder is intellectual slavery—a mental bondage of a kind that said founder himself had given a precedent for 1 breaking. The dead should never be allowed to rule the living except for good—and but too often this rule becomes a tyranny. All religious reformers break away, in some sort, from existing traditions and usages. Religious thought cannot go backward, it dire not stand still,it must go onward and upward toward a better knowledge and a better faith. But here I was stopped by the genial rotundity putting his hand—not over my mouth—but his own to con- ceal a sleep-indicating yawn, so I took my candle and my departure bedward muttering—" If there ,re any after this—let graceless bigots fight. He can't be wrong whose life is in the right."_ .
—Good night. (To be continued.)

4Nt [WITHOUT THB BILBFINETTE.I I. BY JOHN PEERS. (Continued) After a brief call at the museum, to report pro- gress and return thanks,and another all too hurried glance at the many things in which they are so rich and we so poor—notably the 22 feet long specimen of Ichthyreaming platydon—the Fish Liz- ' ard—from Lyme Regis and the fine type specimen ' of Plesiosasurus Convbeari, I again emerge upon the rapidly darkening streets to seek an abiding place for the night rest and refreshment. Now, this is a matter of some difficulty in a strange town to those who wish to avoid the two extremes of dirt and dearness. Personally I am content if I can get the three grand factors in a night's rest—warmth, dryness, and cleanliness. These " premises" being granted the "rest" may be assumed. So set myself to solve the great and pressing problem—where and whither for the night. Now what subtle influence was it that led my wandering steps to the threshold of the Cathedral Hotel ? Was it —could it be some subtile emanation—some philo-ecclesiastic influence per- meating my too susceptible cephalic organ? Again I say was it—could it be—this hat? Had this far too clerical-looking capital covering of mine begun to mislead me as it had so often misled others ? Was, in fact, this hat making me as mad as a hat- ter ? How else can I account for finding myself in such a place, devoted nominally to the reception of episcopalian dignitaries, arguing with myself the question " to be or not to be?" Now, it is well-known that we are endowed with a dual nature; each man and woman has tis or her double. Each man has a good and a bad side, not always with a strictly medial line of division—the good following too closely the proportion of Fal- staff's bread to his " intolerable deal of sack." Man has a sane and an insane side—sometimes the one is outside sometimes the other. Some of us wear our sane side inside and are such adepts at conceal- ment tkat even our best and most intimate friends never suspect us of its possession. With some again, " motley's the only wear," and what, of san- ity exists beneath is jealously guarded as a possess- tion too precious for public display. And have we not an imaginative and a matter-of-fact side in each of us? And does not Mr. Imagination do, say, and think things that his twin brother Mr. Matter- of-fact roundly denounces as extremely foolish ? What, for instance, was it made me in days— now, alas! too far gone to recall, except as a plea- sant memory—why in those halcyon days did I fancy myself a sailor, an incipient Columbus —a Viking—a Buccaneer? Even now at this distance of time I can recal the loving regard I had for a large spot of tar ornamenting my inexpressibles! The possession of that spot of tar constituted me a Jack-tar, and I breathed in imagination the salty flavour of the ocean laden with spicy waftings from Araby-the-Blest. ro have suggested the re- moval of this beauty-spot would, in my then state of mind, have amounted to little short of sacrilege. Ah ! happy, if somewhat foolish days ere yet "the iron " of matter-of-fact had "entered the soul." But all this time I am standing on the threshold of the Cathedral Hotel, while Mr. Imagination who brought me there is debating the matter with Mr. Matter-of-Fact as to the advisability of staying there.
"Well," said Mr. M., " What are you doing here?" „.

"Seeking rest and refreshment," said the other. " Bosh !" exclaimed Mr. Matter-of-Fact, "this is no place for you. Get you hence, and seek more modest lodging. But I suppose it is that inordi- nate vanity of yours has led you here to rub, shoulders with the dignitaries of the Church. Be- ing so often mistaken and addressed as the Rev. Mr. So-and-So, may have fed this vanity, but it is no reaion for thus seeking to hob-nob with bishops. Besides, look at the expense ; is the game worth the candle ?" "Now, don't be savage," interposed Imagination, " if I like good company and good accommodation, and am willing to pay for them, who shall say me nay ?" Whereon Mr. Matter-of-fact stamped his'foot and said, "Well, if you have made up your mind—or what stands in place of it, to commit this folly, there is no more to be said. But allow me to remind you that you have no tithes coming in—no rent charges, rectorial or vicarial. And remember, con- tinued be, "that, although you are by circumstances raised above the hateful necessity of lying for a living—of representing that to be which you know to be not—you-are also unconnected with any branch of lucrative popular delusion; nor have you any means of squeezing your fellow-creatat es to extort from them the means of furnishing you with un- deserved luxuries. The money you spend here will be your own; hence you cannot compete with those who are spending other people's." This did completely for Mr. I. "Matter-of-fact has it," said I," come along." So I went further and fared no worse. For I had the honour of sleep- ing beneath the same roof as "Sammy," the prize cat. Now the reader may think this a sad falling off from a sleek-slabsided Bishop to the furry feline. Times change. Which would the ancient Egyptians have preferred? " Sammy " by odds! In this rule, I am with the Egyptians,

_ - "There is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune." Being here, on the bank of the Avon,from whose recurrent fluxions the "Bard" thereof most probably derived this most beautiful and appropriate simile, I have logged in the quotation, even over the corpse of propriety, in order to be enabled to throw out the idea. Many other more or less probable theories and philosophical speculations I might advance were it not for that inexorable old ruffian " Chr mos," who, like the modern man in blue, bids me "Move on." Now if we do not " move on "with the times, time will move on without us, and I thereby will ensure a great loss of time—and time is money. Now this is the kind of argument to use to the modern grundyan if we wish them to keep pace with the times. You may talk yourself breathless about the loss of honour, or indeed all the virtues, but once get the latter-day Mammonist imbued with the idea that pecuniary loss to him- self will result from any action or want of action and your anxieties and responsibilities, on that point, may cease; he will be upsides with the times "you bet !" Money is the grundyan god—a god of 'Change, whose devotee eats, drinks, and thinks him, to the exclu-lion of better things. In the " Aurum pota- bile " of luctation his little soul finds a congenial death. Be drinks it eagerly as though it were the true Elixir vita whereas it often proves to him a veritable Draught of Death, killing all that is good within him. But now, my business was to tramp the fast-darkening streets in search of accommod- tion for the night. At several places they were "So sorry,but we are quite full I" Now, having neither the sixteen family organ pipes nor the bassinette, it could not be the sight of my too numerous retinue tailing away into the far distance in gradually diminishing sizes and shrillness of tone ! Nor was I insulted by a recommendation to the " Home for Children" fu,ther up the street, or the " Parents' Refuge" round the corner, nor told to seek lodgings under the sign of "The Cornucopia" or "The Qui- ver-full," in Solomon-st. None of these aggravations fell to my lot, but I eventually fell upon my feet in a quiet little place of entertainment—half confec- tion shop, half restaurant, the presiding genius of which was a genial rotund, story-loving mortal of the gossiping type we remember so well in the "Arabian Nights." He could—and did without pressing—furnish anecdotes of most of his late guests. I was not long in finding myself subjected to a process of preliminary extraction to furnish material for a subsequent repetition of the opera- tion with my successors. Though not in these' words, to this effect he addressed me : " I conjure thee by Allah, Oh stranger, to recount unto me the adventures that have happened unto thee this day." To which I replied Verily, Oh master, my adventures this day have been few and simple." So I told him my story as already known unto thee, 0 reader, including the "Incident of the hat, and the reverence paid thereto ;" upon hearing which he fell into an immoderate fit of laughter. Upon his recovery from this seizure he muttered strange words in a strange language—Sartor .Resartus —which require the talisman of learning for their explanation. He then recounted unto me the story of a late guest who ridiculed tailor-made-reverends and was particularly severe on the Salvationists, as a set oh illusionists whose creed consists in a hypothetical damnation, resulting from- a supposit- ious event, and an equally hypothetical redemption from this (suppositious damnation; fanatics whose de- light it is to imagine themselves damned in oidor to have the pleasure of imagining then:lS-We-a laved. "They work' so this cynic is reported to havelaid, "they work in the dark-mines of ignnranc lying as a sub-stratum at the foundation of society, for upon that ignorance alone can they Here I ventured to interpose thg:rematk—" that in this respect. they were no worse_of,(thntl wel:e the

div.head: DUKE OF CONNAUGHT AT JAPANESE BATHS.
div.p: THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT AT JAPANESE BATHS.

What baths they were !—made of wood about six feet long, by three feet wide, by two feet deep. sunk in the flor, and filled with steaming water conveyed through two or three miles of bamboo piping from the bowels of the slumbering volcano above, Oiigoku, which, being interpreted, means "Big hell" The Duke used to say that he never enjoyea a bath so much in his life as at Miyano- shita. One stripped off one's clothing, and wiapped up in a crepe kimono, ornamented with Japan-blue palm trees and storks, was conducted to one's bath by one of the ravishing little musumeg, scarlet- kirtled and gaudily hair-pinned, who waited at the hotel. To a shy man it was a little embarrassing, but, in Japanese ethics, bathing is the merest trifle. —From "The .Taps at Home

div.head: Am CHAMBERLAIN'S NEW PROGRAMME.
div.p: Am CHAMBERLAIN'S NEW PRO- GRAMME.

- -------. The " Star " says :—As was expected, we have not had long to wait fora new programme from Mr. Chamberlain. His energy in making programmes during the last six years has been prodigious, but the new one, unlike his recent performances, is not reactionary ; it goes forward at a pace which will amaze Mr. Chamberlain's fellow Unionists. The following are the proposals in his scheme of social legislation, which he makes as a " socialist " and as a " statesman who has been in office, and who if he again is called to office will be prepared to put into effect"- 1. Legal restriction of hours. a. Eight hours for miners. b. Restriction of hours—(l) of railway men, (2) workmen in dangerous and (3) specially laborious employment. c. Restriction of shop assistants' hours by a vote of majority or on initiative of the munici- pal authority. 2. Provision for old age. 3. Very wide extension of employers' liability. 4. Municipal socialism : The public authorities to
provide work for men wilring to work but who _ cannot get work. _
5. Temperance reform: Support the Bishop of Chester's scheme.

Lieutenant Count on Schweinitz, the leader of the German Expedition to the Victoria Nyanza to establish a dockyard there, and who was wounded at Tabora in an encounter with a hostile tribe, sub- jects of Sultan Sikki, has written a letter to his brother, dated Urguru, now published in the "Kol- nische Zoitung," in which occur the following pas- sages:—" The Sultan Maharuri came to me and asked me to visit his domain. I had expected a hostile reception from all the tribes, but had formed an erroneous opinion of those savages.' The Sul- tans are very intelligent and taking people. I have to-day visited the village of Sultan Wamba, and can assure you that many peasants in Germany do not live in such pleasant dwellings. The rooms the people inhabit are from 91t. to 12ft. high, and from 15ft. to lBft. wide. An exemplary carefulness is exhibited in all their industrial pursuits. Vessels of from 6ft. t 0 91t. high and of 3ft. to Oft, in diame- ter contain the fruits of the fields; the fruit is then carefully selected and placed in small coops on the flat roofs of the houses to dry. There ave goats and fowl in plenty, but unfortunately no oxen, for two years ago a plague came among the cattle and they all had to be killed. lam on good terms at present with all the Sultans. They are powerful rulers, and govern large territories, and commerce with the different peoples is highly interesting."

div.p: THE BISHOP OF CHESTE IPS LICENSING
SCHEME.

The Bishop of London presided over a Church of Eng- land Temperance Society's Conference at Shrewsbury, on Monday. Thu Bishop of Chester explained the nature of the bill he propcsed to introduce, dealing with the licensing question. On the Gothenburg system. A philanthropic company would be formed to manage the husiness, the directorate having small fixed salaries, the surplus profits of sales to go to 'objects of a philanthropic character, but not to reduce the rates. License holders would have, say, five years' notice that their houses would be taken over by the company, with such stocks as might be reduced, and trustworthy servants taken over under new conditions. Landlords who wished to part with their houses immediately might be allowed two years' profit on their business. As AG the licenisng authority he would leave it as at present. He did not propose to introduce int 4 his bill anything as to option of prohibiting. No resolution was arrived at, the pro- posal being left for the consideration of the council. FORMATION OF A TEACHERS' ASSOCIA- TION AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternOOn the teachers of Runcorn district assembled in Greenway-road Board Schools for the purpose of. forming a local association in connection with the Hational'Union of Teachers. Mr..l-. F. Moulton was voted to the chair, and he at Once called upon Mr. J. C. Horobin, M.A., .a member of London School Board; who attended as a deputation from the executive ,of the N.U.T., to address the meet- ing. M. Dorcibin stiongly urged all present to join the Union at once for the protection of their own interests. He pointed out that there are now before the country questioos closely affecting the welfare of every teacher, and teachers must be united, and completely organised in order to secure that their views shall be considered In hesettlement of these questions. In order to obtain redress of grievances it was necessary that. the National Union should be able to speak in the name of the whole of the teachers of the country. There were now up- warps of 20,000 members, and he trusted the number would be greatly. .increased during the present year. Speaking of the Superannuation scheme Mr. Rorobin reMarkedthat in the interests of education, in hOoorable means-arretirement••in old age, should be provided by" the state. There was no profession with which he was acquainted which made such continued demands upon the, energies and resources of mind and body as the work of a teacher, and it should therefore receive suit- able recognition from the State. Other questionswere deOt with•by the speaker in a masterly aud exhaustive manner, and he concluded by Once 'more requesting all those present to joiFf the Union and to use their influence to induce others to join also.—Mr. J. Grundy, general secretary of the Liverpool and District Teachers' Associa- tion also addressed the meeting. On the proposition of Mr. Parr (Whines), seconded by Mr. Epps, it v.otq unanimously decided to form a branch of the N.U.T. The Chairman was appointed. secretary pro Um and authoriFe•l to call a meeting that day fortnight for the purpose of electing officers and selecting a committee. Votes of thanks to Mr. Horobin, and to the Runcorn School Board for the toe,of .Ihe School, brought the proceedings to a close: -.TV, • ,;

div.head: PRIDE OF THE MILL
div.p: PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. Br LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.

CHAPTER XXIL THEY STOOD FACE TO FACE AT LAST, THESE TWO, WHO BOTH LOVED SO FONDLY THE SAME MAN. Frank Lyons drew back, white with wrath, as these cutting, scornful words fell from lonie's lips, and seizing the opportunity, she sprang into the coach unassisted, followed by her chaperon, Miss Carriscourt. He took his place silently beside her, and not another word was spoken until they arrived within sight of the Tresham residence; then he turned to her, and she saw by the light of the carriage lamps a glittering fire in his flashing eyes. "I have one request to make of you, lonie," he said, hurriedly, "and that is that you will not publish to the world by your actions the terms on which we stand. Will you promise me that much 7" "If you keep away from me, I promise," she answered. "That is exactly what I must not do," he said, angrily. "As our engagement has but just been given out, such a procedure would excite comment. Be reasonable, lonie." She saw at once that he was quite right; but she did not vouchsafe him a reply. "Will you dance the first dance with me 7" he asked, as he handed her out of the carriage. "It Is expected of you. I am obliged to ask you in advance, to make sure of you." "It is a matter of indifference to me," said lonie, haughtily. A little later they entered the magnificent ball- room. No wonder a throb of exultant pride that he had won her stirred Frank Lyons's heart as he noted the furore joule created. She was dressed with charming simplicity, which formed a striking contrast to the over-dressed, bejewelled young girls present. He' dress was of while fleecy tulle, without ruffle or tuck, which fell in plain straight folds from the slender waist to the tiny foot. From out of the folds of lace which was gathered into a frill at the throat, rose the graceful head, crowned with its beautiful nut-brown curls. White kid gloves covered the dainty little hands, reaching to the elbow sleeves. There was a total absence of jewels. She wore no ornaments, save the simple cluster of pink rosebuds on her breast and the spray of pink blos- som's in her curls. Many a young man's heart beat faster as he gazed In admiration on that vision of beautiful, girlish loveliness. She was the observed of all observers as she moved among the glittering throng. Miss Carriscourt smiled to see how unconscious lonie was of it. "You are making a most profound sensation, my dear," said Mrs. Tresham, coming up to her, flushed and pleased. "No flattery is intended, but you are by far the most successful dolbutante of the season. I predict that other balls will soon follow in your honour."

She wondered why these words brought no smile to the girl's lovely face. lonie looked slightly wearied. "There is only one young girl present who comes near rivalling you, my dear," she said with a mis- chievous twinkle in her eye, for she had said this simply to arouse lonie's Interest; "and she is,. by the way, a young fiancee, too. She has but 3nst come with her lover, Mr. Arthur Rochester. They gum coming this way. A handsome, distinguished- looking young man, is he not ?" The rich colour faded from lonie Lawrance's face; the little bands that held the cluster of pink roses trembled; even the crimson lips grew pale. Arthur was engaged to another, and so soon ? Ab, how quickly he had forgotten her! And her heart cried out bitterly against the inconstant love of men. lonie rose from her seat, not hastily, but with the quiet grace that always distinguished her. "The scent of flowers is quite overpowering," she said. "I never like helliotrope in a room. What were you saying about the young lady lean. lug on the arm of the—the—gentleman who is approaching? Who is she ? "Miss Elaine Granger, the heiress," returned her hostess. "She is a ward of young Mr. Rochester's father." All the indifference had faded from lonie's face as If by magic, as she gazed breathlessly at the young girl whom Arthur now loved. She saw the gleam of white satin and costly lace, a face, dark, proud and piquant, and jewels that might have cost a king's ransom, swinging from the pink shell-like ears, and running like a river of fire around the white throat and bare, gleaming arms. In that moment she remembered where she had seen that young girl before. Her thoughts travelled quickly bAck to that stormy night when she, penni- less and friendless, stood on the stone, snow-covered steps of the Rochester mansion in the terrible snow-storm, begging of this self-same girl, who had peered at her from behind the footman who had aLswered the bell, to be permitted to see Arthur Rochester for just one little minute, and how coldly and cruelly this girl had refused and repulsed her, and how she had turned slowly away, facing the storm and the darkness again, praying Heaven to let her die and end it all, the world so cruel and hard. Under what strange circumstances they were to meet now, "You two will be rival beauties," laughed Mrs. Tresham, good-naturedly. "Have a care for your laurels, lonie." "She is young, beautiful, and very happy, I suppose—is she? Does her—her—lover love her very much?" The fair face paled as she asked the question, oh, so wistfully, and the crimson lips trembled, but Mrs. Tresham did not notice it. She laughed heartily. "What an old-fashioned question! I do not know. People do not think of that kind of thing. It is about the last inquiry I should ever think of making." " I—l—do not know what I could have been thinking of," faltered lonics. "Of course such a question is highly absurd." "As she is young and beautiful, I should say, yes. her lover must be attached to her. He is not marrying her for her gold, for he himself is quite as wealthy. It is, of course, a love match ; but, then, the attachments of men, dear friend, are matters of little moment," added the lady, with a delicious little laugh. Outwardly, lonie sat perfectly still—perfectly unconcerned—the cluster of roses hardly stirring with her breath • but her heart was beating ; her pulse was throbbing, every nerve thrilling ; her eyes half drooped; she felt the magic of his presence as he advanced, the spell that no one else in this world could throw around her. Just for one little minute she lost her high spirits; she faltered in her speech ; then she was herself again; a careless smile played around her lips. She knew that Arthur Rockester was watching her; their eyes had met. She gave a violent start, and answered at random, half incoherently the question Elaine was asking Mut. "Arthur," cried Elaine, "I do not believe you bear or care for what I am telling you. What are yea watching so intently? You look so white one could almost fancy in this ball-room you had seen a ghost." "Heaven help me, I have," he muttered under his breath—" a ghost of the dead past love." Aloud he said: "Pardon me if I seemed remiss, Elaine. I am ashamed to confess I was lost in thought. I promise you it shall not occur again." A feeling of pique stirred in his heart, ton, as he gazed upon the face of the girl he had loved better than life itself, and lost. "She shall see that others appreciate me," he thought, desperately, and applied himself assiduously to the task of entertaining Elaine. lenie watched them until she grew faint and heart•sick with the pain of it. When the dancing, mirth, and music were at their height, she turned to Miss Cariiscourt with a shud- dering cry. "I am tired of it all, and weary," she said. "1 wish we could go home." "That is impossible, my dear, owing to the fact the ball Is given in your honour," she replied, adding slowly: "I think I know why you do not care to stay. Arthur Rochester is here." "Thai can make no difference to me," returned lonie, proudly. "You know best why you sent him away, dear," returned Miss Carriscourt, pityingly. "A word-4i look would bring him to your side again. Do net be rash where the happiaess of two lives are at stake, child." "if it were to be done over again I should do Jest what I did then," she answered. "Say no Wore,. I—l will stay. I must learn to noliool

myself to meeting him," she moaned under her breath. She turned with a smile to Frank Lyons, who was hovering near her. "You asked for one dance," she said, with a Smile so charming that it fairly dazzled him; "and in return for your consideration, I will give you four. That is your favourite dance—the lancers. Shall we join the group directly in front of us?" He was only too glad to eagerly assent. "I will show him that I do not care," thought lonie, summing up all her bravery, as she allowed Frank Lyons to lead her oat upon the floor, past Arthur Rochester.

No one would have thought to have watched her bright 'eyes and smiling face that the girl's heart was breaking; that the lights, and the music and laughter were mockery to her. The bitterest drop in all her cup of woe was to note how oblivious Arthur seemed of her presence, after that first careless glance and salutation as he passed her by. How quickly he had forgotten her and sought consolation in another's love. . How she wished she had not come to the ball. Life would be so inexpressibly dreary for her after this.
Shortly after, Elaine was brought up to lonie by Mrs. Tresham, and presented to her. . _ _

Elaine held out her hand with a charming smile, wondering at the chilliness with which this young girl acknowledged the presentation, and, saying, cordially: "I hope we shall be the best of friends, Miss Lawrence. I am impulsive—pardon me U I say I like you already."
"She does net know that we both love the same man," lonie thought, looking into the proud, beautiful face.
At that moment one of lonie's partners claimed her, and, with a bow and a few courteous words to Elaine, she turr.ed away. A moment later Arthur Rochester came up to Elaine.
"What are you thinking of 1" he asked, with an attempt at gaiety. "Your face is quite a study." "Ot the new dZbutante—Miss Lawrence," she said, abruptly.
"What .dO you think of her?" he asked, hesitat- ingly. "She is quite as beautiful as report says," she answered; "but she has a heart of marble or ice. I have never met a girl like her."
CHAPTER XXIII. "Ah 1 leave roe not! I love but thee; Blessing or eurse, whiche'er thou be."

"She has no heart," repeated Elaine. "They tell me she is betrothed to Mr. Lyons, who used to be a chum of yours at one time, Arthur, and I marvel at it, wondering how he could ever have broached the subject of love to a girl like that." Arthur Rochester turned away, his fase flushing, then paling strangely. "She has no heart!" How oddly the words struck him. He knew differently. He remembered that scene by the fountain—bow they had watched the rippling waters kissed by the golden light of the stars—and standing there In the white, bright moonlight, with the perfume of the roses round them, how he had told lonie the story of his love; how the colour had flamed into those dimpled cheeks as her eyes drooped from his as she admitted, with sweet, girlish hesitancy, that she loved him as dearly as he loved her. That girl and this seemed two wholly different persons. That one, radiant with the light of love; this one, as Elaine had truly said, like a marble statue. What had so changed lonie ? It was a great puzzle to him. Was she happy with Lyons? He watched them narrowly, anxiously. He had always believed that he could meet her calmly, should they ever by chance be thrown into society together. He found now that it had been a false delusion. As he watched her gliding through the waltz with Lyons a frenzy of jealousy seemed to take possession of him. He felt like going up to them and tearing her from Lyons's clasp. "I cannot bear it," said lonie, coming up to Miss Carriscourt at last; "the lights and the music tire me."

"Come into the music room and rest quietly a few moments," suggested Miss Carriscourt ; "the excitement has unnerved you." " Shall I accompany you?" asked Lyons, eagerly. "Only as far as the door," responded lonie, coldly. He offered her his arm, the other to her chaperon, and they left the glittering ball-room. "There is no chance for quiet even here," exclaimed lonie, disappointedly, observing a group at the further end of the room clustered about the

piano. As she turned away, some of the young girls came hurriedly forward. "Don't go back just yet, lonie," they cried. "Mr. Rochester is going to sing. Come up to the piano and hear him." And glancing in that direction, in the midst of a group of young gentlemen and pretty girls, she saw Arthur.
"No, no!" panted lonie. "I cannot. Let me go." - - - -
"Not until you have beard at least one song. You do not know what a musical treat it will be," they declared. "Mr. Rochester sings divinely. Then you shall go back to the ball-room if you like."

Very reluctantly lonie allowed herself to be drawn toward the group surrounding Arthur. He had been declaring that he oould not sing—he had too bad a cold; but when he saw lonie approach- ing, with a strange expression on his handsome face, he changed his mind at once.
"Your persuasions have conquered me, young ladies," he said, in a low voice, seating himself at the . instrument. "Now, what shall it be?" _
, " Your favourite song," chorused all the young girls in a breath.
He bowed.
" My favourite it shall be, then," he said.

, A dead silence fell over the occupants of the music-room as Arthur ran his white, shapely fingers over the keys. Like the fluttering moth, that seems to insensibly feel the danger of the flame around which it hovers, yet unable to break away, Ioni( drew nearer still to her old lover. The wind stirred among the crimson roses that tossed their fragrant treasures against the open window near where lonie stood, and even the brilliant pendants of the chandeliers seemed to tremble as Arthur's deep, melodious voice thrilled through the room.

_ As the first lines fell from his impassioned lips, he could not resist the impulse to raise his eyes to lonie's face; then, seeing she was pale as death, he lowered the white lids over his scorching eyes, and never raised them again until he had finished, and these were the words he sang: :" I think of all thou art to me ; I dream of what thou canst not oe , My life is cursed with thoughts of thee, • Far over and for ever. "My heart is full of grief and wry; I see thy face where'er I go; I would, alas! it were not so, For ever and for ever. "Perchance, if we had never met, I had been spared this vain regret, This endless striving to forget, For ever and for over. "Perchance if thou wert far away, Did I not see thee day by day; I might again be blithe and gay, ',- For ever and for ever. Ah, no, I could not bear the pain Of never seeing thee again ! I cling to thee with might and main, For ever and for ever. - " Ah, leave me not! I love but thee. Blessing or curse, whiche'er you be' Oh, be as thou best been to me, For ever and for ever !" "Delightful* Charming!" chorused the bevy ot young girls, as the last note of the passionate retrain died away. "Won't you favour us with ona more song, air. itochester i Only one more," they persisted lonic could not have uttered one word to have saved her life. Those thrilling words seemed to have dazed her senses, paralyzed her heart. Like one in a dream she stood leaning against the piano, even after he had finished. She dared not raise her eyes, for she felt, intuitively, that he was gazing straight into her face; and she knew, too, that every word had been intended for her. "Was it meant in deep feeling, or—or sarcasm?" was the thought that whirled madly through her brain. If he had eared so much about her, and mourned losing her, he could never have consoled himself with another love. Ah, it was cruel of him to awaken those old, bitter•sweet memories, now that all was Over between them. She must not listen to his songs. She must fly from the spell while the strength was hers to do it —fly to the protection of the man to whom she was betrcthed, and whom she was to wed without love. lonie took one step forward, turning her white face away as she attempted to pass him with a haughty, careless, indifferent step. Then the room seemed to whirl around her, the chandelier

and the floor to meet. She threw up her little white hands with a gasp, and would have fallen. to the floor if Arthur Rochester had not spiang for- ward just in time to catch her in his arms. "Oh, she has fainted," cried one of the young ladies, in alarm. "She said she did not feel well enough to come in, but I insisted. It's all my fault. I will go•for Miss Carriscourt and Mr. Lyons at once." Frank Lyons was near at hand. A few words briefly explained the sitatiOn. "Miss Lawrence has faint-ear he ejaculated, hurrying into the music room, and up to the startled' group. • His face grew dark as night as he saw Arthur Rochester supporting s her. "Thank you for the assistance you have rendered her. I will relieve you of your care now, if you please," he said, ungraciously. Insensibly Arthur Rochester's arm tightened around the slim figure, lying so still and white against his throbbing breast. " I will relieve you of your burden," Frank Lyons- repeated. "The young lady is my betrothed," he added, maliciously, advancing a step nearer. Slowly Arthur unwound his arms from about her, and the pang that it cost him to resign her to, another, only Heaven knew. He turned abruptly away, and Frank Lyons bore her quickly from the room, summoning Miss Carriscourt. They took her into the conservatory adjacent, where the clear, cool water from the splashing fountain, with which they laved her face, soon revived her. They were discussing the advisability of return- ing home at once, when the lovely dark eyes flashed open wide, with a dazed, statled expression in them. "Was it a dream 7" she murmured. "You fainted in the music-room, my dear," said Miss Carriscourt, anxiously. "What caused it, lonie 2" "Oh, I—l—remember," she whispered, with a shuddering sob. "Tie- room was too warm." "You cannot deceive me," cried Lyons, bending down and fairly hissing the word in her ear. "It was the sight of your old lover's face. You would make me the laughing stock if New York society if this scene was repeated every time you and Roches- ter met." Bitter tears sprang to the dark velvety eyes, and Miss Carriscourt discreetly turned away and walked to the further end of the conservatory. "We were to have been married and you parted us," she sobbed. "Perhaps God can forgive you for It; I never can." "I would not take it so much to heart if I were you," sneered Lyons. "It does not seem to have affected Rochester unhappily, for, if report speaks truly, he was scarcely Off with the old love before he was on with the new.' He is soon to be ittarried to the little beauty he brought here to-night." How dare be taun ther with that Even Frank Lyons had discovered, then, how little he had loved her, after all. The fact was galling to her pride. "I decline to discuss the matter further," she answered, spiritedly. "Take me back to the ball- room, please." At this moment Miss Carriscourt came tIP to them. "You are quite sure you do not wish to go home, my dear 7" she said, anxiously. "What leave the ball that was given in MY honour 7" she said. "it is not to be thought of." Even Lyons was a little surprised at her sudden determination to remain. Frank Lyons escorted her back to the ball-room, and the first person they encountered near the door was Arthur Rochester. With all the pride she could summon lonie swept past him, and as he watched her in the dance, her cheeks flushed, her eyes sparkling, the crimson lips smiling, apparently the gayest of the gay, he turned away with a heavy sigh. "Mad fool that I was I" he mutttered to himself. "I believe that it was old memories that overcame her as she listened to my song. I see my folly now; It was but the closeness, the heat of the room, that caused her to faint." His drive home with Elaine was rather con- strained. "Have you enjoyed the ball, Arthur?" she asked, eagerly, laying a little white, jewelled hand timidly on his arm. "No," he answered abruptly. "I wished you had not persuaded me into going. I hope I shall not be Inveigled into going to any more." "Not if you do not like them," returned Blaine, wistfully. "I detest society," he declared, bitterly; "it is Ifflam and a delusion; it would turn the bead of the best woman living, I believe, for the most part of it is composed of women as false as they ere fair." "What a sweeping assertion," laughed Elaine, good-naturedly; but in her own heart she vtafi wondering why he spoke so bitterly of what here- tofore he had always held up to highest praise. "You shall go to no more balls with me if you do not care for them," she said, considerately ; "but you must not take a dislike to garden parties. I have a plan in my head, Arthur. What do you say to giving a garden party in honour of Bliss Lawrence T" (To be continued.)

In an article on the sense of humour in ani,t°,ft. the" Spectator" tells the following story of a Ja'_A daw. A jackdaw of the writer's acquaintance In": an ingenious method of tormenting the nurnerour' dogs of the establishment, which was most coraie t° behold, and which owed something of its finish to a more artistic conception of the humorous side a teasing than most jackdaws are credited for. It wag an extremely hut summer; and the dogs, of whAic there were three, spent the greater part of the unY dozing peacefully on the lawn. Ling all either dumber spaniels or setters, they had fine sillti coats, which extended to their feet, little tufts o flossy fur sticking out between their toes. Whend° dog was comfortably asleep, with its feet stretch out, dreaming of partridges, the jackdaw would hop gently round, and then make a sudden dive at On° fluffy tassels between its toes, which never failed to wake the dog up with a quick sense of discom- fort, which a tug at the hair anywhere else on its body Vroultt'. never have provoked. At another house al tamemagpie was kept in a stable-yard wii,n , a couple of kestrels. The kestrels were in the hub't .ot sitting on the sides of the water-pails set to warm in the Sun outside the stable doors. The mas:Ple* being in want of amusement, bit on the following plan. Ile cautiously approached a kestrel from behind, and, seizing the bird's long tail in his ben; gave it one or two violent pulls and pn.hes, ana, having worked the kestrel cpiite off its balance, with a good forward push pitched it into the paii,or so far in as its flapping wings allowed. The inagPie then" saved itself" with great haste in the bar rack above the manager. In this case the joke WO paid for ; one of the kestrels,. more widawake that? usual, caught the magpie as It was approaching 811!1. drove its claws into the•practical joker's legs oast his ?creams brought help. . div.head: CHARGE OF MURDEROUS ASSATITZ -AT BIIRTONWOOD.
div.p: CHARGE OF MURDEROUS ASSATITZ -AT BIIRTONWOOD.

At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednes- day, before Messrsdlohn Rylands, and John White, and Major Pickmere, Thomas Dutton, wheel,- wright, of Burtonwood, was charged. after repeated remands from the Occasional Court, with: unlaw- fully and maliciously 'wounding, on the 20th of August, John Garvin, labourer for the Burtonwood Highway Board. Mr. A. Browne 'appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Mulholland,- barrister, of Liverpool, instructed by Mr. P. 'Davies, for the defence. —Mr. Mulholland took the objection that the prisoner was in illegal custody, having been apprehended at one; in the morning, and lodged in jail without a warrant. He appeared there now for the first time, and did so under protest. He applied' that his client should be released, as .he was illegally apprehended.—Mr. Browne said this was the Irst they had heard about appearing under protest. The man was in proper custody, for the I simple reason that the charge might have been onerif 'murder' as at one time his life was in absolute danger, and his depositions had to be taken. He himself and also a witness told P. C. Devlin, who made the arrest, that if he had not come Dutton would have 9m-rendered himself next morning. The sergeant had a perfect right to apprehend him, under the circumstances.-4t •was decided to take the tacts of the case before deciding on Mr. Mulhoiland's objection.—Mr. Browne made his statement of the,case,and said after the defendant had eom ,mitted the assault, he went away and comeback for his bass and inhumanly left him lying bleeding with hid leg broken,and did nothing to help him.Mr.Browne expressed the opinion that the attack did not come far short of attempted murder.—The prosecutor, who had to be as - Mated into a chair, said on the 20th of August hevaras cutting a drain across a footpath. He saw a boy in Dutton's employ pass, and in about ten minutes heoaw Dutton. Witness said to him, "Are you going to pay me what you owe me, or do you ever intend to pay .me 2" He replied, "I will never pay you." Witness said, "If I was able I would pay you it some way." Dutton then put down a bass and can that he carried, and caught hold of the spade witnese had in his hand. He stuck to it. while Dutton pulled him Hine or ten yards front the footpath. He got the spade ,from his hand, and hit hint on the left shoulder with it. He then dropped the spade, and put hint on his hams, :and then jumped twice with his knees on his breast. He then thumped himin the face. He asked him if he was going to kill him, and he said he would kill him before he leftehim. He then got off him. Dutton picked, up the spade again and placed it on witness's throat, -and with an oath said he would cut his head off. Ele dropped the spade again, and jumped with his feet on toovit- ness's left leg. He ehouted to him that his leftleg was broken and that he had him finished. Be replied it would serve him right if his other leg was hi-eaten. Sae remained lying on the footpath with his Slag broken. A few minutes afterwards his son came and he told him his leg was broken and he brought damesDaiatith with a pony and mart from the Limerick Hotel, and he was taken home in the cart. Witness lay about2o minutes in the road. tile was seen next morning by Dr. Smith, of Warrington, and was seven weeks in bed before he could Mt up-lily Mr. Mulholland f. Duttou had employed him to do some sewerage, and had not done it properly at drat. Then heetarted ta do it agaie,. but Dutton would not atar him for the work. He did not. tell George Cooper, farmer, that if Dutton did not pay him he was going to do for hint, or Ma. Prescott, farmer's wife, that he woUld havel it in for Dutton. When he said he would make Duttort pay af he was able he meanthe would force him by law, not with the spade. He 'did not lift his spade to Dutton or shout at the top of his voice "If you stir another yardi will have your life,'!,oer did he say" I will have, your money or your life, you black devil. Dutton did not ea' he could not pay them, nor did he say that he wouldloay before hislife was taken. He hit him with the 'fiat of the spade, and on the shoulder. Wetness did not catch him by the beard then, but when ho was on his back and Dutton was using his fists. Witness fell and 'Dutton on the top of him in struggling for the spade. He did not cry out then that his leg was broker. As he was lying after the, assault Dutton brought Ralr h Cooper and two other men and a .cart. Lane of them bandaged: his leg, and he believed Cooper assisted him into the cart.—Mr. Rylands asked if Mr. Mulholland adhered' to his preliminary objection.—Mr. Mulholland said der Mid, and cited a case in support: thereof.—Mr. Browne' contended that in that case no felony had been estas-1 matted, bat in this case there had been, there might have been ,anurder.—Mr. Mulholland said this was a mere quarrel in the road, and it was absurd to say there .was any power on the part of, the ,police to arrest a man 4 for an offence for which there was no continuous pursuit. This was an important constitutional question. Thai police were not to go and take people out of their homed' because one man went and told a coal and bull story. Mr. eßrowne : Not a cock and hull-story at all. Mr. Browne said he would withdraw the proceedings and' apply for a gammons. Mr. Mulholland: Well do so. 'My friend may take his own course at his own peril •The Chairman ,suggested that Mr. Browne should do bet he decided to go on with the case. Dr. Starkey 'Smith deposed to the complainant's legbeing broken 3 to:4 inches abovethe ankle. The fracture was a com- minuted one and became compound. Gavin complained of painsin his chest and left shoulder, which had a black diseolouration on it. He thought tim in a very critical ,corchtion. It was cot impossible but unlikely that the brokenlegcould have been caused by a twist or a fall. The injurytad been ,caused by direct violenoe, in which be .wouldinclude a heavy man falling on the complain- ant, but .he did not. consider Dutton a ‘heavy man. —PatrickSistvin, theeomplainant's ion, gave evidence, said said he was in the Limerick Hotel, and heard screams which brought him to the spot whereisis father wa,s lying. He met the defendant, who said witness's father ,00mplained that :leis leg was broken, tat said, "What could I,do when-he met me with the spade 2"— Some coaversation took place as to the Court adjourning for luncheon.—Mr. Rylands remarked that there was plenty of evidence to justify committal.—Mr.Mulholland said that appeared to him an extraordinary remark to make at this stage ef the case, on one man's uncorrobo- rated Mary. Whether that fCourt lunched or not was no matter to the prisoner, who was there in peril.—Mr. Ryland': I admit all you say, sir.—P.C. Devlin dee posed to apprehending the ,prisoner at his house at 1 a.m. on the llst Inst., and to his denying the charge,,aad saying that Gavin bad stopped him, threatening his life. —Mr. Mulholland addressed the court for the defence.. He said he had been surprised at the unauthorised F expression from one of the magistrates who had just left the court (Mr. Rylands had now quitted the Bench and Major Piekmere had taken the chair in his place). It was an almost unheard of thing in a court of justice that a magistrate should express an opinion as to the ultimate decision of the Bench before one half the case was heard. He was glad there were two gentlemen on the bench who had not expressed such an opinion. The learned counsel then proceeded to argue that there was no evidence of any kind which pointed to a cutting of the skin, and he cited the fact that Dutton put down the spade was a proof that: he did not desire such an encounter with Gavin as was de- scribed.—The prisoner then made an unsworn stateme.et. This was to the effect that Gavin claimed a balance if 10s. from him for draining in June last, which he would not pay because the work was not satisfactorily done, About 9-a.m. on the 20th of August, be was passing where Gavin was draining, and he came out of the drain in a threatening attitude saying, "Now for your money or your life, you black devil," and followed him threaten- ing him with the spade, and demanding the money. He (Dutton) put his hand in his pocket pretending to get the money, then grabbed the spade. In the struggle for it, it caught his shoulder, and he (Dutton) threw it down. Gavin rushed at him and seized him by the whiskers so close that he could not strike, but wrestled with him, and Gavin fell over the parapet. He did not drag the complainant. He came away, and when Gavin said he had broken his leg, told him it served him right. Mr. Haslem, farmer, gave Dutton an excellent character, and Ralph Cooper, farmer, deposed to Dutton coming to him and others for assistance for Gavin. Jahn Cooper, farmer, and Mrs. Prescott, farmer's wife, testified the former to the complainant saying in July what he would do for Dutton, and the latter to his saying he would have it in for him.—The Bench, after ten minutes private deliberation dismissed the case.

FAT.T,ING FROM A TRAIN. A BOY SERIOUSLY INJURED. A serious accident occurred between Thatto Heath and St. Helens on Tuesday night. It appears that a little boy named Harry Atkinson, seven years of age, of 29, Vincent-st., St. Helens, had been Buffering from a cataract, and had been brought from time to time to the Liverpool Eye Infirmary. On Tuesday morning he came with his father, who is al foreman in one of the St. Helens works, and his brother Norman Atkinson, aged fifteen to this city. Soon after five o'clock in the afternoon the father took his boys to Lime-st. Station and put them in the 520 slow train for St. Helens, expecting that they would reach that town safely without his going with them. They seem, from the statement 3f another passenger named Sephton, to have been playing on the way, and soon after leaving Thatto Heath Station the carriage door was observed to fly open, and the little fellow Harry fell out. The train was then running down the bank at the rate of about thirty or thirty-five miles an hour, and when it arrived at St. Helens Station a few minutes later information was gives to Foremen Porters,Wilding,and Merrill, who were just relieving one another, Merrill at once took his lamp and walked up the line, while at the sametime Wilding telephoned to Thatto Heath signal boa to stop the express train leaving Lime-st. at 550, which was then about due, it being feared that the little -fellow might be upon the line, and would be instantly killed. The spare engine which is kept at St.Helens Station was also ordered to proceed cautiously towards Thatto Heath, so that every assistance and care could be given to him. 'Merrill found the little fellow lying unconscious in the six-foot of the cutting near to Ravenehead Brick Works, rand he was immediately taken to St Helens on the bank 1-engine •

_ .d which had followed Merrill. He was then uncon- scious, and was carefully removed to the Providence Hospital, whit& is about 150 yards from his own home. At a later hour it was stated that he had slightly re- covered consciousness, and that it was not a hopeless frase. It appears that in the carriage in which the boys were travelling there are handles inside the door as wet' outside, and•evidently it was the one inside whichhad :been turned when the door flew open.
[EXTRACT PROM A PRIVATE LETTER.]

It was the latter part of August 1891. A friend and I had come down. from Ramsgate to Minster, to see the venerable church there, which is a thousand years old. I 'entered the churchyard and seated myself upon a nameless grave while he went in search of somebody to unlock the doors of the edifice and show its wonders In a few minutes he returned in company with an elderly lady, to whom he introduced me, saying she was the custodian and guide of the place. I gazed at her face for Berne moments without a word. If my own mother, dead and gone 15 years, had come back to speak to her only son, I should scarcely have been more astonished. For this woman was almost my mother's double ; the same size, the same face, and the same way of parting the hair and combing it in smooth bands from the fore- head. I told her so, and we were friends before either fairly knew the other's name. What a queer world it is. She then conducted us thrcugh the ancient lane, and spoke of the long vanished past, of the monks and nuns who once sang and prayed within its walls, of the quaint carvings on the hard oak seats in the chancel, of that precious relic, the Cranmer Bible, which reposes in a glass box against a pillar, and of many matters be- sides, drawn from the apparently exhaustless well of her detailed and accurate information.

Finally the talk veered round to the wholesomeness of the vicinity, the bracing nature of its sea breezes and so on. Then our guide, Mrs. Sarah Herd, said :—" I have I lived here in Minister 50 years, and seen many ups and downs. One of my sons is now in America, where he is I doing well. He wants me to leave England and make my home with him, but I doubt if I ever shall. lam somewhat like that old yew tree out in the yard, deeply rooted ta this soil, and might be the worse for pulling up. Then lam getting on in life, and ills grow apace with age. In the spring of 1878 I had a serious attac k. At first I scarcely knew what to make of it. There was no disease that I recognised in particular. I felt tired in body and weary in mind. There was much pain at my chest and back, and a kind of tightness at the sides, as though physical force were applied there to restrain me from moving. My appetitte, which was usually good, fell away ; and whatever I ate or drank gave me pain, and I lived almost entirely on bread and water. I was always ia pain and couldn't sleep so as to feel re- freshed by it. After a time I grew so weak as to be unable to go about my work. A bitter and sickening fluid arose into my mouth, and I prespired to such an extent that the sweat sometimes rolled off my face to the floor."

I (the writer) break in upon Mrs. Herd's story at this point merely to say that this tandency to sweat without the provocation of labour or of exercise is always a sign of a debilitated condition of the system. It means that the blood is impure and impoverished, the kidneys working badly, and that the body lacks nourishment and is living feebly on what was previously stored in it. In other words, the stomach has refused its duty and the other organs are in sympathy with it. Now we will let the lady proceed, begging pardon for the interruption.

She went on to say :—" For a time I tried to cure my- self with various domestic remedies which sometimes answer. But they failed, and I consulted a physician. With all respect to the doctors, they occasionally failed , too. This one did. You know there comes a time in all long illnesses when we get in some way used to pain and misery, and make no further efforts to get rid of it. In fact, we don't know how, and se don't try. For about three years I remained wretched and ailing, and dull unhappy years they were. My sufferings were beyond all I had ever known before, yet there seemed nothing to do but to bear them as patiently as I could. At this date, 1881, certain friends of mine spoke to me of the .great benefit they had received from the use of Mother Seigel's Syrup, for indigestion and dyspepsia. This threw light on nay mind, although I cannot say it made M 8 at once a believer in Seigel's Syrup. At length !however, in July 1831, I began to take it. In all I used six bott!es, and futind my health fully restored. Ten years have elapsed, and I have had no attack since. But if I do in futureJ shall know whereto put my hand on the remedy." Our visit being virtually over, we •called for a few moments at Mrs. herd's home, 2 High Street, Minster, Kent, and then wended our way back to Ramsgate.
C. M. R.
THE HALF HOLIDAY AT WARRINGTON
MEETING OF THE SHOP ASSISTANTS.

A meeting under the auspices of the Warrington Shop Assistants' Association was held in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening. Mr. W. Roberts presided, and there was a good attendance. The meeting had been convened for the putpose of bearing an address on organization by Mr. R. James, secretary of the Liverpool Grocers' Employ Ss Association. The CHAIRMAN said he felt that the committee who had conducted the half-holiday movement were deserv- ing of the thanks of every shop assistant in Warrington, and of a large number of tradespeople, who had undoubt- edly enjoyed the holiday. He ventured to say that I there was not a shopkeeper in Warrington who was one I penny the poorer for the inauguration of the movement. (Flear,hear.) He confessed that at the outset he was not in favour of it, but it was ne disgrace to admit an error. He had no hesitation in saying that the great majority of the tradespeople were in favour of this movement,and he gladly recognised the fact that the people of Warring- ton were in favour of it. He thought those who had given up the half-holiday had done so with very great regret. He did not think that half-a-dozen of those who kept open were opposed to the movement. .Many of them had told him that, although they ware keeping their shops open, they were doing no business. That,he thought, was a remarkable tribute to the sympathy and support they were receiving from the public. (Hear, hear.) He desired that they should close earlier every night in the week. A large number of persons in the works were now paid during the week,some on Wednes- day and others on Friday, and he failed to see why they should keep their shops open la:.er than nine o'clock on Saturday night. He could speak in the highest terms of the way in which the shop assistants spent their evening hours. (Hear, hear.) He urged them to be conciliatory to their opponents,to be united in their efforts, and their success was certain. (Applause.) Mr. Green, the hon. Secretary, read a report on the work done by the Association. He remarked that the work had been arduous, uphill and extremely trying to the patience, forbearance and equanimity of every member of the Committee, but throughout the whole of the preliminary and successive work they never lost heart. Mr. Green related how the half-holiday became established, and then referred to the opposition which arose, resulting in a number of the shops reopening on Thursday afternoon. The Committee desired to record its appreciation of the manliness, spiritedness and inde- pendence shown by the tradesmeh who had had the cause of the assistants so much at heart, and its sympa- thy and kind sonsideration were held out to those who had been compelled to open their shops to protect their individual trade. At present they had with them the whole of the boot trade with one exception, the tailoring and clothing trade, with two or three minor exceptions, the ironmongery trade, and several of the grocery trade. (Hear, hear.) The report was adopted, and during the evening, Mr. Rees James and Mr. Stewart gave addresses on organi- sation. On the motion of Mr. Kent, seconded by Mr. Hick- man, the following resolution was passed :—" That the best thanks of the Association be given to those trades- men who have so nobly identified themselves with the half-holiday movement, and earnestly requests that they will continue to support it, and also use their influence with those tradesmen who have withdrawn their sup- port from the movement. We also ask the public to support the association in their endeavours to establish and maintain the half-holiday." A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the meeting. At a meeting a the Committee afterwards it was decided to promote a Ball in aid of the association funds.

div.head: IRAILWAYIEXTENSIONS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: IRAILWAYIEXTENSIONS AT ST. HELENS.

The new double set of rails between Carr Mill, .thinction, St. Helens, and Ince Moss -Junction, Wigan, on the London and North-western Railway, 01/119 formerly opened for traffic on Saturday. The extension has been carried out to relieve the pressure of traffic between the points indicated, which has 'for some years considerably interfered with the satisfactory working of the system from Wigan to Liver- pool. The main line from Liverpool and St. Helens to Wigan and the north is joined at Carr Mill by die branch' mineral line from-Cutton Oak and Widnes, and the ex- cessive traffic is evidenced by the fact that between BO and 90 trains daily, pass over the branch lines. Hitherto there has only been one set of rails upon which to deal with the traffic, and it is known to all in the locality that goods trains have frequently been blocked for hours, while passenger trains have been worked very irregular- ly, especially at • holiday seasons. This unsatisfactory condition of affairs has now been remedied by the lay- ing down of an additional set of rails, and in future one set will be devoted exclusively to the passenger traffic and the other to the goods and mineral trains. The con- struction of the permanent way has been carried out by Mr. C. ißraddock, contractor, Wigan and Southport, while the rails have been placed in position by the tom- pany's own engineers. Fourteen bridges have had to I be widened, the most important of which was the doub- 'ling of the Carr Mill Viaduct, which carries the lines 60 I feet above the bed of a small streanx for a distance of nearly 400 feet. The iron lattice girders and flooring of the new portion of the viaduct have been supplied by 'Messrs. Rankin, of Seaconibe. At lime Moss, where the Manchester, Liverpool, and London main lines unite, several miles of new sidings have been constructed, with I the abject, apparently, of shunting acid making-up all I mineral trains, instead of blocking the main lines with that work as hitherto. The completii in of the work should give great satisfaction to all ti nvellers on the I Wigan, St. Helens, and Liverpool sectio. a. One certain result, according to railway officials, wil I be a nearer approach to punctuality than has been pos iible up to the I present time, and it is expected that a nevi ,er wad better service of passenger trains will shortly i'ae arranged. Colonel Rich, R.E., one of the Roard of Trade inspectors, I visited St. Helens on Thursday week, and m 'in-lately in- spected the new lines.

AN EX-EOLICE CONSTABLE SUMMONED. On Monday, before the Mayor, Dr. Twyford, .Aldermani. C. Gamble, Alderman'T. Cook, and Mr. J.: Forster, Tatrick flenebery, a well-known ex- police-constable in the borough force, was sum- moned for beim,: drank on the licensed premises of the Prince ,ot Wales Hotel, Ormskirk-street ; and, James Woolfall, licensee oi the hotel, was sum- monad for permitting Henebery to be drunk on the premises. Mr.. John 0. Swift defended. The case against Woolfall was first taken, and Henebery, went out of court with the other witnesses. .Sergeant William Strong stated that on Wednesday', night last he was standing at the top of Church-street,' when, from what Constable Tomlinson tclid him,,he went tothe Prince of Melee Hotel and there saw in the par 4 lour ten or twelsre,:persons. Heathery was thensaaated eta small table by himself. He was in a drunken con- ditioa, and had .a glass containing gin before him, Witness told the landlord, who was standing near, that' Henebery was too drunk to be served. The landlord midi." That drink belongs to me," and he was taking it up when Henebery made some alight resistance and said. "It is mine, and I have paid for it." Henebery vas in such a state of *drunkenness as would reasonably Arouse the attention of the publican. Sergeant Hunter, Who went in with Strong, said he heard the landlord say 'that both he and the barmanhad refused cto serve Henebery. Witness knew Henebery, and had. seen him both skunk and sober before. He was drunk that night. Asked what were the signs of drunkennese, witness replied that Henebery spoke in a stupid maudlin way; and had a red bloated face and red eyes. Police-constable Tomlinson said before he told his sergeant he-saw Ileneberyi.nd another man come to the door. The other man was going away when Heathery shouted,'" Come back fora minute or two." The other man said, '"'Jo;; I have had enough—l will go home." The man went away, and Henebery went back into the house. Police-sergeant Sisson, who was on duty in the police office that might, said Henebery came in at twenty-eight minutes past ten, and said the officers had been to him at the Prince of Wales and were going to report him. Henebery was then drunk. By Mr. Swift.: He didn't lock him up. The Chief Constable said he would not be locked up for simple drunkenness, unless he was incapable. Police-constable Johnson corroborated, and that closed the evidence for the prosecution. Mr. Swift said the whole of the evidence was grounded on suspicion and very 'grossly exaggerated. Mr. Alf red Collins said Henebory was sober. Richard Knott, the barman, Mr. Woolfall, the land- lord, and a number of other witnesses denied that Ilene- bery was drunk,—Dr. William Challoner said he saw Henebury at a quarter to eleven, whereas the police had seen him at ten past tea. He talked with him a quarter of an hour, and saw him walk away from the house. He could only come to one conclusion, and that was that he was perfectly sober. Ile had had experience in the London hospitals in discriminating drunkenness. His speech was not thick; he spoke rather fast, but that he was told was natural. If he had taken an emetic before coming he (the doctor) would have smelt it, but there was no sign of such a thing. The magistrates having decided to convict, the Chief Constable said there was nothing against the house, as a similar previous prosecution had been dismissed. The Mayor said Woolfall would be fined 40s. and costs, and after some discussion it was agreed that the licence be not.endersed. Henebery was called and fined 2s. fid. and coats, or seven days.—Mr. Swift said he had been instructed to appeal in this ease, and the magistrates' clerk was instructed to act on behalf of the bench.
