div.head: WARRINGTON SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.

A meeting in connection with the Warrington branch ef the Church of England Sunday School Teachers' Association was held on Tuesday night in the girls' schoolroom, Heath-side, the Vicar of St. Paul's (the Rev. H. V. Pigott) in the chair. There was a good attendance, which included the Revs. J. J. Longhorn, F. Millard, J. Forbes, A. Markham, F. C. Timins, T. W. Cook, T. M. R. Young-Hughes, and the Rev. Denton Thompson, of Liverpool, who attended as hon. clerical secretary of the Sunday School Institute to deliver an address on "The Sunday School as the handmaid of the Church." After prayers, the Chairman said that at their last meeting the propriety of joining the Diocesan Institute was discussed. The conclusion arrived at was that they had nothing to gain particularly by doing se, but something to lose perhaps. That night light would be thrown on the subject by the representative of the central authority. They would hear what he had to say, and be in a position afterwards to come to a decision upon the subject. The Rev. J. J. Langham remarked that one other parish had joined them since the last meeting, namely, the parish of New- ton-in-Makerfield, so that at the present time they included nine parishes. Every parish in Warrington belonged to them with the exception of St. Peter's, but they hoped that before long that parish would not be standing outside. (Hear. hear.) The Rev. D. Thompson then addressed the meeting, and, referring to the remark of the Chairman, said they had nothing to lose in Warrington by joining the Institute, but, perhaps, something to gain. A discussion followed and it was understood that the association would ultim- ately join the Diocesan lastitute. A vote of thanks to Mr. Thompson was carried. and Mr. Thompson briefly returned thanks for the compliment paid to him.

div.head: NEGLECT OF A DYING MAN.
div.p: NEGLECT OF A DYING MAN.

On Wednesday Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy-coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall on the body of Henry Wharton, 69 years of age, joiner, 60, Peter- street, St. Helens, who died under somewhat singu- lar circumstances on Monday morning. The evidence showed that the deceased had been sub- ject to fits of apoplexy. He lived with his married daughter and her husband, a Mr. and Mrs. Leonard. About nine o'clock on Saturday night the deceased fell at the foot of the stairs. As Mr. and Mrs. Leonard could not lift him up he was left lying on the floor when they retired to bed, but Mrs. Leonard wrapped him up Ma shawl. He remained on the floor all night, and next morning was attended to, but he died suddenly on Monday morning. Several jurors strongly con- demned the conduct of Leonard and his wife in leaving the deceased on the door of the house all night.—Mrs. Leonard said she came downstairs several times during the night to see her father, but she could not waken him. He appeared to be comfortable.—The Coroner: Do you know that you and your wife were lying drunk in bed when the inspector called to get some particulars of the death ? Leonard : I don't remember the inspec- tor coming.—Dr. F. Knowles stated that in his opinion death was due to apoplexy.—The jury returned a ver- dict of " death from natural causcs," but were of the opinion that Leonard and his wife should be censured.— The Coroner informed the jury that the Leonard's would be entitled to about £5O as insurance money by the old man's death.

div.head: GLASGOW ATROCITY.
div.p: THE GLASGOW ATROCITY.
AN ALLEGED CONFESSION.

The suspected murderer, M'Ewen, who still lies in the Glasgow Royal Infirmary, suffering from the self- inflicted wound on his throat, is making satisfactory progress, and as soon as his removal can be accom- plished, the police proceedings against him on a charge of killing the woman O'Connor in West Lodge, Pollok- shields, Glasgow, will be begun. It has transpired that when M'Ewen was stripped in the infirmary his clothes were found to have been almost soaked in blood. When arrested, M'Ewen, it is understood, had in his possession a piece of paper, on which were a few hastily-scribbled words. What the exact words were has not been allowed to transpire, but there is reason to believe that they were of a very incriminating nature. It is sup- posed that krEwen, having made up his mind to take his life, wrote what amounted to a practical confession of his guilt. His excuse for his fearful act is believed to be that he was "forced to do it." A belief in the pro- bable innocence of the sailor M'Neilly, who is also in custody in connection with the crime, seems to be gain- ing ground, even among the police. It is now alleged to have been proved almost beyond doubt that the woman and M'Ewen had tea together after M'Neilly's departure from West Lodge on the morning of the tragedy. When M'Neilly rose to go away, it is said that M'Ewen was in the act of making tea for him; but according to the story of the sailor, he had no time to take it, as he wished to get on board the ship as soon as possible. The cups were afterwards found to have been used by two persons.

THE BISHOP of CHESTER is evi- Bishop Jayne's Scheme. dently very much in earnest in advocating his important scheme of licensing reform. It is best described as the Gothenburg system as carried out in Norway and Sweden, with such alterations as may be deemed necessary for adapting it to the requirements of this country. That system involves a complete revolution in the control of the drink traffic ; and it is a revolution with which, so far as the principle is concerned, we, at any rate, are very much in favour. It is when it comes to the ques- tion of the conditions under which it is applied, that we find ourselves more or less in disagree- ment with what the BISHOP of CHESTER propo: to do.. He explained his scheme at considerable length, at a meeting at Shrewsbury, on Monday, of the Council of the Church of England Temper- mice Society; and it is understood that he is pre- paring a bill which wilt be laid before Parlia- ment at an early date. Briefly stated, the Gothenburg system means that all houses in the town or district used for the sale of intoxicating liquors shall he owned and directed by philanthropic companies, Which shall provide the money for the purchase of the houses, and for carrying on the trade, while receiving no profit from the undertaking beyond 5 per cent. interest upon the capital invested. Having no inducement to encourage the sale of drink, and • being on the contrary anxious to do all they can to lessen drunkenness, it will be parceived that licensed houses may in this way be converted into 1 houses of entertainment to which little or no :objection could be taken. The plan has succeeded in Norway and Sweden, and it is believed that it would succeed in this country. Mr. CHAmeeaLAIN expressed himself in its favour as far back as 1887, and in a recent letter to the Bishop of Chester says—" The system has done marvellously for Sweden, and it would do the same for this country, if it could have a chance." With regard to the question of surplus profits, it is understood that these should be applied to philanthropic undertakings which are not sup- ported by the rates. It is feared by some who have considered tile subject that if the profits went in reduction of rates the ratepayers would to this extent have an interest in encouraging the sale of intoxicating liquors. They would not, therefore, be as anxious as they would otherwise be to suppress drunkenness. Besides, there is. a class of persons who are so strongly opposed to having anything to do with the liquor traffic that they would altog,ether object to being partners in the business end receiving money in this particu- lar way. All sections require to be considered in introducing a reform of such magnitude, and Dr. JAYNE is obviously anxious to proceed on such lines as will best unite his general supporters. Still, if he does not mind ba will carry the pnciple of accommodation to a point which will involve the sacrifice of some other and not less. important Iprinciple.. In this way he may find himself left , stranded. For instance, he says he will not, as at present advised; touch the existing licensing authority. This means that magistrates are to be left to decide who shall and whc.shall not have , licenses, thus disregarding the pr4iciple of local option which has found such favour throughout the country. Indeed, we cannot but think that unless his Grace advances beyond this untenable position, he will find himself deserted by a large body of teraperince workers, who would otherwise he in a position to give him invaluable support. Further, he seems to be "sitting on the fence" in the matter of compensation. He speaks of what he calls " Equitable consideration for licensed victuallers" ; and from what can be gathered as to his views it would seem that he is disposed to give some sort of compensation to the holder of a license while denying it to the brewer who happens to be the owner of the house. We are quite certain that this country will not tole- rate any proposal for compensating brewers ; and we have our doubts as to whether it will commit itself even to a mild form of compensation to pub- licans. Dr. Jayne thinks differently; he is inclined to give as much as five years' notice, or to offer ompensatiou equal to two years' profits; for he

says :—" When a company was formed and a desire was expressed to make a start before the expiry of the five years' notice, was there any reason why the company should not offer a respectable publi- can two years' profits, calculated on the average of the preceding four or five years, if he would at once hand his house over to them and allow them to get to work?"

It is well to recognise that the scheme will never be adopted if it is to be heavily weighted with com- pensation. The law has decided that neither the Publican nor the brewer has any vested interest, ill a license; and that being the case, the ratepayers,. who are already heavy sufferers by the drink traffic, will not her disposed to amend the law, in order that large sums of money may be take° from the pablie treasury. Another -point which will require consideration, is whether the Gothen-- burg system ought to he worked by Town and County Councils, or by separate bodies of men, upon which Town and County Councils, would fully represented. Dr. Jayne favours the latter proposal as one best calculated to insure 3.13 efficient carrying out of the scheme, and in thus we are inclined to agree with him. The question is a vast one; and it bristles with difficulties. It is greatly to the credit of the Bishop of Chester that he looks these difficulties in the face; and, as he " menns business," it is extremely desirabl! that his,proposals should be well considered sal thoroughly ventilated.

Our Yankee cousins have been trying to borrow the " blarney stone " from Sir George Colthurst, the owner of Blarney Castle; but they have failed. They should have kissed the blarney stone before making their application. What next will they try to rake in ? Jupiter's latest-found moon ?

The money-thief, the jewel-thief, and the watch-thief are intelligible; but what of the man who has a weakness for stealing wheel-barrows ? At the Knutsford Quarter Sessions, on Monday, an old man named Thomas Benjamin West was convicted for the fourteenth time for wheel- barrow thefts. He was sent to gaol for a month for he was "only a labourer." There was no lawyer at hand to prove that he suffered from kleptomania.

There are in the lives of most men crises when it is deemed absolutely necessary to " take some- thing." Tom Hood was advised to take a certain medicine on an empty stomach F "Yes, but whose stomach P" the wit asked. This _answer is
akin to that made by the younger Sheridan when his father said the time had come for him to take • a wife. "Yes, but whose wife ?" asked the chip of the old block.

"Her Imperial Highness Princess Eugenie di Cristoforo Palaeologae-Nicephorae-Comnennae," is the " style and title" of a new vocalist, who is ex- pected to make her appearance in London during the winter. The "divine William" asks " What's ih a name ?" and the answer is—"a good deal when it well-nigh exhausts the alphabet."

The Corporation of Salford are responding to the appeal of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, for a proposal was considered, on Tuesday, by the Town Council to advance £1,000,000 by way of loan on reasonable terms, and on the understand- ing that Salford should be adequately represented on the directorate. So far as the Corporation of Manchester are concerned, they will require to have a majority on the Board as a condition of a further loan.

What of Warrington? There is no likelihood of a proposal being made to join in the new loan. The idea seems to be that the best relief it can afford will be in the direction of constructing Warrington docks out of Warrington money. Already the General Purposes Committee and the Chamber of Commerce have had the matter under Wnsideration ; but, as to what they suggest doing, "Mum's the word."

" Mum" is doubtless a good word in its place, but this is a 'natter which may seriously affect the pockets of the ratepayers, and it is natural for them to be desirous of knowing what is going on. It may he that such a scheme as is being mooted will be best alike for Warrington and for the Ship 'Canal Co.; and, if that he so, it will he none the worse for an exposition of its merits. This much is certain —Warringtoi. cannot aflord to blunder in the matter.

A Runcorn boy has lost his life at Antrobus through another lad being allowed to meddle with firearms. From all we can hear, there is a growing tendency for youths to carry either a pistol or a r,volver. The other day one Warring- ton schoolboy was amusing himself by pointing a loaded revolver at a comrade. It was an accident that there was not an accident. With the ap- proach of the sth of November, " Paterfam " and the police should keep a sharp look-out.

If King James had known anything of the acci- dents resulting from smoking in coal-mines, he would have been able to give additional force to his " counter-blast " against tobacco. Three colliers were each fined 40s. and costs at Ponty- pool, on Saturday, for being found in a fiery mine with pipes and matches upon them. The magistrates intimated that in future the punish- ment would be imprisonment. And quite right too. It is bad enough for miners to risk their own lives in this way : but it is criminal in the highest degree to endanger the lives of perhaps hundre..ls of other men.

Another life lost thro ugh the brutal practice of kicking during a fight. Two Warrington lads quarrel and have " a set to " ; one 'kicks the other in the stomach, and death ensues. It seems im- possible to break Lancashire lads off the murder- ous custom of striking with the feet as well as the fists; and yet the task should be attempted. Couldn't something be done at school to promote a feeling that kicking is an act of cowardice? There is a strong sense of fairness amongst boys, and if kicking was once recognised as unfair it tnight be stamped out.

Trade is bad, and the Fair Traders, who never forget and never learn anything, are beginning to raise their voices and assert that the cause is Free Trade. Very good, but how about France, which has been having an "extra special" in the shape Of Protection? Hera is the answer as given by a Paris correspondent :—"The best indication of the loss inflicted on the trade of the country by the application of the new tarifts appears in the re- turns just published as to the foreign trade of Prance. The September imports declined over 130,000,000 f., while the export trade decreased nearly 14,000,000 f. as compared with September, 1891. This looks like the road to ruin. Shall Ire follow it ?

The "screw kick" in football is fascinating, but his not without its dangers. A youth of 16 missed his "screw kick" on Saturday, gave him- self a violent twist, and so seriously injured him- self, that he died within an hour afterwards. Internal rupture is suggested as the cause of death. If he had struck the ball, he would, most likely, have been little or no worse. Who has not experienced the shock and wrench which have resulted from more or less similar failures in the transmission of energy? Even in the mild exer- cise of going upstairs, it is not a little disturbing to make an extra step when there isn't a stair. Moral to footballers : Be sure of your kick— Whether fancy or plain.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BRAKEMAN.

About eleven on Tuesday morning, a young Oiarried man named William. Gee, of St. Thomas's- a.treet, Sc. Helens, was engaged shunting waggons In Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks, when he slipped off. the buffers and falling with his legs across the rails two waggons went over them. Toe engine- driver had been shouted to, but could not prevent the accident. The injured man was placed on fl Stret c h er, after first aid had been rendered, and taken to the surgery of Drs. H. and F. Knowles, Where it. was found that both legs were nearly severed from the body. One leg was set, but the f3t,ther required amputation, an operation for which us patient was found to be too exhausted. The unfortunate man died on Tuesday night.—At the Town Hall, on Wednesday, Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy C°lloty coroner, held an inquest on the body. It was stated that deceased acted as signalman as well as shunter. He would ride on the buffers, and on ileanng the points would drop off and run to .t"hloge them. He was attempring to get on the .9:llEers on Tuesday, when he slipped, and two • aggons went over. his legs.—The jury returned a ve_rdict of" Accidental death." ul4°T WATER FITTER.—GARLAND, ironmonger, Warrington ; raaoll—Barlestown.—Adv.

BARRACKS, _RUNCORN.

Special meetings were held at the Salvation Army citadel, on Sunday, in connection with the farewell of Captain and Mrs. Helms, who have been labouring in the town for four and a half months with considerable success. The meeting in the morning was conducted by Captain and Mrs. Helms, and m the afternoon Major and Mrs. Wright gave stirring addresses to a good con- gregation. The evening meeting was well attended, a large crowd being present to bear the farewell addresses of those who were about to leave. On Thursday, at Widnes Police Court, a middle aged widow, named Ann Govern, of Windle, near St. Helens, was charged with wilfully neglecting to maintain her four children who had become chargeable to the com- mon fund of the Prescot Union. Mr. A. F. Mann prose- cuted. It appeared that the woman was in receipt of parish relief, and on the 27th September, 1891, she de- camped from Windle, leaving her children in the closet of a house in Barrow-st. Nothing further was heard of her until Wednesday, when she was apprehended iu Widnes by P.C. Worsfold. The maintenance of th children had cost the ratepayers £4O us. sd.—The pri- soner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. _ GOSPEL MISSION AMBRIDGE-ST. RUNCORN. _ . .

. ... Last Sunday the harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Mission Hall. The Hall was tastefully adorned with the marvellous gifts of God, in the shape of bread, meat, fruit, flowers, plants, vegetables, &c. Three sermons were preached by Rev. J. Pulford Williams and Mr. J. Thompson, of Liverpool, and their powerfullysearching and appealing remarks will be long remembered by those who had the pleasure of listening to their excellent and appropriate discourses. On Mon- day evening a'. entertainment was given, presided over by Mr. D. Bisbrown, assisted by Rev J. Martin, Messrs. Marshall, Suttoe, and Tickle, who gave excellent addresses, each reier, log specially to the object of the meeting, and the woe.: of the Mission. Several special songs and duets were iendered by Mr. and Mrs. Burn, Mrs. Richardson, Mr. and Miss Tickle, assisted by the choir. The singing throughout the services was well rendered by the choir, and efficient aid was cheerfully given by Mr. and Miss Beckett, and other friends. The harmonium, kindly lent by Mr. Clough, was presided over by Mr. Musgrove, which greatly added to the efficiency and success of the festival. The unanimous and hearty thanks of the meeting were given to the Chairman, speakers, singers, and generous givers of all the produce, also to all who assisted in the decorations, &c. The congregations were moderate, and the result of the festival, financially, was very satisfactory.

EXCITING INCIDENT AT RUNCORN STATION.

Considerable consternation was caused at Runcorn railway station, last evening, when the 4-55 train, from Crewe to Liverpool, rushed through the station without stopping. A number of Runcorn passengers put their heads through the carriage windows and gesticulated, but without avail and it was understood that the driver had lost control over his engine. A stoppage was made at Ditton, however, and the Runcorn passengers trans- ferred to the dodger, which was just about to start. It was a fortunate circumstance that the line was clear.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION AT WIDNES. As the date of the first municipal election for the borough of Widnes draws nearer, the list of candi- dates increases in length, and up to the present time the burgesses have 32 names from which to select eighteen gentlemen to represent them. There are sixteen Independents, seven Nationalists, six Liberals, and , three Conservatives; and a fore- cast of the probaide result of this peculiar contest would puzzle the powers of a thought-reader. Tile complete list is as follows : Farnworth Ward.—(3)„ Mr. C. E. Barlow (C), Mr. P. Longton (C), Mr. T. Shuttleworth (C), Mr. F. Heyes (Ind.). "Halton Ward.—(3), Major Waring (L), Mr. J. Fitz- patrick (N), Mr. ft O'Donnell (N), Mr. T. A. Bullougb (Ind.), Mr. D. Wright (Ind.), Mr. W. Christie (led.). Simm's Cross Ward.—(3), Mr. J. Midwood (L), Mr. S. Sadler (L), Mr. S. Owens (L), Mr. G. I. Neil (Ind.), Mr. R. Hirst (bad.), Mr. J. Hulme (Ind.), and Mr. J. Beach (In .1 .). Victoria Ward.—(3l, Mr. S. Quinn (N), Mr. T. Tilley (N), Mr. H. Singleton (N), Mr. F. Neil (Ind.). Waterloo Ward.—(3), Mr. H. 11. Shores (L), Mr. T. Carney (Ni, Mr. J. Williamson (N), Mr. J. C. Crawford (Ind.), Mr. C. Hemingway (Ind.), Mr. D. J. Brookes (Ind.). West Bank Ward.—(3), Mr. W. Hodgkinson (L). Mr. W. W. Gossage (Ind.), Mr. H. S. Timmis (Ind.), Mr. B. Brown (Ind.), Mr. T. Smith (Ind.). A number of the addresses of these gentlemen may be perused in our advertisement columns. Mr. W. W. GossaFze whose name has been mentioned In connection with West Bank Ward does not intend to stand. Another candidate for Farnworth Ward has appeared in the person of Mr. J. Horabin (I), and the rumour that Mr. P. Longton intended to retira is with- out foundation. Mr. F. H. Gossage, the provisional mayor, has fixed Monday next for the nomination of candidates, and withdrawals will be received up to two o'clock on the following day. From that hour up to four o'clock Mr. Gossage will sit at the Town Hall to receive and decide objections, which may be taken to the nomination of any of the candidates.

The thanksgiving services were continued at the above church on Sunday, commencing with an early celebration of the Holy communion. The pulpit was occupied both morning and evening by the Rev. W. W. Whitelegge, M.A., wto was formerly vicar of Widnes for upwards of 20 years. In the aftesnoon a children's service was held, and an appropriate address given by the Rev. G. H. Garrett, 8.8., (vicar). Special hymns, kc., were sung by the choir, Mr. J. C. Crawford presid- ing at the organ. The church was crowded at each ser- vice. A special service was held on Monday evening, when the Rev. Mr. Whitelegge preached another telling sermon. The collections amounted to upwards of £l7, and will be devoted to the church roof repair fund. When in want o 'a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S. 51, High-st.—Advt.

Total WIDNES COUNTY COURT.

At this Court, yesterday, before his Honour Judge Shand, George Cook, travelling showman, brought an action against his son James Cook, also a travelling showman for £2O for damages for assault, loss of time, 1 and injury to his show, on the 4th August last at the Ball of Ditton, Widnes.—Mr. T. J. Peters appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendant. Father and son had a dispute with respect to the posi- tion of their shows, which terminated in the defendant assaulting his father and damaging his show,—His Honour gave a verdict for £3 and costs.—Michael Small, 33 Albert-road, sued Thomas Cross of Warrington for £9 balance of value of a horse purchased from him by the defendant.—Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. A. Browne defended. The defence was that plaintiff had given a warranty that the animal was sound, but three weeks afterwards it was condemned by the assistant borough surveyor of Warrington. It trans- pired that the horse had an attack of influenza. The Judge held that a warranty could not cover this and gave a verdict for the full amount claimed, with costs.

BRAVERY REWARDED AT RUNCORN. On Sunday, the 21st August last, three boys named Allred Cox, John Wilson, and Charles Jones, went to bathe is that part of the Old Quay Canal which is now blocked up, and forms a lake. The three boys undressed, and went into the water, and splashed about there some twenty minutes. Cox then got beyond his depth and went down ; he did not rise,and,it is thought, his feet stuck in the mud. Wilson,who can swim a very little, tried to get him out, Cox caught hold of WileOn, and pulled him under the water. Wilson struggled and got clear of him, and came out of the water, and fell upon the bank exhausted. Jones then tried to save Cox, He waded beyond his depth, and caught hold of Cox's arm, and gave him a pull, but could not Move him,and then himself began to drown, for he could not swim. A boy, Robert Rowland Harrison, seeing this, slipped off his trousers, and with his shirt and socks on, leaped into the water to Jones' assistance. Whilst in the water he divested himself of his shirt, and with great presence of mind held one portion of it, ex- tending the other within reach of Jones, who caught hold of it, and was drawn by Harrison to the bank, and saved. Harrison can swim a little; he is 13 years of age, and of dimunitive stature. Mr. Robert Dobson, of Warrington, deputy-corcner for the Honour and Fee of Halton, held an inquest on the body of the unfortunate boy, Cox, and complimented Harrison, Wilson, and Jones, on their excee'lingly plucky conduct. Mr. Dob- son has now received an intimation from the Royal Flumane Society, stating that their honorary bronze medal and certificate have been awarded to Robert Rowland Harrison, and testimonials on parchment to Jones and Wilson, for their humane exertions.
MASS OF T. CECILIA.-BY TIIE REV. J. E. TURNER, 0.5.8.

This is a fine musical composition for four mixed voices, with accompaniment, composed by the Rev. J. E. Turner, St. Mary's Buttermarket-st., Warring- ton. It is not at all pretentious, and yet it is marked by freshness and originality. Like all solid music, it grows upon the listener, and it is there- fore exceedingly likely that this composition will become popular with Catholic choirs throughout the country. Some of the solos are very tuneful, and the climax in the" Gloria "is most impressive. It should be added that the accompaniment is in every respect satisfactory, and that the mass itself has been sung with effect both at St. Mary's and St. Alban's in Warrington. It may be stated that Father Turner has been several times before the public as a successful composer.

NARROW ESCAPE AT HAYDOCK.

On Monday night, a young fellow named William McCoy, living at Newton, and employed as a fitter by Messrs. Evans and Co., at Haydock, had a very narrow escape from being killed. He was doing some repairs to one of the engines, being at the time underneath it. Ile told his assistant to block the wheels, but he must have neglected to properly throw on the brakes, and while McCoy was pro- ceeding with his work, he noticed the eccentrics begin to move. With great presence of mind he threw himself down out of the way, just in time for the eccentric to crash within an inch or two of his head. The engine being in motion continued on until it reached the shed doors through which it crashed, smashing them in splinters, and injur- ing the man who was assisting McCoy. Had not McCoy observed the motion in time, and quickly got out of the way, he would assuredly have been , killed.

div.head: -ep- WID NES WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: -ep- WID NES WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

A social gathering in connection with this Associ- ation was held in the Drill Hall, on Thursday even- ing. The proceedings commenced with a tea party, at which about 400 were present, and after- wards there was a public meeting and entertain- ment. There was a large attendance. In the absence of Mrs. Stewart Brown, the president, Mrs. Robinson, presided. In a letter of apology, Mrs. Stewart Brown referred to the general election, and said she trusted that though defeated and grievously dis- appointed, their members would not feel discouraged, but rather stimulated to further effort to advance the cause of Liberalism in the constituency. The large reduction of the majority against their candidate, this time, encouraged the hope that if they were so fortun- ate as to secure the same candidate again, when the next election came, they would be able completely to Isweep away the Tory majority. After a few words from the Chairman, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, C.C., delivered a speech, and afterwards proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Robinson for occupying the chair. This was seconded by Mr. Hartland and carried. A pro- gramme of music was admirably gone through.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

To-day the ratepayers of Widnes are again asked to choose the members of the School Board. There are twelve candidates for eleven seats, of whom five are Roman Catholic, four Churchmen, and three Progressive, or undenominational. The last Board included only two Progressives, and they are seek- ing at the present juncture to obtain another seat. It cannot be said that the .ProgrAssives are making an extortionate demand; in fact they are rather too modest in their claims; anti, in the opinion of many thinking men, they ought on principle to possesa the balance of power.

That the Board Schools should be managed by gentlemen who are avowedly opposed to the system of education given there, and whose chief aim is to protect and conserve the interests of schools under their personal control, is an anomaly which it is hard to understand. The only conclusion that can be arrived at is that the ratepayers do not understand the question at issue, or are frightened from dealing with it in a spirit of independence because of the religious bogie which is held before them. urely those who have no denominational interests to serve would make better governors of our Board Schools, and be pre- pared to administer them on a wider and more extended basis than those who are wishful. if they could, to keep them at one unprogressive level.

TI a ratepayers ought to have just as much right to n-anage the denominational schools as the denom- inational school managPrs have to manage the Board Schools, but at present the law does not give them that right. The recently published financial statement of the Runcorn Denominational School shows that for one pound of private money sub- scribed to these schools ten, and often a larger proportion, is derived from the public taxes; and when there is an opportunity to obtain the figures a like state of affairs will be found to exist in Widnes. There is a petition of independent candidates for the Town Council, and they are applauded for breaking away from the trammels of political caucuses, but if ever there was need of independent or progressive members, it is on the School Board, and without having any personal objection to the other candidates, it is to be hoped that the progressives will capture the one extra seat they seek. It is highly gratifying to find the proposal to construct a vehicular Bridge across the Mersey, .te connect the districts of Widnes and Runcorn, taking a practical shape. Each town is prepared to provide thirty thousand pounds of the estimated cost, and it is hoped and expected that the respective County Councils will provide the balance. The cost according to estimate will be £200,000. Of this amount .£140,000 is put down for the erection of the Bridge; ..C50,000 for parliamentary expenses, and .ClO,OOO for com- pensation to property owners. As the Bridge will be not only of local benefit, but of great import- ance to the trade and intercourse of the two counties, it is expected that the County Councils will help forward the profit financially and other- wise. It is generally admitted that the investment would be one of the best ever entered into by any town or county. . _

The figures given by Mr. Wiswall at the meet- ing of the Free Library Committee with reference to the proposed Runcorn Technical Institute, ought to have the effect of reassuring those who had doubts as to the feasibility of the Board of Com- missioners building an institute at the cost of £3,500, with only a penny rate to administer. The County Council have made a grant of .£5OO, the grant for the Science and Art Department will certainly reach ..£l,OOO ; then there are promises from Mr. Brunner and Mr. Speaknaan • and at the- worst there will not remain more than .£l,OOO to provide out of the rates, and as this would be spread over 30 years, the annual charge would be very light. And this would he one of the very best investments Runcoin Commissioners ever made. It is too much the custom to reckon suc- cess or failure on merely a financial basis, as Mr. Pritchard did a few days ago. The success of an educational institute can only be weighed up by the advantages conferred, and the benefit received by the students in increased knowledge ; and the Technical Institute will be an incalculable boon to the rising generation. The. Committee vro have the matter in. hand ought to go forward with energy and perseverance, and let us have the Insti- tute at the earliest opportunity, notwithstanding the opposition of its misnamed.' friends."

div.head: SHOCKING GUN ACCIDENT AT ANTROBITS.
div.p: SHOCKING GUN ACCIDENT AT ANTROBITS.
.DEATH OF A RUNCORN YOUTH.

On Saturday, about-n(To-n,FeCil. Jo-h-n-s;n7aged 14 years, of 105, Shaw-street, Runcorn, met with his death under melancholy circumstances. From the information obtained regarding the accident it would appear that deceased, as well as Wm. Wright and Geo. Lightfoot, both of Antrobus, were on Mr. Lightfoot's farm. Wright was carrying a double-barrelled gun when, it is stated, Johnson took hold of it, and the hammer caught Wright's jacket sleeve. The firearm went off, and the contents of both barrels entered the stomach of Johnson, whose death took place immediately. The discharge of the weapon was purely accidental. The receipt of the news of the sad occurrence caused a sensation in -Run- corn, where the deceased was well-known.
_ The inquest on the body was held on Monday evening, and a verdict of accidental death was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
THE COST OF FREE EDUCATION.

A special meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr. James Pritchard. Present-the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. ?ticDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, Mr. T. Handley, Mr. G. Moss (clerk). The chief business was the consideration of the statement of receipts and expenditure for the year ended the 29th September, 1892. The receipts included the following items :-Balance on September 29th, 1891, £373 ss. 9d ; annual grant from Education Department, £BO7 , 16s. 10d. ; grants from the Science and Art Department, £2B 10s. ; fee grant from the Education Department Act, 1891, £260 16s. Bd.; contributions from local auth- orities (undeL the Technical Instruction Act, 1889) £420; other receipt l, £54 ls. 9d. ; school fees, £2l is. ; sales to children of books and other articles, £2B Os. 7d. ; from the rating authorities, being equivalent to a rate of 4d. in the pound on £58,413, the rateable value of the dis- trict according to the valuation lists in force,£9so ; legal costs refunded 7s. ; for use of school rooms. £l6 Ifis ; loans received during the year, £180; total £2,93895. 7d. The expenditure was as follows :-Salarie.s of officers of the Board, £296 us. Bd. ; legal expenses, £7 10s. 10d. ; other expenses of administration, £9l 11s. Bd. • salaries and remuneration cf teachers, £937 6s. jOd, ;books and apparatus, £B6 17s. 2d. ; fuel, light, and cleaning, and replacement of furniture, and repairs to buildings and furniture, £134 16s. 2d ; rents, rates, taxes, and insur- ance, £8 2s. 10d. ; other expenses of maintenance, £3 3s. ; contributions to industrial schools' £2O 18s. 2d. ; spent under Technical Instruction Act, £403 16s. 11d. ; furnishing of school buildings. £6 18s. 10d. ; paid in respect of loans, £159 15s. 10d. ' • and interest, £l6B 7s. 7d. : making and sewering of Victoria-read £lBO ; total, £2,507 17s. Bd.; leaving a balance in hand of £430 12s. 14. The outstanding liabilities of the Board were £4,477 Os. Id. In moving the adoption of the statement, the Chairman remarced that the amount received from the rates was the same as in the previous year, so that notwithstanding Free Education they had not had to ask for more money from the ratepayers. Having had one complete year of Free Education it might be of interest to know the actual loss upon the work of the schools. Upon their schools in Greenway-rd. and Mill-brow the total loss was £146. Out of that amount £4O might be attributed directly to Free Education.- Free Education had cost the Board £40.-Mr. Taylor : But we have not had more from the rates this year than last year.-(The Chairman No:) The balance sheet showed the deficiency in actual working to be £146, so that their schools were that far trom self-supporting. Greenway-road ach Nal was certified to accommodate 481 scholars, taking 10 square feet for each child. In the older denominational schools the space required was only eight square feet, which meant one-fifth more accommodation and if they were permitted to take in scholars to the same extent in Greenway-road Board School, they could accommodate 600, and with this large number the fee grant and also the examination grant would have gone a long way towards liquidating the amount of the deficiency. Very often the expend- iture of Denominational schools and Board Schools per scholar was compared, but it was very seldom that the one-fifth advantage of the older schools was taken into account. Notwithstanding that Board Schools were a little more expensive in working in consequence of be- ing compelled to find more space the ratepayers' children had the advantage of it in having more breathing room and, therefore, conducted their lessons under more healthy conditions.-Therefore, taking everything into consideration they might claim for the Board good management and economy in the conduct of the schools. -Dr. McDougall seconded the motion, which was car-. Tied unanimously.
It was resolved to issue a precept upon the overseers for £3OO for the ensuing half year. The Board then went into committee to consider the question of providing more school accommodation.

div.head: SPEECH BY THE REV. J. HIRST HOLLOWELL.
div.p: SPEECH BY THE REV. J. HIRST HOLLOWELL.

A meeting in support of the Progressive candidates was held on Thursday night in the Baths Assembly ROOM. There was only a moderate attendance. Mr. G. Davies presided.—Mr. F. J. Poole explained that the Rev. G. H. Hughes was absent through illness, but he had sent an assurance that he had great interest in the work and would do all he could to secure the trium- phant return of their candidates. (Applause.) Mr. R. Shaw moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting of electors of Widnes is in favour of the Board School system of educat:on and thinks that the time has arrived that there should be fuller represent& tion of unsectarian educationalists on Widties School Board." Mr. Shaw said if any argument was wanted to support that motion they had it in the fact that half the school-going children of Widnes were in the Board Schools. Dean Finegan charged the Nonconformists with having forced the School Board system on the country; he (Mr. Shaw) would hardly like to take credit for it, but if they did, it was the best dav's work for England the Nonconformists ever did. (Applause.) The School Board system was forced upon England because it was found that foreign nations were better educated than our own, and that their workmen wire beating lours in the markets A the world, and because there I was not accommodation for the children of the masses. He contended that those who did not believe in sectar- ian teaching in day schools had a right to more repre- sentation on the Board, in order to see that the children got the best education possible, and he urged those present to do their duty and attend at the poll to-day. (Applause.) Mr. B. Brown seconded the motion, and said he must take exception to a remark made by his worthy col- league, Dean Finegan, that they were forcing the elec- tion. They were not forcing the election. Those people were forcing the election who had an unreasonable num- ber of representatives upon am Board. (Hear, hear.) If all thoelectors voted as squarely as the Roman Catholics did the latter would not get anything like the represent - atives they had on the Board. He quite agreed with Dean Finegan when he said that they went to the Board to stop the Nonconformists putting their hands into the ratepayers' packets. From what he knew of history the clergy always had objected to any- one putting their hands into the ratepayers' pockets if what was to be done was for the benefit of the people; but when it had beeri, for their own benefit he had not , heard such strong objections from them. With regard 'to the 22 millions spent on Board schools, he said England had never spent 22 millions to better advantage —(loud applause)—and he was quite prepared to say that she would never get better interest for her money than she got on that. (Hoar. hear.) Referring to the School Board rate in Widnes, he said they must take into account that they had to pay £2OOO a year in interest and repayment of capital for the building of the schools which when paid for would be their own. But Dean Finegan said nothing aboilt the money given by Gov- ernment towards the erection of denominational schools, prior to 1870—grants which were not made now— schools over which the ratepayers had now no control whatever—(applause.) The Rev. J. Hirst Hollowell. of Rochdale, supported •the resolution and said his attention had been c.ailed to a sort of manifesto speech by the Rev. Dean Finegan. It was a fighting speech and he was sorry there were so many mistakes in it. (Applause). In the first place he said that the assisted Education Act of 1891 was looked unon by Nonconformists with delight, which was abso- lutely untrue, for they looked upon it with suspicion and dislike, and results had justified them. The Dean also said that the Widnes taxpayers were overtaxed al- ready. Well the School Board rate was 6.7 d. in the £, which was lower than the average School Board rate for the whole of the country, including the very small- est and poorest villages, the average being 7d. in ths £. (Applause.) Dean Finegan had worked against free education in Widnes, but he (the speaker) hoped they would get it in spite of him. The addition to the rates if the schools were made free would not be 2d. in the £, which would mean is. 4d. a year to a working-man occupying 'a house assessed at £B, so that it would be a saving to working-men of several shillings. Then the Dean had said that they ought to make it easy for the children not only to get to school but to remain there. Quite so, and he only knew one policy that would do it. If they wanted to get the children to school and keep them there they must have free education, and make the schools as good as they could, get as good teachers as they could, and pay as good salaries as they could—(applause)—because they could not get good teachers by paying bad salaries. There were thousands of head mistresses in the Church of England schools who did not get more than £4O a year. They must also teach science in an interesting manner, they must have popular control—(hear, hear) and they must respect the conscience of both teachers and scholars. ,'Applause.) The nine denominationalists had five schools of their awn to manage, and besides that they did not believe in Board Schools, and there never would have been any Board Schools in Widnes if they could have helped it. The best man to look after a School Board was the man , who believed in it, and he urged them to elect men of that class. (Applause.) Mr. D. Lewis, also supported the motion II in a speech, and it was afterwards carried unani- mously. _ .
A vote of thanks to the Chairman, concluded the meeting.

div.head: ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC DAY SCHOOLS,
div.p: ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC DAY SCHOOLS,
RUNCORN.
VISIT OF ARCHBISHOP SCARISBRICK.

The annual services in aid of these schools wEre held at St. Edward's church, Irwell lane,on Sunday, and were attended with much success. The event was invested with greater interest by the visit of his Grace Archbishop Scarishrick, recently ot South Africa. His Grace arrived in town on Saturday night, and at once was taken to the residence of the pastor, Dr. Gastaldi, and the. brass band of the League of the Cross signalised the occasion by playing several selections of music on the lawn. There was a large attendance at the morning ser- vice, when solemn Mass was said, and his Grace afterwards delivered an eloquent discourse. There was again a large attendance in the evening when the Rev. J. Chapman, 8.A.., of Widnes was the preacher. In the course of his sermon the Archbishop dealt with the question of education. He said the education of the poor was a question which had for a long time, and still. agitated the public mind. The destinies of the people were necessarily bound up with and made dependent upon the education of its youth. To the absence of good Christian education might be traced almost all the evils of life, and these were many. The work of the day was to educate. But there was education and education. There was first of all secular education, which banished religion from the schoolroom, and excluded the name of God during school hours, not perhaps with irrever- ence prepense, but with an avowed intention of prac- tically ignoring the divine law as the motive power in the wheel of life. He need not tell them that the Catholic Church never could and never would accept any such system of education. She knew too well that intellectual culture without religion would only propagate a race of self-constituted men and women ; would only encourage a spirit of rebellion and a love of independence, and certainly the world of the 19th century had no need of such impulses as those. Education was essentially a moral question. It was intended not only to make ef the rising genera- tion men of loyalty to the State, but it must be looked up to in its connections and bearings on their future existence. Their schools must not be dechristianized, and should not be. It would be better to be banished altogether 'from the country, which outraged public conscience than to allow their children to be surrendered into the hands of the State.

After benediction in the evening, the members of the League of the Cross assembled in their club room for the purpose of presenting an address to Archbishop Scarisbrick. The room was crowded. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi presided, and he was supported by the Rev. J. Chapman and the officers of the League. In opening the proceedings, the Rev. Doctor said it was with the greatest pleasure that he, as their pastor, was in a position to be present that evening with his Grace Archbishop Scarisbrick, who had been in South Atrica, ministering to the people the same religion and same feelings they as Catholics held so dear. His ear- nest wcrk had been of immense benefit to those people, and it was to those present not merely a gratification, but a pride to them that they had his Grace amongst them, and to hear a few words, whioh no doubt every one of them would in future days remember the special favour his Grace had bestowed upon him. The Secretary, Mr. Quinn, then read the following address :

We, the members of St. Edward's Branch of the League of the Cross, most cordially welcome your Lord- ship on this the first occasion of your visit to the town lof Runcorn. All hail our glorious Archbishop. Some four years have now already flown away since the establishment ot our Total Abstinence Society in this parish. Aided by the hearty and generous co-operation of our beloved and respected pastor, Dr. Gastaldi, we , have worked earnestly and zealously, and we trust not in vain, in the laudable effort to implant in the hearts lof many of our Poor toriorn Catieine nrethren the principles of teMperauee, wnereby• they might become once again good honest citizens, and worthy ornaments of the glorious and imperishable religion to which they profess to belong. My Lord,it is therefore with feelings , of great love and respect that we humbly approach your Lordship upon this important subject of temperance, and we would deem it an everlasting favour if you would kindly condescend to bestow your blessing upon our Society. A blessing coming from such a leading light of the Catholic Church would undoubtedly have a beneficial and satisfactory effect, not alone upon the Society, but with the great Creator above, who shapes the future destiny of us all. In conclusion we heartily wish that God will in His infinite mercy, spare your Grace many more years of happy life and sacred office, and at the end and closing of a long and useful career, your Grace shall reap the just reward of your labours and services in the Catholic Church, a work which alone is reserved for the righteous in Heaven. Signed on behalf of St. Edward's Branch of the League of the Cross.

IRichard Clynch, president, James McMoran, vice- president, John P. Quinn, secretary, Thomas Byrne, C. W. Runcorn, Sunday, October 16th 1892. 'Hie Archbishop in replying said lie was not conferring a favour upon them by coming amongst them :it was they who had favoured him by giving so many proofs of hearty zeal in the holy cause of religion in that town. The address made a slight mistake in stating that was his first visit. It was not quite his first visit, but the last time he was here was in 1838, that was 54 years ago. He was a boy then, and he did not remember what was the religious state of the town, but he was sure that since that day religion had made great strides, and everybody was very much better than they were then. It had been a great joy for him to see how reli- gion had taken root in this once bigoted town. There was great prejudice against the holy faith once, and per- haps there were a great many still who held prejudices, but he was sure that advanced pregress was being made. Their healthy state and influence was owing primarily and principally to the great zeal of their pastor ; they had been greatly blessed in having such a pastor. It was a great blessing to a congregation to have a priest according to God's heart, full of zfial in his work, and such a priest ought to be backed up, as no doubt he was backed up, by a generous and sympathetic congregation. He considered one of the great works they had to promote in that society was not merely the cause of temperance—they would all be temperate men as Christians—because it was impossible to call themselves Catholics, or even Christians, if they did not observe the laws of God, and one of the greatest was to restrain their appetites. So that he need not encourage them to persevere in good resolutions, and to walk soberly and wisely throughout life; otherwise he was sure they would not be welcome members of the League of the Cross in Runcorn. (Applause.) Another duty was to help their Pastor ;in every good work he took in hand they must be his backbone and support when he had any great function on hand, any great work to promote as had had that day, to stand by him loyally, and try to let the inhabitants of Runcorn see that the Catholic body were as united and as strong-willed a body as any other dissenting body in the town. (Applause.) He congratulated them upon the success of that day : the result of the offertories was an improvement on the past. In conclusion his Grace blessed the league, the members and their families, and at their request they renewed their pledge for twelve months. Mr. Clynch, the president, then delivered a brief. address in which he depicted the evils arising from the drink tralic, there were hundreds of houses in Runcorn which were homes of poverty and misery, through intem- perance, and he urged those present who had not joined the League, to do so at once. A. number of new members were enrolled.

The Frodsham Parochial Committee reported that at the time of their meeting on the 14th inst., there were two bands practising in the Town Hall, which made it almost impossible to conduct the business of the Com- mittee and this having frequently occurred on previous occasions, it was resolved that the clerk write to the secretary of the Town Hall Company and point out that unless this can be remedied the Committee will have to look out for another room in which to hold their meetings.—Mr. Heywood gave notice that at a special meeting to be held on Wednesday the 26th inst. he would bring forward the subject of urban powers, with the view to an application being made to the Local Government Board, under section 276 of the Public Health Act, 1875„ to declare the provisions of the said Act in force, in the contributory places of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, and to invest the Authority with all the powers rights, duties capacities, liabilities and obligations of an Urban Authority under the said Act within the contributory place or places in respect of which it shall be determined to make the appli- cation.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Williams.

MEDICAL OEFICEIC'E REPORT.

The Medical Officer reported an outbreak of small-pox at Stockton Heath, Appleton. The infection appeared to have been derived from Warrington. He had visited and issued all the precautionary measures possible. Two cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Appleton, one at Stockton Heath and two at Manley. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Helsby, where the sanitary ar- rangements of the house were defective, quantities of sewage lying stagnant- There was evidence of the drainage having become blocked. The water was derived from a well, the surroundings of which afforded opportunity for contamination. He would suggest that the water be analysed and in any case the cesspool should ke at once abolished, or removed to a distant site.—lnstructions were given for remedying the nui- sances mentioned.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

This contest will be decided to-day. There are twelve candidates for eleven seats, viz.. Church : Rev. G. H. Garrett, D.D., Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.y., C.C., Mr. C. E. Barlow, and Major Waring; Catholic Very R3V. Dean Finegan, Rev. J. C. Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. S. Quinn, and Mr. C. Flynn; Pro- gressive : Messrs. if. Brown, R. Shaw, and David Lewis. Polling takes place from 8 a.m., to 8 p.m., and there are ten polling stations, viz., Farnworth Girls' School, S:. Bede's School, Simm's Cross Board School. Albert-road We-leyan School, Warrington-road Board School. St. Mary's Catholic School, Lacey-street School, Waterloo-road School, Blue Ribbon Gospel Hall, and West Bank Board School. Voting will be by ballot, and voters can give eleven votes to one candidate, or divide them as he chooses, but he must not give more than eleven. The counting will take pla..sa in Widnes Town , Hall on Monday. Each of the three parties are work- ing hard to return their candidates. The canvassing , has been of a thorough description, but only the Progressives have held public meetings in support of the cause.

..,.....,,. MR. CRAWFORD AND THE CHURCH CANDIDATES. ' Speaking at a reception meeting at the National Schools, on Tuesday evening, Mr. ..T. C. Crawford re- ferred to the School Board Election. He said theve iseemed to be a feeling of confidence amongst the elector- ate that the church candidates were safe. They had in Mr. Deacon a gentleman who had shown that he could

not be excelled as a guide in educational affairs. They had also beside him upon the Board Mr. Barlow, who had given a a great deal of time and ability, for the furtherance of education in Widnes, and who under- stood fully the denominational education given in Wid- nes, and was thoroughly in favour of working the denominational schools side by side with the Board schools. Then they had Major Wareing, who had been a member of the Board far the past three years, and they would agree that his action had been not to lower the standard of the Board Schools or crush the dedorninational • schools but to practice econ- omy with efficiency. Then they had their new candidate, the Vicar who had to be tried, Their friends the Nonconformists said that the denom- inational schools were not public but private schools ; but he contended that their schools and the Catholic schools were as much public schools as any of th. Board schools. They said they would not allow outsiders upon the Board of management. Nothing of the sort. They did allow outsiders to be on the Board of management. Their friends seemed to thank that they were living in the antiquated times of twenty or thirty years ago. The churchwardens were managers, and they had outside men on the Board, and everything was carried i out n the same way as to incorue and expendi- ture as it was in the Board schools, therefore he regretted entirely the idea that the denom- inational schools were not public schools. They were governed by the same code as the Board schools, taught the same subjects, and taught them as well, therefore he said, they were exactly in the same position as the Board schools. Re believed the election would be a very stiff one. Both of the parties would strain their utmost to carry their men, and it behoved them as Churchmen to carry their men. lie felt certain that if they were all joined together they could carry five, and if they did not carry four thJy, would be thoroughly disgraced. (Applause.)

div.head: COUNTY ABYII3II QUESTION.
div.p: THE COUNTY ABYII3II QUESTION.

A letter was read from Mr. Proctor, of the Cheshire County Asylum, Parkside, Macclesfield, stating that he had now the permission of the Local Govern- ment Board to forward a copy of a letter which they had sent to the Cleaks of the Northwich, Wirral, and Chester Unions all of which had now paid the difference between the charge made for maintenance at Upton and that made at Parkside. The course which the Commit- tee at Parkside were following was quite in accordance with the opinion of Mr. Dolby, the district auditor. The reasons given by Mr. Delby,were enclosed, one of which was to the effect that the institutions were provided and maintained out of the general county rates, and each asylum was in law to the extent of its accommodation, available for the reception and maintenance of lunatics, belonging to any parish or union within the county.— Several members commented on the injustice of Runcorn Union having to bear the extra expense of sending their lunatics to Parkside, and also to pay an extra charge of ls.sd. per head, because Upton Asylum waslargely occupied by patients from the city of Chester, which was outside the county.—The clerk was instructed to lay the whole matter before the Local Government Board and to ask the clerk to Upton Asylum for a reply to a communication he had forwarded to him on the subject.

div.head: IMMIGRATION OP FOREIGN PAUPERS. -• • •
div.p: THE IMMIGRATION OP FOREIGN PAUPERS. -• • •

Mr. Williams said there could be little doubt that they had run great risks in regard to public health and pub- lic finance, through the immigration of vast numbers of people who were paupers, and also afflicted more or less. He did not think it advisable that any public body should pass a sweeping resolution for prohibiting the immigra- tion of all paupers or all people. He should very much object to do anvtning which would in any manner affect the character and very enviable position they had held as a nation, with regard to aliens. Up to the pre- sent time it had been a free country to all corners, and he desired it should continue to be so under certain restrictions with regard to the health and capacity for maintaining themselves when they arrived on English shores—something like that which had been passed by the United States Government. He therefore moved that, "Having regard to the grave danger which has existed of late by reason of the prevalence of cholera • . . .

abroad, and its importation into this country through the medium of insalubrious and often destitute foreign- ers, as well as to the general depression of our trade and agriculture, and consequent increase of poverty amongst our own people, this Board respectfully urges that the time has arrived when our Government should take stepsto check the immigration of such destitute or in- sanitary foreigners, as are likely to spread disease, or to become chargeable to the ratepayers of this country."— McWilliams said there could be little doubt that we had run great risks in regard to public health and public finances from the immigration.—ln reply to Mr. Bran- dreth, Mr. Williams said everything at the present time pointed to a period of depression in agriculture and trade, accompanied with poverty amongst our own people. The point of his resolution was that, taking into consideration that they had something more than usual to face at home, they did not want to add to their troubles by the importation of disease and poverty.— The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the motion; which was carried unanimously. FIXANCH.

The Finance Committee reported that the balance ia the treasurer's hands was £2,378 19s. 3d., and they re- commended the payment of accounts amounting to £.394.15.--In moving the adoption of the report, Mr. Bmndreth said he was glad to observe there was a re— duction in the amount of the outdoor relief given in Runcorn, the amount for the last fortnight being £BO..

In connection with the above, a series of revival services have been held in the chapel. The services are being conducted by the Rev. T. Ross. div.head: WARRINGTON DOCKS.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON DOCKS.

A special meeting of the Council of the Warring- ton Chamber of Commerce was held on Monday, for the purpose of considering the question of the con- struction of the docks at Warrington. The meet- ing was a strictly private one. As we have before mentioned, the Corporation are also moving in the matter, and at the meeting of the Coun- cil to be held on Tuesday evening next the General Purposes Committee will submit the following resolution :—" That the following members of the Council be appointed a sub-commit- tee to consider and, report upon a proposal from the Manchester Ship Canal Company respecting the construction of the Warrington Docks .—The Mayor, Aldermen b‘rancomb, Platt, Sutton, Wright, Councillors R. T. Fairclough, Greening, Monks, and Henry Roberts. We understand that though no definite arrangement has been arrived at, there is a prospect of a satisfactory outcome of the negotia- tions with the Car.al Company.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW ROAD ACROSS ARPLEY MEADOWS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW ROAD ACROSS ARPLEY MEADOWS.

The General Purposes Committee of the Corpora- tion having passed a resolution instructing the Town Clerk to arrange an interview with the Lon- don and North Western Railway Company, on the subject of the proposed new road across Arpley- Meadows, a deputation consisting of the Mayor„ Alderman Burgess, Alderman Francomb, and the. Borough Surveyor, have proceeded to London, and. were yesterday to see the directors. It may be re-. membered flint the Railway Company have recent- ly acquired powers to divert "Slutchers"lane. tnd Part of their scheme is the construction c 4 a vehicular bridge over the railway near the end_ of Winmarleigh-street. The intention of the Railway Company was to make this bridge only 21feet wide, but the desire of the Corporation is to have the width considerably increased, hence the inter- view with the directors. From this bridge a road is to be constructed across Arpley Meadows_ in the. direction of Lower Walton, and this read will, with-, out doubt, ultimately be connected with the new road that is to be made by the Ship Canal Company from Lower Walton to Wilderspool Causeway near the level crossing. It will be seen from this that the road which is to take the place of Sluteber's, lane will become a very important thoroughfares affording a much shorter route from the Chester. road .to Bank Quay Station, and the parts of Warrington which lie adjacent. It is therefore, of Icourse, highly desirable that the new bridge to be made by the Railway Company should be of a good width, and capable of accommodating a large amount of traffic.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

They refused a license to Mr. Thomas.—Jonathan Broadhurst, who was late in reaching the court, now applied for a music and dancing license for a room above the Burton Cycle Works.—ln reply to the Chairman, he said he charged people 3d. apiece for admission.—The Ghairtnan : We can't entertain anything of the sort.—The applicant : I have had it for two years now.— The Chairman: Yes, well it will have to be closed.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATI7RDAY.—Before Mr. L. Voisey, and Mr. J. Geddes.

WANTED TO BE LOCKED T/P.—William Barker was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street on the previous evenin,..;.—Sergeant Chantler said he saw the prisoner outside the police station at 20 minutes to ten. lie was making use of bad language, and wit- ness asked him what was ths matter. He said he wanted to make a complaint, but asked what it was he replied, " I shan't tell you ; I'll tell the Superinten- dent." Witness told him to go away, but he became disorderly and said be would be locked up. At length witness took him into the police station.—The Bench ordered the man to pay the costs, 3s. 6d. WIFE ASSAF/LT.—Frank Maloney, of Dial-street, was charged with assaultin; Sarah Maloney, his wife, in that street, the previous night. It appeared from her evi- dernce and that of P.C. Alderman Harrison said the best thing to do with a man like the defendant would be to strap him up and flog him, and he wished the Bench had power to do this. nothing but physical punishment would meet such cases. —The prisoner was sentenced to 21. days' imprisonment with hard labour.
