div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SF-9SIONS.
WEDNESDAY. —Before .Messrs. John Rylands (chairman),

and John White, and Major'Pickmere. DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.—Thomas Jeffrey and Peter Ashcroft, at Orford on the 7th inst., Ss. each. ALLOWING Cows TO STRAY.—James Gleave was charged with allowing a bull and a heifei'to stray on the high- way at Croft, on the 15th inst., Mr. Jenkins appeared for the plaintiff,—A police constable said two or three
young women complained about the bull straying iis Heath-lane. 2s. and costs. _ _

.. AN UNSTAMPED WEIGHING MACHINE.-Wm. Royston chemical manufacturer, of Poulton, was charged with, having in his possession a large platform weighing mac- hine unstamped.—lnspector Spencer proved the charge. ss. and costs.

POACHING. James Harrison, farm labourer, was charged with trespassing in pursuit of conies, at Axton, on the 6th inst.—The defendant said he was pursuing his own rabbit, which he had turned out.—A game- keeper proved the case,and said the defendant was half- a-mile from where he had a right to be.-2s. 6d. and costs. _

ASSAULTING Tax POLICE. Herbert Barlow was charged with assaulting P.C. Callaghan, on the 16th inst., in Heath Lane, Croft.—The constable said the prisoner was with another man and they were both chunk, and en his coming up to them and complaining of their conduct, the prisoner's companion put him down on the ground, and the prisoner kicked him. He kicked him again after he was secured, was very violent all the way to the station. The other man got away. bs. and costs. ABSEN CE Faost SCHOOL. —Allan Tickle, Robert Robin- son, and William Worthington, for not sending their children regularly to school, were each fined ss.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. SexuanAT.-_-_Before Mr. John Rylands.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Two rivetters, employed on the Ship Canal at Rixton, named John Stewart and Thomas Gar- vin, were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting at Rixton on the 15th inst., and were bound over to keep the peace for three months. P.C. West proved the case.—Joseph Walker was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk at Rixton, on Saturday night. —Herbert Barlow was charged with being drunk at Croft, on the 10th inst., and further with assaulting P.C. Callagan.—For the first offence defendant was fined 23. 6d. and costs; the hearing of the second charge was postponed to the next County Petty Sessions. It ap- peared with regard to the charge of assault, that the prisoner and other men were in the village of Croft creating a disturbance. They were asked to go away, but they refused to do so. One of the men threw the officer down, and all the others assaulted him, but they managed to effect their escape. Barlow kicked the officer who succeeded in arresting him.—For being drunk at Golborne, on the 16th inst., Patrick Callaghan, a labourer, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: RUNCORN PE HY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PE HY SESSIONS.
MONDAL—Before Mr. A. Thomas, Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handlcy. _ .

A BREWER'S DRAYMAN AND HIS Ho RSH.—Joseph Grounds, a drayman in the employ of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., was summoned for having on the 6th inst. cruelly illused a horse.—P.C. Werth deposed to see- ing the horse shy near the new gas works at Runcorn, when the prisoner kicked the animal about the ribs and legs in a disgraceful manner. Afterwards; on examina- tion, he found scars on the legs and the front of the horses mouth was quite torn.—The defendant denied kicking the horse, and said the bit was too keen.—A witness corroborated this statement.—The defendant was fined 10s, and costs 11s. 6d.

DRUNK.—AIf red Hughes, a navvy, was fined 53. and costs for being drunk. A Safe CANI-L NUISANCIL—Thomas Clarke, William Nash, Thomas Davies, and George Twish, were charged with wandering abroad and lodging in an outhouse on the Ship Canal not having any visible means of subsis- tence.—P.C. Boyle proved the case and said the men were in a hut and had a roaring fire.—The prisoner said they had been unable to work because of the weather.— Superintendent Atherton said the prisoners appeared all working-men and not ordinary cadgers, but there had been great complaints made of this practics.—The pri- soners were committed to gaol for seven days. ONE MORE Caatrce.—Elizabeth Deans, pleaded guilty to having on the 12th July last stolen a quarter of a lb. of Berlin wool from the shop of Elizabeth Cockcroft of 7 Regent-st. The prisoner had since been away from the town.—Mr. J. Burton acting on behalf of the parents who are respectable people, asked the Bench to give the girl one more chance. She was only 17 years of age and had been married 831E0 montbs.—Superintendent Ather- ton said the prisoner was sentenced to 14 days imprison- ment in 1890 and 21 days in 1891 for felony.—The Bench decided to give the prisoner one more chance and only imposed a fine of 10s.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ITHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

Referring to the classific,ation of clubs in the Lanca- shire County Rugby Cup Competition, the "Athletic News" says it was not to be expected that the c )rnmit- tee's choice would please everybody, and apparently they did not even try to satisfy the critical spirit abroad; but we think they might have displayed a little more discernment, and have made themselves better ac- quainted with the status of many of the clubs before determining the position they should occupy in the list.

The plain fact of the matter is that the County Com- mittee attempted too ranch in one evening, with the result that several organisations which have been striv- ing, and with some success, to rise in football circles, have been put back a few years, and cannot now take that place amongst clubs which their records entitle them to and their play justly merits.

We do not say this with any intention of disparaging the labour of the gentlemen who were engaged in the arduous task, but merely to point out the injustice which certain clubs will suffer if the county do not affect some alteration before the fixtures are settled. It is, we be- lieve, intended that secretaries shall meet next Wednes- day for the purpose of arranging matches on the basis of the classification, but we would ask before that meet- ing takes places—why should fixtures be settled so pre- maturely? There is ample time between the end of the present season and the beginning of the next to make all arrangements, and the results of the games played dur- ing 1892-3 would be a far better criterion of the stand- ing of the clubs than those of the years 1891-2.

As an alternative, however, we would suggest that, in order to give the juniors a chance, instead of four divi- sions the thirty-six clubs be divided into three classes of twelve clubs each. This would have the effect of con- centrating the interest, and it would lessen by at least one year the chances of a club rising, and getting into a nigher class.

Accrington certainly did well to run Sunderland to a couple of goals on the banks of the Wear. It is all very well to say that the champions took things easily, but the fact remains that the Lancashire team held their own after the interval. The excitement reached a high pitch when Accrington drew level, for which they de- serve more than a passing word. That they failed to maintain this form to the end does not detract from their excellent display, as Sunderland are very formid- able antagonists indeed on their own ground.

The aspirants for county honours in Cheshire received a shock when the team selected to do honour for the cheese county against the Midlanders was made known. The Possiblos—or the unknown ones—had on the pre- vious Saturday beaten the Probables—or the known ones —by a goal to nothing after having the best of the game throughout, yet not a single player from the Possibles had been marked out as worthy to wear a County jersey. That is not very encouraging for the ambitious youths who reside in Stockport and such places, and a Blight like that rankles deep in the bosoms of the boys of Cheshire, wherever they were born, or whatever county they learned their football in.

The League games of Saturday last furnished one tremendous sensation. As Newton Heath could not manage to beat the Albion a week ago, not even their dearest friends believed them capable of muzzling the " Wolves " from Wolverhampton, and yet how complete- ly they did it was in everybody's mouth during the even- ing. Ten to one almost takes one's breath away. Rose and other good men were absent from the ranks of the Wanderers, but Hassall has been keeping goal in such clever style during the season that the extent of the score is all the mere a matter of wonderment.

Double figures were only twice reached in the League all last season. West Bromwich beat Darwen by 12 to 0, and Aston Villa scored 12 to Accrington 2. Strange to say, in the Alliance, Newton Heath vanquished Lincoln City by 10 to 1, and now they serve the" Wolves" with the same sauce in the more important business of the League. The performance is all the more significant seeing that the " Heathens " had never previously tasted the sweets of victory. They have done the 3ob properly, now they have started.

Next to the performance of Newton Heath in the shape of a surprise came the turn-up at Ewood Park. It was natural for the followers of the Rovers to believe them capable of holding their own with Sheffield Wed- nesday, to say the least. In this, however, they were grieviously disappointed, as the Sheffielders not only beat them in getting goals, but beat them as regards the play generally. Southworth has been no great shakes this season' but the match served to demonstrate more forcibly than ever that with the International centre away the forwards are practically useless.

div.head: SHOCKLNG ACCIDENT IN A GOLBO.RNE
div.p: SHOCKLNG ACCIDENT IN A GOLBO.RNE
COLLIERY.

A Golborne youth named John Turner met with a frightful accident at Golborne Collieries on Monday evening. While following his duties as a pony boy down the pit one of the animals bolted, and in attempting to arrest the pony- it is believed that it lashed out with its hind legs, striking the boy between the temples. On being picked up he presented a shocking spectacle. One eye was knocked out, his nose smashed, and his face almost battered into his skull, fie was removed to the Wigan Infirmary in a critical condition, little hope being entertained of his recovery. The authorities report the occurrence was purely an accident.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 22, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 22, 1892.
RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

This, one of the best of the Runcorn home matches, was completely spoiled by the inclement weather, and Runcorn was robbed of a good gate. Runcorn also hav- ing to play three men from the A. Team, Crompton, Faulkner, and Robinson being off, and Houghton played after pressure, he having had an accident at his employment. The players turned out at four o'clock and were as follows : Runcorn : Houghton, back ; Rogers, Warder, and Hughes, three-quarters ; Abrams, and Robinson, half backs; Williams, Sampson, Davies, Derbyshire, Farmer, Taylor, Moores, Langley, and Riley, forwards. Wigan : Halliwell, back ; Wallwork, Seddon, and Clarke, three-quarters; Taylor. and Mitch- inson, half hacks ; Webster, Ferguson, M`Master, M'Natnara, Wardle, If nsworth, Dempsey, Rigby,Grundy forwards. Seddon started at four o'clock, and Rogers replied splendidly. The Runcorn forwards played grand, dribbling finely, the ball going ever the Wigan line, Williams scoring grandly, Houghton failing at goal. On the resumption the home players came up to the home line, Halliwell saving again in the nick of time. The play Was fast, Rogers kicking finely and gaining a lot of ground. Wallwork was in evidence, but preferred to kick. The game was fought out with great spirit, and for a time the play was even. Play was grand. The Cheshire men showed fine form, pushing the Wigan forwards all over the ground, and from a pack on the Wigan line Halliwell kicked dead again. The drop out brought no relief. Seddon mulling, let up Sampson, Williams, and Farmer in the visitors' quarters. Here a free kick to Runcorn was allowed to roll dead, the play being feeble on the part of Wigan. The backs soon touched down again, when they again repeated imme- diately after. Runcorn to- a man were now playing splendidly, keeping Wigan on their lines all the first half. Half-time :—Runcorn 1 try 5 minors, Wigan nothing. Riley started after the interval, and the play was of the same fast nature as characterised the first part, the for- wards really playing magnificently, fairly out-playing the Wigan front rank. Awakening up, the Wiganers dribbled over the home line, and during a scramble Taylor scored a lucky try. Afterwards play was keen, both sides trying desperately to score, but the play of Runcorn was brilliant. Final result :—Runcorn 1 try 5 minors, Wigan 1 try. CHESHIRE v.. MIDLAND COUNTIES. The first ef the series of county matches arranged by , the Cheshire County Committee was played on Wednes- day, on the ground of the Runcorn Club, the home side being opposed to a team representing the Midland Counties. Alterations in the original selections were numerous on the side of the visitors, with the result that their forward rank was somewhat uneven, two or three light men being mixed up with the big, heavy division that usually represent the Midlands. The Cheshire side could have been made a little stronger, as Fred Hughes and W. Faulkner were absentees, but, at the same time, they received exceptional help from the Scottish International, P. R. Clause, who has recently joined the Birkenhead Park Club. It was a pleasant afternoon, and with the ground in fair order, a good " gate " assembled to witness what was expected to be a keen contest. In this they were not disappointed, as after Cheshire had taken a decided lead in the first half, they fell off considerably towards the end of the game, and the Midlanders were at one time very near drawing level. The combination of the Cheshire team was ex- cellent, but the feature of the game was the play at Strauss and Crompton, the latter scoring a try and drop- ping a goal. Hope scored the try for the visitors. The final score was Cheshire 2 goals (one dropped), Mid- tends 1 goal. ASSOCIATION.

Waanmerrox ASSOCIATION Y. BIRKIIALM. —These teams met for the first time at Birkdale, on Saturday. The visitors had a very weak team, and each side played ten men, T. Dutton, T. Mather, E. Mather, and T. Parrott, acting as substitutes for Jones, Davies, Norman, and Fennolly, who were on the sick list. The visitors kicked off very late with the wind, and experienced hard lines, forcing no fewer than five corners in succession, but without result. The Warringtonians severely pressed the homesters, but half-time arrived with no score. Restarting, the home team took up the pressure, but found the visitors' defence too good for a time. After about 15 minutes play, hands off the visitors resulted in Dutton heading through his own goal, thus scoring for Birkdale. The play after this reverse was very even, and no further scoring being done, time arrived with the score—Birkdale, one goal ; Warrington none. War- rington team :Goal, J. Mather; full backs, J. Kinnard (captain), and T. Dutton; half backs, J. Bannon, and H. Lawton; forwards, S. Pierpoint, 'l'. Parrott, T. P. Forbes, E. Mather, and T. Mather. WARRINGTON CRICIERT ASSOCIATION V. ST. ELPRIN'S.— The above clubs met on Saturday on the cricket ground, the match having a local interest because the Cricket Club had beaten Warrington by five goals to four a fortnight ago. The " Crickets" with the wind went down the field, but were sent back by Colley, and the Saints had a look in, Scarisbrick being finely robbed by Chidlaw when within an ace ef scoring. After a spell of even play Williamson scored a grand goal, and after the Saints had been driven back, Isherwood by splendid play again beat Bates, half-time arriving Cricket, 2, St. Elphins 0. After the change of ends the Saints improved being continually round the Cricket goal, Cook finally scoring finely from a free kick. After this the game was very fast, the Cricket forwards being sent back by Cook who kicked well towards goal. Prancomb only parti- ally cleared, Taylor taking advantage to equalize. After Smith had scored a third for the Saints from a combined rush, the Cricket played hard to equalize, but the splendid defence of Cook, Colley, and Bates effec- tually prevented further scoring, the Saints, who had the better combinatioa, winning a hard game by 3 goals to 2.

div.head: RUGBY. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE MATCHES. OLDHAM ,r. WARRINGTON.
div.p: RUGBY. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE MATCHES. OLDHAM ,r. WARRINGTON.

The most attractive fixture in the Manchester district on Saturday seemed, says the " Athletic News," to be that at Watersheddings between Oldham and Warring- ton, a pair of clubs that play the Rugby game .3 it should be played. It was to Oldham that I therefore decided to go, although it did seem like throwing a chance away to turn out on such a miserably cold, wet day. Oldham was certainly not seen at its best on Saturday, and at Watersheddings the headquarters of Oldham Club presented a dismal apwarance. Bad the weather been fine we should have seen a very big crowd and some attractive football, but as it was, we got neither the " gate" nor the other thing. Both clubs naturally turned out their best teams for so important a fixture, but the less said about the play the better, for it seemed to take the men all their time to stick on their feet, whilst the efforts made to catch or pass the ball were more amusing than anything else. About a couple of thousand spectators waited in the rain until about a quarter to four, when the following players entered the field ready to do or die : - . . _

OLDHAti.—W. H. Pennington, back ; W. M'Cutcheon, D. Gwynn, and J. Hurst, three-quarters ; J. R. Mills, and J. Thomas, half-backs ; T. Ingham, E. Blomley, 13. Andrew, J. Chadwick, T. Holden, S. Holden, J. Board- man, J. Tuhor, and J. Murrell, forwards.

WARRINOTON.—J. Boscow, back; F. Plumpton, J. Neesom, and H. Webster, three-quarters; J. T. Bate and W. Evans, half-backs; W. Ashton (captain), J. Jolley, Fair Turner, W. Bandies, T. Donohue, H. Teare, J. Holmes, W. Nevins, and T. Thornley, forwards. Referee : Mr. J. Mills, Swinton F.C. It must have been a great effort of endurance for the thirty players, uot to mention the referee, to scamper through the wet, slushy turf for seventy minutes, and to some of the combatants the " no side" solo on the I whistle would be the sweetest music imaginable. At first it seemed as if the Warrington men were going to have matters all their own way, for they carried the packs, and it was only owing to the fine play of the Oldham backs that the visitors were kept at bay. First M'Cutcheon showed some cleverness, and Gwynn followed suit, whilst Jack Hurst fielded the ball admir- ably, and exhibited a lot of speed as well. After a while the Oldham forwards warmed to their work, so to speak, and for the remainder of the contest the play was about as even as it well could be, each line being visited in turn. Both clubs had near shaves of scoring, Evans, the Warrington half-back, on one occasion getting within a yard of the line, but when time was up, and the half-drowned and starved players were able to go and get a bath, a change of clothes, and a drink, it was another case of honours even, neither side having scored anything of greater value than minor points, which, I may remark, are not now recognised in the competition for the Lancashire Ragby championship. When the Oldham Club first came into prominence they had a fine lot of forwards and a poor collection of backs. After a few years the backs were as smart as the front division was slow and unskilful, but from what I saw on Saturday the Old- ham team is strong and well balanced both fore and aft. Ben Andrew, as far as I could see, is a useful scrum- mager, and uses his weight besides being able to follow up fast. Chadwick is another good player, and the Hoidens struck me as being able to play a very fair game. At half-back J. R. Mills, locally known as Jim Bob," was a street in front of his companion Thomas, apparently being always in the right spot. Hurst started well, but fell off a bit, for which there was some excuse, but the two Welshmen, M'Cutcheon and Gwynn, showed all their old resource under great difficulties. The last- named player is going on so well this season that he will very likely get another chance of being included in the Lancashire fifteen. He did some very smart things despite the we weather on Saturday, and one bit of play that he started from midfield almost resulted in it try for Oldham. Warrington, who have not yet got " Smack " Bate fixed up after his accident, have a sterl- ing full back in Boscow ; and a promising centre three- quarter in Neesom. The lengthy Webster, who was one of the wing three-quarters, started indifferently, but when he got into his stride—and it is something like a stride, too—was of good service to his side, until the concluding stages of the game, when he made several mistakes. One of the features of the game was the wonderful manner in which our old silent friend, Fred Plumpton, kept his jersey and white knickerbockers clean. All the other 29 players were literally bedaubed from head to foot, and it was an extremely difficult matter to distinguish the red and white hoops of Oldham from the yellow and black vertical stripes of Warrington. Plumpton, however, managed to present a beautiful spotless appearance from first to last, and how he did it no one seemed able to understand. In the last few minutes of the game it seemed a certainty that he would be rolled in the mud, and great was the excitement and heavy the betting; but, to the disappointment of the spectators, he escaped, and eventually walked off the field in triumph. Evans made a smart half-back, and Jim Jolley, Ashton, and Nevins were always in evidence among the forwards.

WARRINGTON T. OLDHAM A.—Owing to the flooding of tho Wilderspool enclosure this match had to be played on the Rangers' ground, which was found to be in a fearful state. Warrington having won the toss, took advantage of the blustering breeze, but Oldhem having kicked off, at once began to force their way towards their opponents' goal, Hampson saving daringly. A fine run by Lees gained for his side a strong attacking posi- tion ; but this was not the sort of thing generally expected, and at a critical moment Ashurst cleared grandly. Quickly the homesters forced back Oldham, a splendid rush, headed by Bailey, Antrobus, Glover, and Davies, being only saved on the line. There was a stiff I struggle for supremacy in this dangerous vicinity, until a foolish piece of play by one of the Oldham back gave I Edwards a try, Ashurst kicking a goal. With this I advantage, the home team, urged on by the soddened spectat•Nrs, again rushed in the fray, Edwards, Hampsonl Higham, and Lally being notable until Bryan came to I the rescue with a capital piece of work. A long kick by Daniels, although partly returned by Lever, enabled Warrington to gain another foothold in the Oldham territory, where Hampson again saved in daring fashion. Then a fine display by Antrobus, Daniels, and Potts enabled the latter to dash away to the line. Warrington almost scored here, a long pass from Bate to Lawless almost having the desired effect. At this interesting , stage, however, Oldham got away with a fine dribble, j forcing the leather over the Warrington line, aud a try was allowed, and at half-time the home team led by one goal to one try. At the outset of the second half Oldham were penalized for their eagerness, but Lees recovered the lost advantage. A powerful punt by Ashurst was supplemented with a kick from Potts, when Bate got away, only to see his pass missed. A lot of indiscrimin- ate and indiscribable play in the mud occupied the attention for some time, and then Ashurst cleared a dribble in marvellous fashion. Again Oldham returned to the attack, and when their chances of scoring were of the brightest, Lally dodged away, threw to Bate, and the last named, exercising his line judgment, passed at the right moment to Lawless. This player took the ball finely, and getting rid of a couple of opponents headed the team almost the length of the ground, winding up with a brilliant try behind the post ; Ashurst placed the goal. Directing after the resumption Bate made &grand run, and Lally took up the running into the visitors' 25. Ashurst, who had played a magnificent full back game, again delighted the drenched onlookers. A capital bit of work by Daniels being supplemented by Antrobus, Molyneux, Bradbury, and Bailey, the visitors' quarters were again reached, but nothing further was scored, and the referee's whistle brought the match to a welcome close, Warrington winning by two goals to one try. WARRINGTON 2ND V. BIRKENHEAD Sr. ANNE'B.—The above match took place at Birkenhead, on Saturday, in wet weather, and the visitors had to wait on the field fully half-an-hour for the home team. Consequently it was 4 10 when Birkenhead kicked off uphill. Gibson re- turning in touch. For a time the home team had the best of the position, and from loose play, F. Smith scored, no goal resulting. This roused Warrington, and by the aid of Rowe they took play to the home 25, but the St. Anne's again rushed up the field. From a scrim- usage, Smith (Warrington) got hold, and after dodging two or three of his opponents passed to Gibson, who eluded his opponents in grand style, and scored a splendid try under the posts. Owing, how- ever, to the sloppy state of the ball, Boldsworth failed to notch the coveted point. This brought about half- time, each side having scored a try. In the second half Warrington played somewhat better, exchange kicks between Boldsworth and Basnett resulting in a minor for Warrington. The Warrington forwards now came on with a rush, and Forster had hard lines, a touch in goal resulting. Shortly after Monks scored for Warring- ton, but the point was not allowed. The home team rushed down the field, Smith getting over, but the try was not allowed. Time was called shortly afterwards, leaving the game drawn, the final result being--War- rington 2nd 0-1-3, St. Anne's 0-1-1. WIDNES v. TYLDESLEY.—PIayed at Widnes, before 1,000 spectators. The homesters turned out as selected, whilst Tyldesley were without Hanson. Tyldesley com- menced operations in a heavy downpour of rain. Brennan returned well, and Barber further improved his team's position. Alford attended to Berry, and a scrimmage ensued on the visitors' goal line. Wright had a good chance, but failed to hold the ball, and Fernley cleared, but Widnes returned to the attack, and Fernley again relieved. Alford somewhat retrieved his team's position. The sloppy state of the ground militated against a good exhibition of football, but the game proved thoroughly exciting, the teams being very evenly matched. Another scrimmage on the Tyldesley goal line was well cleared by Bell, the midgeld exchanges were then the order of the game, after which grand play placed Widnes on the attack. Final result Tyldealey, 1 penalty goal, (3 points) ; yidnes, pil. , 1

div.head: LAMBETH POISONING CASES.
div.p: LAMBETH POISONING CASES.
THE TRIAL OF NEILL.

The Central Criminal Court was crowded on Monday, when Thomas Neill, 38, was indicted before Mr. Justice Hawkins for the wilful murder of the girls Donworth, Shrivell, Marsh, and Clover ; also for attempting to murder Louisa Harris, and for sending blackmailing letters to Drs. Harper and Broadbent. The Attorney- General prosecuted, and Mr. Geoghegan defended the prisoner, who is an intelligent-looking man, and who appeared self-possessed, scrutinized the jury as they were sworn, and pleaded not guilty. From the opening statement of Sir Charles Russel, it appeared that prisoner who was English by birth, obtained a medical qualifica- tion in America, and came to England in October, 1891. He met at a music hall Eliza May, an unfortunate, and afterwards wrote to her making an appointment. • May and another girl named Masters met prisoner in Lambert Palace-road with Matilda Clover, one of the girls subsequently poisoned, and they went in Clover's house. Clover let prisoner out, and afterwards left, returning at five o'clock next morning. Later she was found in great agony, and died four hours afterwards. Prisoner wrote to Dr. Broadbent, of St. Thomas' Hospital land to Dr. Harper, father of a student there, endeavour- ing to extort money from him. He also wrote to Mr. F. I Smith, sen of the late Mr. W. H. Smith, respecting I another of the poisoned girls, demanding money to sup- press evidence. Elizabeth Matthews positively identified prisoner as the man whom she saw with Clover. Dr. Broadbent produced the letter received, from prisoner, and the case was adjourned. On Tuesday, John George Kirby, chemist's assistant, proved that at the beginning of October the prisoner purchased from him Dux vornica, which was scheduled as poison, capsules, and opium. Lucy Rose, servant. 27, Lambeth-road, said that in October last she admitted Clover and a broadly-built gentleman in the evening. Dr. Stevenson, Government analyst, proved finding strychnine in Clover's body after exhuma- tion. Evidence was afterwards called as to the receipt of several letters accusing innocent persons of poisoning women. On Wednesday, the witness Haynes, to whom the prisoner is alleged to have made certain remarkable communications, admitted that throughout the case he had been employed by the police as their agent for ob- taining information. Amongst other witnesses called were Miss Sabatini, who was at one time engaged to Neill; and " Loo " Harvey, whose ready wit in throwing away two "long pills" or capsules given her by the prisoner while she pretended to swallow them, possibly stood her in good stead at the time. The case was again adjourned. On Thursday the court was crowded. Many ladies attended, an early arrival being Miss Sabatini, the prisoner's late sweetheart. Dr. Stevenson, Government analyst, said he discovered strychnine in the contents of the stomachs of the girls Marsh and Shrivel!, and attri- buted their deaths to that poison. Mr. Geogeghan, with the concurrence of the judge and the prosecution, sub- mitted a written question to the witness, explaining that he did so in the interests of public morals, not from consideration for those present. Detective Ward deposed to seeing the prisoner with a loose woman in Westminister Bridge-road, on May 12th. She had since been missing from her customery haunts ; but it was not suggested that the prisoner was responsible for her absence. After further evidence the prosecution closed. Mr. Geoghegan opened the address for the defence, stating that no witnesses would be called. Mr. Geoghegan contended that the evidence did not clearly establish either that Glover died by strychnine, or that the prisoner poisoned her. He submitted that unless absolutely satisfied on these points the jury must acquit the accused. The Attorney General then com- menced his reply for the Crown.

COLLISION OF A TRANSA.TLANTIC LINER.

The Anchor Line steamer Ethiopia arrived at Greenock on Thursday, from New York. The captain reports that when off the Cumbres the Ethiopia had her plates dam- aged in collision with the outward bound steamer Walden. The Walden received considerable damage, but proceeded on her voyage. ,

div.head: WRECK OF THE BOKHARA.
div.p: WRECK OF THE BOKHARA.

20 PASSENGERS AND 102 OF THE CREW MISSING. HONG KONG, Oct. 18. H.M. cruiser Porpoise arrived here to-day with the survivors of the ill-fated steamship Bokhara, which was lost upon Sand Island, in the Pescadores group, while on the voyage from Shanghai to Hong Kong. The Bok- hara, which left Snanghai on the Bth inst,eticountered a furious gale on th• 10th inst. The sea ran mountains high, repeatedly sweeping the decks, and finally extin- guishing the engine-room fires. Being thus rendered quite helpless, the Bukhara drifted towards Sand Island, upon which she struck at midnight, and sank immedi- ately afterwards. All on board were lost except two of the passengers, three of the vessel's officers,-two of the European, and sixteen of the native crew. Altogether, 125 persons perished, including 11 Hong Kong cricketers returning from Shanghai. The survivors, after passing two days on Sand Island, a desert spot, were taken off by Chinese to Wakung, where they were found by the Douglas Line steamer Thales, which took them on board, and subsequently transferred them to the Porpoise. The Peninsplar and Oriental Steam Navigation Com- pany have received the following telegrasm from their superintendent at Hong Kong, dated 1.40 p.m., Oct. 18th :

Chief Officer Bokhara reports : Bokliara struck on Monday midnight, 10th October, vessel becoming help- less at 10 p.m. Monday owing heavy seas putting fires out. All deck fittings and boats gone before vessel struck, she sinking immediately. European and native crew behaved splendidly throughout. One hundred and two of the crew missing :—Namely, Captain Sams ; Second Officer fogies ; Engineers O'Bryan Covan, Paton, Hills, Boilermaker Houston, Winchman Kendal, Carpenter Brennan, Boatswain Reeves, Quarter- masters Gaskin, Friend, Hudson, Field, Phillip ; Steward in Charge Ward, Stewardess Barstock ; Stewards Poppy Wilson, Mitchell, Elliott, Pettit, Chips, Reading, Briscoe, Goarwood, Boxall, and 70 native seamen and firemen.

" The following is a list of passengers missing : Major Turner, Captain Dunn, Captain Dawson, Lieutenant Boyle, Lieutenant Burnett, Sergeant Jeffkins, Sergeant Donegan, Sergeant Mumford—above belonging to garrison—Mr. C. Wallace, Mr. G. Taverner, Mr. G. Purvis, Mr. C. Ralf, Mrs. Carnes, Mrs. Hawley (Bom- bay), Mr. G. Bishop, Mr. H. Lalmia (Ismailia), Mr. and Mrs. Chaiu (Loadon), Mrs. Cunnify and infant.

" Passengers saved :—Dr. Lowson and Lieutenant Markham. Of the crew saved :—Officers Prickett, Parry and Sweeny. Quartermasters Wood and Lewis ; also 16 native seamen and firemen. " Swatow officers report two more landed South Pescadores, probably Europeans. Will be forwarded as soon as weather permits. " The cargo consists of treasure 200,000 dole., 1,300 bales of silk, and 800 tons of tea and general cargo." The Press Association says: The names of officers aboard the vessel make it practically certain that they and some of their companions were members of a Hongkong cricket eleven returning from Shanghai after playing the annual match against the northern port. There has always been keen rivalry between Hong Kong and Shanghai, in the matter of cricket, despite the 800 miles separating the two places. In 1889, and again in 1891, a team from Hong Kong largely com- posed of officers belonging to the garrison visited Shanghai. On each occasion the match was played about the middle of October. Captain Dunn, Lieut. ' Boyle, and Dr. Lowson were members of the eleven last year, the first-named officer being the captain. Quar- termaster-Sergeant Jeffkins played against Shanghai when an eleven from that settlement visited Hong Kong in February last. C. Ralf, in the published list may stand for C. Barff and C. Wallace for S. Wallace, both prominent local cricketers. Major Turner, Captain Dawson, Lieutenant Burnett, Lieutenant Markham, ' Sergeant Donegan, and Sergeant Mumford .-were I without doubt also members of the team returning II from Shanghai, the Hong Kong eleven being I usually composed almost entirely of military men. If the two persons reported as landed on South Pescadores turn out to be civilians, the small garrison in the colony will have been suddenly deprived by this calamity of five officers, warrant officer, and two r sergeants, whose places will have to be filled either from India or from home. Official telegrams have been received at the Colonial Office and War Offica confirming the details of the wreck.

As an illustration of the long lives for which iron ships of the Peninsular and Oriental Company's navy have distinguished, it is interesting to note that, though the Bokhara was little short of twenty years old, many others built before her are still running in the Eastern seas or trading between Europe and India. The Surat, built so long ago as 1866, is now on a voyage between Ceylon and Shanghai. To her passengers outward bound were transferred from the Malwa at Colombo a week ago, and she should be somewhere near Singapore by this time. Notwithstanding her age, she is still credited with a speed of fourteen knots an hour. Indeed, the P. and 0. Company has not a really slow ship afloat. The Bokhara could do fourteen knots an hour, while of thirteen ships built either before or in the same year as she was five are credited yet with a speed of 14i knots, four can go at a rate only half-a-knot less, and the remaining four can keep up their thirteen knots an hour pretty regularly. LOCAL HARVEST FESTVLALS.

div.head: LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The annual harvest festival in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel was observed on Sunday. The chapel had been beautified with flowers, fruit, and corn, the arrangement of which produced a very pretty effect. Appropriate sermons were preached morning and even- ing by Mr. Roscoller, and the services were made bright and attractive with special music rendered by the choir. In the afternoon there was a children's service, at which suitable addresses were delivered by Mr. Roscoller and Mr. Moss. The collections were in aid of the chapel funds.

div.head: WARRINGTON RIGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RIGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The harvest festival in connection with the above institution took place on Saturday and was con- tinued on Sunday and Monday. The building in Bewsey-street was suitably adorned for the occasion, and much credit is due to the decorators for the comfortable nature of the surroundings. On Satur- day evening Mrs. Law, of Blackpool, who was inscribed on the posters by the attractive title "Black Pudding Lucy,' gave a history of her early life and the method by which sha was brought to recognize the Great Truth. The services were very well attended. Serviees were also held on Sunday, in the morning, afternoon, and evening, all of which were well attended. Collections were made at the close of each of the services in aid of a new school. On Monday evening a fruit banquet and entertainment was held. The programme which was given was of a very attractive character and the several items were loudly applauded. DARESBURY. _ .

The annual harvest festival -services were held In the Parish Church, Daresbury, on Sunday, when two ser- mons were preached by the Rev. Charles W. Markham, rector of 4ughton, near Ormskirk. The morning service was commenced at 10.30, at which a large congregation listened attentively to an excellent discourse, from the words, "Be net deceived ; God is not mocked ; for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." The church was decorated with fruit, 3m., in a very neat manner, especially the belfry screen, which was the work of the ringers. The pulpit decoration was done by Mr. Calder, gardener at the Elms ; the font by Mr. Sanderson, gardener at Moore House ; the east end by Messrs. Flamblett and Hartley, the lectern, windows, &c. by Miss Whiteley, Misses Rodger, Miss Darbyshire, Mrs. Wright, Miss Darlington, Miss Horrabin, and Messrs. W. Darbyshire, T. Billingten, and H, Hayes. The musical part of the services were well rendered. The collections for both services amounted to over £l5, which sum will be devoted to the three Sunday schools of the parish. ORFORD.

The annual harvest festival in connection with this church was held on Sunday. The church had been beautifully decorated for the Gcnasion by Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Phillips, Mrs. C. Grounds, and the Misses Pollitt, Fisher, Richardson, Monks, Grounds, Mather, and Massey. In the morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Isaac Phillips (vicar), who preached from the words," Whilst the earth remaineth, seedtime and har- vest, cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." There had, he said, been failures in crops, but there never was a time, and never would be a time, when God would look down upon a vast extent of desolation and starvation. At the even- ing service, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington, preached to a large congregation. Special hymns and psalms were sung during the day. ' The anthem" Fear not, 0 land" (Simper), and at the morning service ; and " Praise the Lord, 0 ray soul" (Simper), at the evening service, were admirably rendered by the choir. Mr. John Cann presided at the organ. Offertories were taken at both services in aid of the church expenses fund and diocesan institu- tions.

div.head: PORTSMOUTH COURT-MARTIAL.
div.p: THE PORTSMOUTH COURT-MARTIAL.

The Court-Martial on the drivers Robinson and Rogers, charged with cutting saddles, concluded at Portsmouth on Tuesday. The Court convicted, but sentence was deferred for the Duke of Connaught's confirmation.

THE UGANDA QUESTION. Lord Rosebery, replying to an influential deputation from the Anti-Slavery Society which waited upon him in regard to the contemplated evacuation of Uganda, said he could not pledge the Government to any course of policy with regard to that territory, but, among many considerations to be weighed,the great cause they advocated would have a commanding place.

It is understood in legal —circles that the judgeship rendered vacant by the retirement of Mr. Justice Den- man will be offered to Mr. R. T. Reid, Q.C. who has represented the Dumfries district since the general elec- tion of 1886.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

THE NEW LOAN.—DECISION OF MANCHESTER* I A meeting has been held of the Special Ship Canal Committee of the Manchester City Council. 'rue com- mittee had under consideration the correspondence be- tween the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Leech) and Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the Ship Canal Co. It is understood that the committee re-affirmed their willingness to receive the co-operation of any other Cor- poration. A sub-committee was appointed to confer with Mr. Moulton, the legal adviser of the Corporation, in regard to the terms on which the Corporation could lend further financial aid to the company. One condi- tion which will be inserted in the enabling Bill to be submitted to Parliament is that the Corporation shall have a clear majority in the directorate of the company. SALFORD CORPORATION AND THE NEW LOAN. A well-attended meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee of the Town Council of Salford was held on Wed- nesday—the MATOR (Mr. Alderman Keevney) presid- ing—to consider a communication received by the Mayor from Lord Egerton, of Tatton, chairman of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, with reference to a loan from the Corporation of Salford towards the cost of completing the canal. The meeting was held in private. We are informed that in opening the meeting, the Mayor stated that he only received the letter from Lord Egerton last Saturday, so that he had lost no time in calling them together. It was the more necessary to call them together soon, for, as Lord Egerton pointed out in his letter, it would be necessary, if Salford was disposed to assist, to go forward at once with a bill to be promoted by the Corporations of Man- chester and Salford in conjunction with the Ship Canal Company. Proceeding, the Mayor reminded the Council that on the previous occasion when the 'Manchester Corporation proposed to give a loan to the Canal Com- pany Salford expressed its willingness to join. but Manchester seemed at that time desirous of undertaking the whole matter itself, and it was thought that the in- tervention of Salford might jeopardise the passing of the bill by Parliament. Now, however, the matter assumed a different form, as the Salford Corporation had been asked by the Company to assist. He briefly explained the effect of the proposed loan on the financial position of the borough. £1,000,000 at 31 per cent. would represent, he said, an actual charge of £32,500, which on the rateable value would be equal to tenpence in the pound, and to repay the money over a period of 60 vears,would require a further sum of £6,000 per annum, which would represent another twopence in the pound. These figures represented what they would have to meet assuming that the canal did not earn any income, and that the Corporation were called upon to meet their entire liability. But he firmly believed that the canal would eventually pay. —'Fhe Mayor's remarks were favourably received, and the tone of the two hours' discussion which followed appeared to indicate that the majority of the mem- bers were disposed to view favourably the proposal that an advance of a million should be made to the Canal Company, under satisfactory conditions.—A motion was submitted declaring it desirable that the Corporation should give the proposed financial assistance, but this proposal was rejected, not so much because the members were hostile to the lending of the money, but because it was thought desirable to obtain further information before coining to a final decision. Eventually a sub- committee was appointed to make certain inquiries. The inquiries have relation to the measure of representa- tion on the directorate the Company will be prepared to concede to the Corporation should the advance be made; and to the terms on which the Corporation might be able to borrow the money it.is proposed to advance. The sub-committee was instructed to submit its report to a further meeting of the General Purposes Committee to be held a week hence.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Latchford Hospital, on Saturday, touching the death of Samuel White, aged 32, of 45, Sewell-st., Runcorn. Mr. R. D. Maddock, of Messrs. Jol!life and Maddock, solici- tors, Runcorn, watched the proceedings on behalf of the relatives of the deceased.—Henry Taylor, who is em- ployed at the Old Quay, Runcorn, said that early on Thursday morning, the deceased entered the engine house, and while replacing a dubbin can under the en- gine, the belt of the engine broke and struck him on the head. Witness had examined the belt twenty minutes previously, and found nothing wrong. It had broken a fortnight ago, and had been repaired by witness and the engine man with rivets, It broke where it had been re- paired.—Evidence having been given to the effect that deceased died on the night of the accident, the jury re- turned a verdict of " Accidental death." A RUNCORN LAD KILLED ON THE SHIP CANAL. On Monday afternoon Mr. T. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, Con- cerning the death at the hospital on Saturday night, of Wm. Parker, aged 13 years, a greaser on the Ship Canal, and son of George Parker, labourer, residing at 65 Sur- rey-st., Runcorn. Mr. Newman, solicitor of the firm of Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., Manchester, represented the Ship Canal Co. Alice Parker, the deceased's mother, said on Saturday morning he left home about a quarter past five to go to work at Weston. He had worked about five weeks on the canal. She heard of the acci- dent on Saturday afternoon. James Mather, 75 Surrey- st.,Runcorn,a lad aged 16,a greaser employed at Weston Point, said he left work for home with the deceased and two ether boys, Mather and Johnson at one o'clock on Saturday. At Weston Park they saw the " mail " train which conveyed the workmen to their homes. Johnson said "there's the mail coming ; let's get on and ride home." They all said "yes." and Parker went to the first truck and got hold of it to get on, and witness got on to the last. Parker missed his hold, and fell un- der the second truck, the wheels of which went over him, cutting his legs almost off.—By Mr. Newell: There were certain stopping places for the " mail " for passen- gers to get on.—W. Johnson, aged 15,a greaser, corrobor- ated Mather's statement, and admitted suggesting that they should get on to the train, though he said he did not attempt to get on, because the driver shouted to them not to do so, and he did not try to prevent his companions from doing so because he thought they heard the driver shout. When the deceased was run over witness sig- nalled to the driver to atop and the train was stopped, and the deceased taken at once to the hospital.—The Coroner strongly rebuked Johnson for suggesting to the other boys to get on to the waggons.—Frederick Shaw, labourer, who had been riding in the "mail," gave evi- dence. He said the deceased's legs after he was run over were hanging by the skin only. He brought him to the hospital. He was unconsclous.—Alfred Bullock, the driver, deposed to shouting to the lads to keep off. The deceased fell through not getting proper hold of the ladder up the side of the waggon. The train was going about five miles an hour.—By Mr. Newman : He had instructions to prevent lads getting on except when the train stopped.—The Coroner, in summing up, observed that Johnson wanted to pose as a very good boy, though. he brought the other lads into mischief. He hoped the sad occurrence would be a warning to lads, and men also, not to attempt to get on to the trains while in motion.—& verdict of accidental death was immediately returned.

ANOTHER DEEMING. A dreadful discovery was made at Oldham on Wed' nesday. At ten o'clock in the morning Mr. Jobs Walker, who owns some property in Hollins-road, had occasion to visit it. He found the house, 412, Hollins - road, tenanted by a man named Joseph Mellor, a twiner minder at Melrose Mill, Butler-green, locked. Mellor, who is about 40 years old, had lived there with his wife. On looking through the window Mr. Walker's suspicions were aroused by seeing that the flagged flooring had been disturbed, and at once went to the Police-constable Anbrook, who lives near, and informed him of what he had seen. Anbrook went with Mr. Walker and a water- man named Booth to the house, and by forcine'oPen the window of the kitchen, obtained an entrance. 'The first thing that drew their attention was a large hole dug.in the centre of the back kitchen floor. The flags with I which the place was covered had been taken up and a hole dug about the length and breadth of an ordinary grave and about three feet deep. The flags had heel; placed at the side and covered with the soil brought Oa' of the trench. On looking round Anbrook found a woman's corset covered with blood and penetrated' in several places as though with a knife. 131°°d was found in several parts of the kitchen, and under the stairs the party came across a woman's body. Tirl throat was cut and there were four stabs on the le" , breast. Anbrook immediately placed a guard over the house and went for Joseph Mellor, whom he found work- ing as though nothing unusual had occurred, and eOll- - veyed him to the Central Police-station. In the mean- time the chief-constable and other officers arrived (in the scene, which is about a couple of miles from the centre) of the town. They found the place as described, and the smell being unbearable disinfectants were seat for. By this time the startling discovery • ecame noised about, and attracted large crowds of people. On Mr. Peacock, the Chief-Constable, making an examination of the house he came across a large carving knife covered with blood. A medical examination of the body revealed that the head had almost been cut off. There w rre alae • found four wounds in the left breast about the region of the heart. The woman was half-dressed, and the b0(1.7 was covered over with carpet. The doctor gave opinion that the crime must have been committed several weeks ago. The neighbours state that the lAA time the woman was seen was on September 2nd. There was also found en the premises a barrel of quicklime. On VVedner h day morning, in reply to the question from one of - 1 fellow workers, Mellor said that he had just received letter from his wife stating that her mother was rather better and that she was coming home shortly. gelll did not appear to be at all surprised when called out 0 the room at Melrose Mill, where he was employed O' being informed that he was "wanted" on suspicion 0_ having murdered his wife, he at once expressed a desire that he should be taken to the Police Station in a cal's' A conveyance was obtained and he was driven to till Town Hall. div.head: SELECTED READINGS.
div.p: SELECTED READINGS.

ME USE o FLOWERS.—FIowers are used much More sensibly than they used to be. The absurd fashion of loading a woman down with a dozen or more huge bouquets, every one measuring from • SfA.epie swenty incluse across, lane longer in vogue. Theatra6ons custom died of its own inappropriate- ness. It is possible 'even with the most delicate blossom, which are the essence of grace and refine- ment, to be positively vulgar. The large corsage bouquets, which were so popular for two or three Years, seem to have vanished, not to reappear, from the very fact of their oversize mid overuse. This is true as well of the bunch of flowers for the street dress as for the ball toilet. Flowers are not so worn bec iuse of their wide and exaggerated use, when , the ygot out of the hands of women of taste and re- finement, into those of the sort who bleach their hair and daub their faces. The fashionables now Permit themselves only a bunch of violets in the Spring, when a craving for flowers cannot be stifled. More colouring is used in funeral flowers than ever before. Set pieces are no longer used; loose flowers furnished by members of the family are the only ones considered appropriate. This is a sensible departure. Why should the stiff, waxen camellias and the tube-rose be always used? To some sensi- tive minds these flowers are so associated with death that, seen at any time, they only recall a scene of mourning. Flowers at a funeral are intended to console the living with their loving touch and gracious softening of the grim outlines; there is more tenderness in the droop of one La France rose than in forty stiff, inodorous Japonicas. , A SENSIBLE Womex.—Sbe takes a healthy interest in her neighbours, but she is by no means a gossip, still less a scandal-monger. At no time Will she be brought into the folly of discussing Motives, or judging of things by the seamy side of aPPearances. And if persistently bored by those Who find a pleasure in seeing all things at cross purposes and all people more or less scoundrels undetected, she does her best to naitigate what she cannot prevent. She has strong principles, but she is not an active proselytizer. tale lets others think for themselves, and, 13111 y when called on to testify, raises her awn private flag aloft. She knows the dif- ference between constancy and aggression, Which, with the courage of her opinions, has also the modesty of reticence. She treats her servants as, in a certain sense, her friends, her children, While still keeping the reins of home government in her own hands. But they all know that when they do their duty she will reward them, or, at least, recognise by kind word and hearty acknowledgment that they have done well, and when they neglect it She will rebuke them. She will be neither indifferent on the one side, nor remiss on the other; and thus her household always feels and knows that her eyes are open and her heart is warm.

There are some who never seem to believe themselves capable °I anything; they see others press forward to attempt and achieve, and shrink back into a desponding inactivity. Having no faith in them- selves, they undertake nothing and effect nothing. If they are convicted of some fault or bad habit, thEIY have so little hope of being able to cure it that they scarcely make an effort. If some avenue Of usefulness and honour opens up before them, they draw back, almost sure that they should not lalcceed, and decline to enter. If some duty presses ,Urgently upon their conscience, they try to quiet tte nremptings by pleading inability. Thus their 'lves pass away in uselessness, their faculties do not develop, or their characters improve, their abilities are wasted, they dwindle into insignificance, and ail this, not for lack of power, but for the want of 1„4 confidence and courage that would set that power into good practical working order. A person in the west of Scotland, who flia engaged in the manufacture of a certain description of goods, then recently intrOduced into that part of the country, found it necessary, or conjectured it might be profitable, to establish a permanent con- nection with some respectable mercantile house in London. With this design he packed up a quantity of goods, equipped himself for the journey, and departed. He travelled on foot to the metropolis. Upon his arrival, he made diligent inquiry as to those who were likely to prove his best customers; and, accordingly, proceeded to call upon one of the most opulent drapers, with whom he resolved to establish a regular correspondence. When Saunders entered the draper's shop, he found it crowded with purchasers, and the clerks all bustling busily at the back of the counter, handing out their several wares to their respective customers. Saunders waited, what he thought, a reasonable length of time, then laid down his pack, his bonnet, and staff, upon the counter, and inquired, in his broad Scotch dialect, for "the head o' the house." One of the clerks asked what he wanted. The Scotchman's answer was, as usual, a question: "Want ye ought i' my line, sir ?" "No," was the prompt reply of the person interrogated, who accompanied his monosyllabic negative with a look of contempt for the mean appearance of the itinerant Scotch mer- chant. "Will ye no tak a look o' the gudes, sir ?" was Saunders's next query. "No, not at all; I have not time," replied the clerk; "take them away—take them away." "Ye 'll alblins [perhaps] find them worth your while; and I doubtna but ye 'll buy," said Saunders, as he coolly proceeded to untie and unstrip his burden. "Go away, go away," was reiterated half a dozen times with great impatience; but the persevering Scotchman still persisted. "Get along, you old Scotch fool," cried the clerk, completely out of temper, as he pushed the already exposed contents of the pack off the counter; "get along." Saunders looked up in the individual's face with a wide mouth and an enlarged pair of eyes, then looked down to his estate that lay scattered among his feet; looked up again, and ex- claimed, "And wull ye no really buy ought; but ye dinna ken; ye hae'na seen the gudes yet ;" and so saying, he slowly gathered them up, and replaced them on the counter. "Get out of the shop, sir," was the peremptory and angry command that fol- lowed his last appeal. Saunders, with great gravity and self-possession, said, "Are ye in earnest, frien' ?" "Yes, certainly," was the reply, and that reply was succeeded by an unequivocal proof of sincerity on the part of the person wko made it, when he picked up Saunders's bonnet, and whirled it out into the street. The cool Scotchman stalked deliberately and gravely in quest of his Stewarton "head-gear. After giving it two or three hearty slaps upon the wall without the door, he re-entered very com- posedly wringing the moisture out of it, looked over to the person who had served him so, and said, with a geninne Scotch smile, " Yon was but an ill-faured turn, man; yell surely tak a look o' the gudes noo." The master draper himself, who was standing all the while in the shop, admiring the patience and perservance of the old man, and feeling a little compunction for the unceremonious manner in which he had been treated, examined the contents of the pack, found them to be articles he stood in need of, purchased them, ordered an additional regular supply, and thns laid the foundation of an opulent mercantile house that has now flourished for some generations.

div.head: PARISIAN BARBER'S BOY.
div.p: THE PARISIAN BARBER'S BOY.

There was once a gentleman in Paris, who was the terror of all the barbers' boys, as one whom it was next to impossible to shave, and who was yet so extremely fastidious about his beard that he would have killed any barber who left a single hair standing on his chin. As he paid largely, the master barber whom he generally employed was anxious to keep his custom. But then he could scarcely get a garcon who had a heart stout enough to encounter a task which threatened such con- sequences. A Gasson at length presented himself, who, being informed of the great difficulty of the business, and the wrath which the gentleman generally fell into on being ill-shaved, declared lustily that, thouczh he were the devil himself, he would not be afraid to try his hand upon him. He went to the gentleman, who, opening his great eyes upon him, saw a man of good stature, and who had all the appearance of one who had seen much of the world. Indeed, the gentleman was a good deal struck at first with the mien and countenance of the Gagnon. "My good fellow," said he, "are you aware that I am very ill to shave ? " "Oh, yes," said the Gascon readily; "but I also know that I am a thousand times more expert than you are difficult." So, with- out giving his customer time to think further, he applied the napkin to his neck, Laid his razors on the table, and began to shave with such exquisite nicety that the patient scarcely felt him touch the skin. From time to time he quitted his work, and raised his eyes to heaven, as if invoking a blessing from the Almighty upon his work. The gentleman was surprised at his conduct, and asked what a prayer to God should signify in shaving. "A prayer," said the pious barber, "is a good thing at all times." "Very true," said the gentleman bluntly; "but I wish you would remit your prayer till another time." "No time so good," said the Gascon, "as when one feels he has need of it." "How," cried the gentleman, mere bluntly still; "how can there be need for praying just now?" "If you really wish me to tell you," said the shaver, "I will. It is because I feel at this moment a violent temptation which I can scarcely get the better of—a temptation to cut your throat." "The devil I" exclaimed the patient; "a temptation to cut my throat I" and his colour rose to a pitch unexampled on even that fiery countenance. "Get you gone, you rascal, if you do not wish to be thrown over the window." "Softly, softly," said the Gascon, with great coolness; "I have overcome the temptation, and will now proceed with my work without more disturbance." "You scoundrel cried the ahatee, his rage still inc.-easing "begone, If you wish to save your life." The Gascon only replied with greater coolness than before, "I am not afraid of you; if I pleased, I cou'd shave you in spite of yourselt. But what signifies it after all? If you wish to have only the half of your beard done, I bid you good day." The gentleman was actually so much subdued by the firmness of the man, as to permit him to depart with the last word. When the Gascon got back to the shop, he said to his master, "Yon told me that this gentleman would storm if a si')gle hair was left on his visage; I found him quite in another humour to-day; he has made me leave half of his beard unshaven."

div.head: RULING PASSION STRONG IN DEATH.
div.p: RULING PASSION STRONG IN DEATH.

A late German newspaper related the following anecdote :—ln an imperial city, lately, a criminal was condemned to be beheaded, who had a singular itching to play at nine-pins. While his sentence was pronouncing, he bad the temerity to offer a request to be permitted to play once more at his favourite game at the place of execution, and then, he said, he would submit without a raurmur. As the last prayer of a dying man, his request was granted. When arrived at the solemn scot, he found everything prepared, the pins being set up and the bowl being ready. He played with no little earnestness, but the sheriff at length, seeing that he showed no inclination to desist, paivately ordered the executioner to strike the fatal blow as be stooped for the bowl. The executioner did so, and the head dropped into the culprit's hand, as he raised himself to see what had occurred. He Immediately aimed at the nine, conceiving it was the bowl which he gra.ped. All nine falling, the head loudly exclaimed, "Well, I have won the game."—This reminds us of a story which has been told in proof of the amazing dexterity of the German executioners in cutting off heads with the sabre. A culprit being bound and prepared for the blow, and not feeling it when it came, coolly asked the man what hindered him, since the signal had been duly given. "Shake yourself," said the I executioner; and, on the criminal doing so, his head, which had been severed but not displaced, tumbled on the scaffold.
