div.p: iC ettero to tbt Obitor.
EIGHT HOURS FOR MINERS.
Sir,-

Eight hours' work, Oght hours' play, Eight hours' sleep, and eight bob a day, was the victorious labour war note first sung by our Australian brethren about fifty years since. And, lam Convinced, that in the near future, England will triumphantly send the echo back again And all the labouring world ere long will join in the achieve- ment of the eight hours, if not of the eight bob a day. As Carlyle profoundly said "The condition of the major- ity of the people of a country, is the condition of the country itself." Where the eight hours is not now in force, the rest of the horny-handed sons of toil are an the move for it, which is an infallible sign of its accom- plishment. Let" Cyrnro," and all his class, read much, and think deeper, about the signs of the times. The mercury in the glass of time shows the storm is coming before it overtakes us. Wise men, see it ; fools, heed not, nor prepare for it. Labour International Congres- ses, payment of members of Parliament, one man, one vote, nationalisation of the land, are signs that the voice of the people is the voice of GA. "Men do not deny their Christ, but they sell Him," deplored Ruskin. True, Ruskin ; and they still clamour for Barabbas the Robber, and put him on the throne, as France did, or , send him to make the laws in his own favour as England has too long done, and feeds her children with sour grapes, that have set their teeth on an edge. And they are crying' aloud for an eight hours working day to be made sure by law. But Barabbaa again, as of yere, wants to rob the over-worked labourer of the needful boon. If an eight hours working day , in the mines is long enough, and essential to health, sr,c., it ought to be secured by some means. Then why not make it sure and binding by legal enac..ment P The late Professor Thorold Rogers states emphatically that in the fifteenth century the working day was eight hours. But robbers of the Barabbas tribe effected a change, until, in 1817, even children had to " work in the mills for fifteen or sixteen hours a day," twice as long as " Cymro " wants personally to work. His class have good wages, can support their Trades' Union, and so keep up a high rate of wages, whick I hope they will always be able to maintain, and get as few hours per day as they ought to have, for health, &c. But it is heartless to oppose other labouring classes having such advantages. His type are our worst foes, and their own also. They put out their own eyes, and then cry as " Cymro " does. He "Cannot see how the vast army of the poorest class of men can be brought under organisa- tion as to any number of hours." Then he says, we must not let" any Government tinkering in the busi- ness—no penal enactments." So that he cannot see that Trades Unions can accomplish an eight hours system. In " Cymro's " logic the case is boneless. The bless- ings of the Ten Hours Act, &c., accomplished by legal enactment hitherto, teach " Cymro " and his class no- thing but opposition and despair. Has the Empire been commercially rained by the passing of the Ten Hours Bill? Are the wages of the toiling masses less since it passed? Are the people worse fed, clothed, or worse housed? All " Cvmro's " doubtful contentions were urged against the whole of the legal enactments for the shortening of the hours of labour hitherto, and history has given them the lie. The wealth of the Empire is in too few hands, that spin not, nor work for what they have. Are we then to continue helpless in the hands of Barabbas ? who defrauds the labourer of his just hire. No, the cries of them that have laboured have" entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth." " Be ye also patient, establish your hearts ; for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh." Whatever is just and right, will triumph, for the God of law, orders justice, and love, whose hand is on the lever which moves the world, gives no high-toned cravings to men to mock them, but for self-preservation.
Cymro," let history teach thee more, Study Nature's unerring store, One Element in all is found, One God, who brings perfection round.

div.head: Yours faithfully, RICEIARD STOREY. Oct. 18th,1892. 160, Orford-lane, Warrington.
div.p: Yours faithfully, RICEIARD STOREY. Oct. 18th,1892. 160, Orford-lane, Warrington.
THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.

Sir,—Your issue of the 15th inst. contains a letter from R. Storey. He heads it with the query" Why not obtain a legal eight hours day ?" For a more satisfac- tory reply than I can give, let him ask the Durham miners, or the railway workers, or, if I must answer, I can only say as they do—" It will not work."

He charges me with rint; from my concealment,under the pretence of friendship and goodwill, on all those struggling victims, hard and overworked miners. I can assure him that I have as much sympathy—practical sympathy—with the miners and other hard-worked people as ever he has. Where then, is the pretence he talks of ? Nowhere, but in the distorted imagination of a splenetic mind. He says " Cvmro " prides himself on 'knowing something of coal-getting—its difficulties and dangers." True, Ido know something, but I do not pride myself on such knowledge, and if Mr. Storey's letter was as free from spleen as my letter was from pride, it would read more like common sense. Another distorted statement, quite destitute of fact— that I oppose a legal eight hours day "on the mere base £ s. d. ground." Very good, Mr. Storey, if there were no other, this would be a very strong ground—this base Es. d. As it is, we cannot do without it. I doubt not Mr. Storey is as fond of the base £ s. d. as any other man—notwithstanding its baseness. He charges me with false pretences, pride, and baseness. He has copied a great part of my letter, and made hist extracts a peg whereon to hang a doleful string of baseless charges and socialistic cant. He says I complain that the world is getting more lazy than formerly. This again is a misconstruction ; I have made no complaint. I have asked a simple ques- tion and uttered no complaint. Did I touch a sore place in asking that question ? Does the galled jade wince? I ask that question again in all seriousness and deliberation ; and seriously and deliberately I say there are a great many people in the world who are not ashamed of parading their laziness. If they could. they would persuade or coerce the rest of the world to follow them • and when Mr. Storey says that I oppose the eight hours day, or any measure for the amelioration of my fellow toilers, he is deliberately wrong. What I oppose if there is any force in words, is the legal enactment of any number of hours as a day's work for adult man- hood. _

He advises me to think deeper than to taunt Jack with wanting to be as good as his master. I have uttered no tatint. Why, may I ask, should he not be as gsod and in many cases better than his master? What does the • man mean by thinking deeper? I believe I have thought out this subject to a better end than Mr. Storey. I have for many years advised my fellow- workmen to adjure the drink shop and the betting book. to study the political history of their .country and to find out which of the two great parties in the State has passed mast measures for his political and social advancement. Why should not Jack be as well behaved and as intelligent as his master? He may not have the wealth, " the base £ s. d." that his master has, but he may have that which wealth can never purchase—a goiid character, a conscience void of offence towards God, and the respect of his fellow-men. Mr. Storey asks—why should the men who sink the shaft, hew the coal, spin the silk, &c., &c., ad infinitunt. Why should they not, I ask, do all this if they are paid for it ; and why live in hovels if they have work and wages? I never have lived in a bevel, and why should an industrious sober man, with any respect for himself and regard for his family, live in a hovel ? If he is a competent workman and sober, having work and health, he can make it worth while for his employer to keep him, and see that he earns good wages. Mr. Storey launches out into a string of social- istic phrases which I cannot follow or endorse. His theological peroration may be sublime, but I cannot soar to such heights. lam of the earth earthy, and can only behold and wonder. Still I think there is a good deal of claptrap and humbug about it. Given an eight hours day by law established and Mr. Story may be ookmg out for an inspectorship, or he may turn in former, and rummage every working place from found- ation to ridgetile,and woe betide the unlucky wight who may be caught encroaching on the ninth hour.

What about the great army of domestic servants? Has Mr. S. no sympathy for them? What about our wives? Are they to knock off at eight hours, and not get tea ready when we get home from work ? And serve us right too. Shall the baby be left to cry in the cradle because the mother's eight hours are up ? This is not Jack as good as his int -ter, but Gill as good as her master. He must find her a substitute when her eight hours are up, and if the lords of creation are to be free with eight hours why not the ladies ? They are the weaker vessel—and if the lord's back and limbs ache with the terrible exertion of fatigue of the day, hew must the lady feel? Cannot she follow suit, and go to the legislature for legal protection and reduced hours ? She has as much right to legiilative protection as ever the man has, but then she is" only a woman." Anxiously awaiting your Saturday's issue with the solution of all these to me inexplicable problems, lam, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, October 17, 1892.
CYAIRO.
A LESSON FOR ".t LEARNER."

Sir,—The opinions of a man (?) who dare not back them with his name—are worthless—very much less, caeteris paribus, than those that are so backed. The us of a pen-name is quite admissible when discussing gen- eral principles; but if we wishto descend to vituperation we ought to do it above eur own signatures. He who does otherwise is less than a man, and is distinctly not a gentleman. Your not too brilliant correspondent, " A Learner,' has an excellent memory. He cannot forget that I once likened him to a too ripe red herring leaving its malo- dorous trail across the track of our argument. Now memory is often in inverse ratio to intellectual capacity. Not seldem is the meanest capacity coupled with a retentive memory. A mind to which the simplest pro- position is an intransitive porta astnorttm, may yet be the storehouse of a multitude of trifling, details:

As far as I am able to follow the " ccnfusion worse confounded" in his latest lucubration—which would be much improved by smelling more of the oil—he imagines that because animals act in accordance with certain physical laws—which also affect man in his natural savage state—that man, in his present state, must be actuated solely by these laws. Now is it not evident to the merest tyro that man by assuming a higher intellec- tual status—with the advantages therefrom accruing— has also assumed higher moral responsibility, a respon- sibility to himself, to society, and to " the Power, not ourselves that makes for righteousness ?" " A Learner" is too backward in his studies. to know anything about moral evolution; else he would know that man has advanced—that this advance has come about by some 'form of evolution, and that it is impossible to conceive that his moral faculties have been left out in the cold by this agency of improvement ! Is man, because he shares with the animals certain merely animal functions, there Ifore merely an animal ? He is an animal plus certain moral and intellectual faculties—capable still further of improvement. Hence will appear the utter puerlity of " A Learner's" dictum :—" The Agnostic Evolutionist,' In order to be consistent, should destroy all such unfortunates by death." That is the weak and dying must be put to death as being unfitted for life. But the Agnostic does not take upon himself to judge as to who is and who is not so fitted; he is content to leave our com- mon mother to do that, and she does it very effectually. , It is the natural savage man whe thus assumes nature's prerogative; when he rises to become an Agnostic and an Evolutionist, he ceases to do this or anything so immoral. One essential feature in the Agnostic creed is —" Be happy—make others so." And this they try to effect not by striving to attain to illusory "mansions in the sky "or in avoiding its equally illusory antithesis,but by paying better attention to the more important and imperative—" Now." While the last paragraph of " A Learner's "letter con- tains no such "very serious difficulty "as he imagines, it does contain something timt justifies my contention that man has no moral right to torture animals for any purpose—that, if experiments on the Hy mg body be per- -1 missible, man should select the victims solely from hisi own species. If—as I quite believe—the lowest man is lower in the scale of intelligence than the highest 1 animal—why should the latter be immolated on the altar of scientific butchery, while the thing with the form, but without the soul or sentiments of a man is exempt? I ask where or from whence does man get his rFght to kill either one or the other ? All living creatures have one invaluable and irreplaceable possession— life. To kill creatures, rich only in this and their capacity for its enjoyment, may be a justifiable necessity. But the right to kill, if it exists, does not confer the right of torture. Finally, if the lower rungs of the human ladder are to be the subjects for vivisection, my advice as a "Sage" to "A Learner," as a tyro is" Be Sage, and Rue in Thyme."—l am, Sm., Penketh, October 16th, 1892.

div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

The monthly meeting of Runcorn Free Library Committee was held on Wednesday morning at the Town Hall. Mr. T. Riley presided, and the re were present Messrs. W. M. Sowerby, F. Wis wall, W. Leach, W. Hankinson, W. J. Grice, and J. D. Jones (librarian). The librarian reported that there had been 1801 issues during September, classified as follows : —Theology, 36, philosophy, 10, science, 52, history, 113 poetry, 22, fiction, 1392, miscellaneous, 178.—Mr. Sowerby moved the following resolution, 'That the Free Public Libtary Committee, recognising the need of books of a technical character in the various branches of science, which would be invaluable in promoting the technical education of the youths of Runcorn, but which their funds will not enable them to purchase without crippling the general work of the library, request the Commissioners to make a special grant for this purpose out of the funds which they hold for technical education." Mr. Sowerby spoke of the great value that literature on technical subjects would be to the youths who were studying in the various classes, and said the, Committee as far as their limited income would permit them, and without injuring the other departments of the Library, had purch- qed a number of books of this description. There were, however, some very expensive books which they could not afford to obtain, which ought to be in the library for the use of students, and he urged that the Committee had claim upon the funds in the hands of the local authority for the purposes of technical Instruction—Mr. H. J. Grice seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Leach. —Mr. Wiswall explained the financial position of the Commissioners in relation to technical education. The Commissioners were endeavouring to save all the money they could for the purpose of building the Technical Institute, and he deprecated any attempt to get money from them for other purposes, because such a course I would injure the prospects of the proposed institution., The important thing to aim at was to get the institute built, so that they would have a suitable place in which I to teach and train students of technical subjects. Be did not oppose Mr. Sowerby's proposition, but he did not see how he could support it at the Board under the circumstances. The Commissioners had now practically £1,500 offered to them for the Institute—£soo from the County Council, and £l,OOO, or more frcm the Depart- ment of Science and Art. There were also other offers made, and the practical result was that for every pound contributed by the public of Runcorn for the Technical Institute, the Commissioners would get another pound, so that every pound subscribed really meant two. Be depicted the immense benefits which would arise from the institute, and urged the ratepayers to support it by every means in their power. He suggested that Mr. Sowerby's resolution should be amended by the addition of the words, "or to endeavour to obtain a grant of £5O from the County Council for that purpose.' This sug- gestion was agreed to,and the resolution as amended was carried.

div.head: -•-• ANOTHER DARING BURGLARY.
div.p: -•-• ANOTHER DARING BURGLARY.

THE 'LADDER" THIEVES AGAIN. A daring burglary took place on Wednesday night at Longford Hall, Stretford, near Manchester, the residence of Mrs. Rylands, whose purchase :of the Althorp library recently came into note. On Wednesday night. Mrs. Rylands, who is the widow of a well-known Manchester merchant of vast wealth, was away from the house, which was in charge of the servants. A ladder seems to have been placed against a bedroom window, and access was thereby gained to Mrs. Rylands's room which was ransacked and plundered. Jewellery to the value of £2,000 and other valuables were taken. The thieves fastened the outer door of the hall to prevent egress from the premises if an alarm had been raised, but no one discovered the burglary. The police believe the bur- glary to be the work of an accomplished gang, who had carefully matured their plans.

div.head: COTTON TRADE CRISIS.
div.p: THE COTTON TRADE CRISIS.

HEYWCOD. On Wednesday notices were posted at about a dozen i mills n Heywood stating that the operatives wages will be reduced five per cent, on the 7th of next month. The operatives will resist the proposed reduction, and they are now paying increased levies to their societies, which are preparing for an extended stoppage.

STALTBRIDGB. At a special meeting on Wednesday night the Staly- bridge Operative Spinners Association resolved to pay a special levy of 23. a week above the levies now in force to the central account. Manchester. The payment is for three weeks up to the sth November, and in the event of a strike taking place the levy will be increased to 4s. a week. A meeting of piecers was also held, and it was agreed to pay a contribution of 6d. for full timers, and 3d. a week to half timers.
Cholera is reported to be raging at Sanchow, in China, and carrying of hundreds of victims daily,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1892.

Warrtington,there was no man in the long list of men who had stood for their suffrages who had so commended himself to them as he litd done in the recent election. They felt that while his defeat must have been a dis- appointment to him it was an irreparable loss to them— that if they could only have returned him to Parliament he would have conferred upon their town by his repre- sentation of it, a lustre of which none of them had had any idea. They believed that the Liberals of England had lost through his defeat—(hear, hear)—that the Government had lost through it—(hear, hear)—and they sincerely hoped that the opportunity would offer itself by which his undoubted ability and great experi- ence might be taken advantage of, for the benefit of the legislature, and the amelioration of the condition of the people across the water. He was sure there was not a man in the party thi oughout the borough who did not feel that if Dr. Houston could be of assistance to him in any capacity he would willingly and gladly do it. Therefore, although that meeting brought to a climax the efforts of many months, it by no means con- cluded the acquaintance which was begun a few months ago. They would take great interest in watch- ing his future, and would only be too pleased whenever the opportunity occurred for him to take his natural place in the House of Commons, and whatever they could do in any way for him they would de as for a man , whom they respected and loved. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: PRESENTATION TO DR. HOUSTON. INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO DR. HOUSTON. INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS.

On Thursday afternoon a deputation from the Warrington Liberal Association met Dr. Houston, Q.C., by appointment at the Queen Hutel, Chester, tor the purpose of making a presentation to him on behalf of the association, in expression of their appreciation of his high character and of the admir- able manner in which he conducted his recent electoral contest in Warrington. The deputation consisted of Mr. John Hylands, J.P., president of the a 'dation, Councillor H. Fleming, president of the Lioeral Club, Councillor H. Roberts, hon. secretary to the association, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, hon., treasurer, Mr. Thomas Birchall, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. George Clay. Mr. James Tomkinson, late Liberal Candidate for the Eddisbury Division was also present. Mr. William Pierpoint, Chairman of the Executive was prevented by indisposition from attending, and a blank had been left for his signa- ture to an address to be presented to Dr. Houstor. The presentation was to have taken place in the Winwick-street Co-operative Hall, Warring- ton, but it was thought that considering the pre- valence of disease in that neighbourhood it would not be advisable to hold the meeting there. It was therefore decided to have the ceremony at Chester. On reaching the hotel the deputation were most cordi- ally received by Dr. Houston, and ushered iato his private room, where luncheon was provided for the ccmpany, prior to which being partaken of the cere- mony took place. PRESENTA l'IoN SPEECHES.

Councillor H. ROBERTS invited Mr. Rylands to make the presentation. Mr. RYLANDS said: Dr. Houston, I have great pleasure in doing anything in the way of expressing our grati- tude to you, and in the first instance I will, as requested, read the address to you. Mr. Ryland; then read the following illuminated address contained in a handsome album, and which was as follows To Arthur Houston, Esq., Q.C., Liberal candidate for the Parliamentary borough of Warrington, general elec- tion, 1892. Dear Sir,—On behalf of the Liberals of War- rington, and in testimoty of our sincere regard, we desire your acceptance of this address and the accom- panying cheque. As a Liberal candidate for the borough, you conducted the recent campaign always with cour- tesy and tact, and displayed a zeal and energy which were only equalled by the exceptional eloquence and ability with which, on every possible occasion, you championed the great principles of justice and freedom. Not only to you personally do we feel ourseives laid under the deepest obligation,tmt to Mrs. Houston, your charm- ing and devoted helpmeet, who contributed so largely to the interest and enjoyment of our meetings, and by her example stimulated others to greater efforts. For our party, we desire to accord our warmest gratitude. We hope that before long you may attain that high position in the legislature of our empire which your great at- tainments so eminently qualify you to hold, and which your earnest and disinterested attachment to the cause of political progress so justly merits. Signed John Fylands, president of Warrington Liberal Association, C. Jackson Holmes, hon. treasurer' Henry Roberts, hon. secretary, John Crosfield, Thomas Starkey Smith, John Walker, Charles J. Holmes, J. Rymer Young, John H. ' Gornall, Julian Winser, J. Shaw Green, William Roberts, Henry Thornton, William Beswick, George Holford, Joseph Mounfield, Saml. Dunbobbin, Jos. Atkinson,VV.m. Hefty Hurst, Arthur H. Lee, Joseph S. Garland, James Procter Jones, Joseph Titchett, D. 0. Sullivan, Joseph Longland, Thomas Grime, James Strange, John Toft, ' Edward Moore, Charles Lyon, Matthew Knowles, H. C. Jones, John S. Hill, George Clay, George Weaver, E. J. Guest, Thomas Birchen, P. Caldwell, W. H. Dutton, Edwin Jc:m Mitchell, Ziba Armitage, Robert H. Pear- son, John Yenge, J. H. Fleming, T. B. Kiernan, F. Jen- kins, Ben.' Thomas Hawthorne, James Dodds, A. H. Crosfield,Samuel Dunr, Arthur Browne, William Win- stanley, Edward Pickavnnce, Robert Garnett, Thomas Morris, F.G.S.

Mr. RYIANDS prcceeded : Well, sir, I have during my political life freqtkntly been in a minority, and I have had the satisfaction of finding that with patience that minority generally turne3 into a majority. I could give you a large number of instances, but you know them quite as well as I do, in which the Liberal' party have had to fight a long battle, but have always Is ad victory in the end. The history of the Warrington Parliamentary elections has shown that at one time the Liberals were in the minority, and at other times in the majority, and I think in Warrington the great difficulty we have is with the publicans. I think the first time I saw you I mentioned that. However, you were bold, and I must say I was sanguine. I thought that there was teally a wave in the right direction. We never could calculate how far that wave would carry us, but I fully anticipnted that it was possible, especially as we had the Irish with us, that we should win by a small majority. However, I did not allow enough for the the drink interest, which, I am sorry to say, appears to be increasing rather than decreasirg. However, we fought as well as we could, but unfortunately we could not command success, though you, sir, endeared your- self to us, and conducted your contest in a way which astonished us all, and personally I feel disappointed and grieved at the defeat. I have pleasure in presentinr, you these with our best and kindest regards to yourself and Mrs. Houston. Mr. Rylands than, amidst applause, handed to Dr. Houston the album, and a cheque for a handsome sum.

Mr. Summit', said he must say that of all the public men he had met in his lifetime he thought Dr. Houston had made a deeper impression on him than any man in a similar position. As a politician he admired him through- out the contest, and he had carried it out in a manly and a splendid manner. He did not believe the bitterest of his opponents could put his finger upon a single blot in the whole campaign, and say he had done anything unworthy as a man and a gentleman. It was an old saying that a man did not make real friends after 40, but with regard to Dr. Houston he himself felt after 60, a deep friendship and respect, and affection that he believed would never be obliterated as long as he lived. The past campaign, though it had ended in defeat, was, he believed, not all loss. He believed it had made Dr. Houston such a reputation as a politician that eventually —probably before very long—they should see him tak- ing his natural place in the House of Commons. With regard to Mrs. Houston, he believed there was only one feelirg, that of gratitude to, and admiration of, her as a woman of a most genial character, and admirable capa- city; and he was sure that the memory both of Dr. and Mrs. Houston would be long cherished in Warrington. He believed the doctor had made many hundreds, he might say thousands, of friends, who would always think of him with a sincere respect and affection. (Applause.) Dr. GORNALL said he could only reiterate what Mr. Birchall had said, and say that next to the death of the late Mr. McMinnies, he did not think anything cut him so much as the defeat of Dr. Houston. He should feel it all his life, because his ambition as a politician had been to live in a town represented by a Liberal ; and, as far as he could see in the near future, Warrington was doomed merely to represent the drink ti—ffic and that alone, he was afraid. With regard to Mrs. Houston, he could only say that she had endeared herself to every- one, and though he regretted more particularly the villainous expressions made use of by the Tory party towards her and Dr. Houston, he believed that the pre- sent member for Warrington expressed himself in such a kindly manner concerning them, at the Mayor's dinner, the other night, that he might forget their villainy for ever.

Mr. FLEMING said he as ranch as anyone regretted the loss Dr. Houston had sustained in Warrington. He sup- posed they must go on struggling. Dr. Houston was about the finest example of a man they had ever had to fight their battle in Warrington, and he did not see that they were likely to find such another. To his good lady they were indebted very much. She was a noble example of a woman. He wished Dr. Houston long life and prosperity. He also wished him some high post, which he was sure his attainments would lead to before long. _

Mr. CIAy said he re-echoed the remarks passed by the previous speakers. He had heard expressions on all sides, as to the gallant fight Dr. Houston had made. Although he did not succeed, he laid the foundation for future success. The moral tone and eloquence of his sneecties, had raised the standard of politics in Warrington ; and he thought there was no doubt that on some future occasion, a Liberal candidate would succeed.

Mr. HOLMES said he agreed entirely with the ex- pressions made use of, and he was sure that Warrington had never realist(' and never would i realise the loss t had sustained in rejecting Dr. Houston. They ought to feel that it was an honour to have been allowed to work side by side with him ; and the expressions of regret at his defeat had been so num- erous ever since the election day that it would be im- possible to gi—e anything like the number of them. He regretted that they had not the pleasure of seeing Mr. Houston ther• "ley wculd have liked to renew their acquaintance with her, and assure her of the great esteem in which they held her. Mr. H. ROBERTS read a telegram from Mr. John Cros- field, from London, stating that he and his son, Mr. Arthur Crosfield, regretted inability to be present. He also read a letter from Mr. E. J. ("nest who regretted he could not attend, the more because he had formed a very high appreciation of Dr. Houston's ability and sincerity. Had the electors of Warrington done them- selves the honour of electing him they would have been in the van of progress, but they had missed their oppor- tunity, and must be content for the present to drag miserably behind. The letter concluded "Let us hope for better days in the future when the light shall shine upon the dim vision of our opponents." Mr. Roberts also read a telegram from Mr. W. Pierpoint excusing himself with regret, on account of being con- fined to the house with a bad cold, from attending. Mr. Roberts said he could only repeat most cordially every expression that had been trade there as to Dr. Houston both of appreciation of his abilities and of personal regard for him. Proud as they were of the Liberal candidates who had been put before the electorate of

div.head: DR. HOUSTON'S REPLY.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON'S REPLY.

Dr. HOUSTON, in reply said :—" I accept with heartfelt thanks the beautiful address and handsome gift you have kindly and generously presented me with. So marked a recognition of the merits of my candidature at the general election is, if I am not much mistaken, al- most unique. While, therefore, it is most complimen- tary to myself, it is highly creditable to the consti- tuency. Though I dare not flatter myself that I merit the encomiums bestowed upon me in your address, I yet venture to think that I endeavoured to deserve them. From the earliest moment of my candidature I felt that the Liberals of Warrington were worthy of all the efforts and all the sacrifices their candidate might be called upon to make. Their robust Liberalism, their earnest and unselfish devotion to the cause of justice and progress, in face of constant difficulties, frequent dis- ceuragements and repeated reverses ; their sympathy with my fellow-countrymen in the struggle for self- government, their loyalty to the man whom they honoured by choosing as their champion, gave them a title to the utmost exertions he was capable of patting forth. Under the bracing stimulus of those feelings, our contest was conducted. Though we failed with honour to ourselves and without detriment to our cause, never, I am convinced, was the position of Liberalism in War- rington stronger than to-day. The campaign through which you have passed has consolidated your organiza- tion, drawn your remit; together, improved yonr disci- pline, taught you where lies y our strength, and where lies your weakness. Furthermore, that campaign has had a great moral and educational effect. Interest and enthusiasm have been awakened ; delu- sions have been dispelled, misapprehensions have been dissipated, -ejudices undermined, where not entirely removed. It now only remains to take care that the good seed sown shall grow and ripen, and bring forth its natural fruit. I need not say that if I can be of any assistance in this work, you may always rely on my poor services. lam most gratified to find from the terms of the address, that you regard my action in the late contest as having been characterised by courtesy, as well as tact. It is only fair to say that had I been disposed to act differently, the behaviour, not only of our own followers but of my opponent and his suppor- ters generally would have left me without justification or excuse. The bearing towards each other of the two parties in Warrington, throughout the electoral struggle was such as both may justly be proud. On behalf of my wife, I have to thank you for the kindly referyce made in the addt-st, `n the part she took in the election, and to assure you that she felt it a pleasure and a privil- ege to be permitted to share in that memorable contest. Moreover, the friendships we have formed and the kind- ness we have experienced through my relations with your borough, would of themselves be an ample reward for our endeavours, such as they were, for the advance- ment of Liberal principles in Warrington. And now let me assure you that your individual welfare and the prosperity of your ancient and now happily thriving and growing town, will always be very near to my heart, and should the wish expressed at the close of your address, that I shall attain the distinction of a seat in the Imperial Parliament ever be realised, it will be a plea- sure to me to employ whatever influence such position may confer to further and to protect the interests of Warrington and of its people without distinction of party. Dr. Houston then proceeded to thank those present for their spoken references to him and Mrs. Houston, and claimed that he had passed from being a mere candidate into the rank of a personal friend of the Liberals of Warrington. He regretted that his wife was unable to be present, and she had requested him to express that regret, and her apprecia- tion of the kindness she had experienced in Warrington. If people had spoken hardly both of her and himself in Warrington, why he supposed they could both afford to despise it. (Hear, hear.) There was one drop of bitter- ness in his cup,and that was the untoward circumstances that had prevented him from receiving the presentation at the meeting that was intended to be held in Warring- ton that night. But he thought a wise and prudent course had been taken by those who had the management of the matter. It was right that they should refrain from bringing together a large concourse of people,which would have been calculated to spread the maladies which unfortunately mere or less prevailed in Warring- ton. He deeply lamented the fact that the town had been visited by the epidemics now more or less preva- lent there, and felt the deepest sympathy with those who had been struck down, and had been bereaved through them, and he trusted that the abatement which he understood had already occurred would be maintained. and that the outbreak would disappear shortly, and Warrington be restored to its usual health, prosperity, and happiness. (Hear, hear.) After expressing his thanks most heartily to the promoters otand subscribers to the presentation, he assuring them that it did not require a very beautiful volume and a very handsome 1 gift to endear the people of Warrington to him, he pro- ' ceeded to make some observations on the present political position. Although, he said, their efforts had failed in Warrington, the cause was triumphant. (Hear, hear.) The Tory and Unionist party after clinging desperately to power for six years, had bee., replaced by a Liberal ministry, with Mr. Gladstone at their head. That was not any ordinary occurrence in the history of political changes ; it marked an epoch, and inaugurated an era. It appeared to him that the democracy of the country had arrived at full age, and were about to enter upon their heritage. The current of reform had been , dammed for several years. It was now swollen and turbid, and no obstacle, no antiquated forms,no ancient institutions could arrest its progress. (Hear, hear.) And in his opinion, before long they would see a large 1 number of popular, democratic reforms carried out. S. far as any indication could be obtained from the acts of the Government they were thoroughly prepared to proceed upon popular and democra- tic lines. (Hear, hear.) Then again it wauld be found that the magisterial bench would be im- proved by the infusion of a large number of men im- bued with popular opinion, and of a considerable number of men taken from the working classes. In Ireland they had still greater reason to know that the Government were prepared to stand by their pledges. Mr. Chamber- lain, with a singular want of foresight, had proclaimed that Home Rule was as dead as Queen Anne. Home Rule was not dead ; ft was living and would live, but another thing was dead, and that was coercion. (Hear, I hear.) Dr. Houston urged the Liberals of Warrington not lose heart, and to keep out of their minds the idea that they were to lie down and be trampled by the beer interest, though he knew what a power it was in War- rington. The whole licensing system in Warrington, he said, was a huge machine worked only for the benefit of a few brewers. (Hear, hear.) They had a network of public-houses spread all over the borough and the neigh- bourhood, and which was so complete that it was almost I impossible for the poor victims to escape.- They knew where the spiders were that grew fat upon the poor people of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The public-houses of Warrington did not exist for the benefit of the people who stood behind the bars ; they were the mere jackals of the great brewers, and were glad to exist upon the crumbs that fell from the rich brewer's table. The brewers had thrown dotvn the gauntlet, and the Liberal party must take it up. After speaking of the necessity of reform in the licensing system, Ito remarked that there were many other reforms which the Liberal party were pledged to carry out, and they were determined to carry them out if possible, and he expressed the belief that the alliance between the Liberal Unionists and Tories must fall to pieces. In conclusion he said that if ever an opportunity occurred for his being of service politi- cally or otherwise to Warrington, or any person in War- rington, they might always call upon him to do it. (Loud applause.) The company subsequently partook of luncheon with Dr. Houston.

div.head: NEW WIRRAL RAILWAY'.
div.p: THE NEW WIRRAL RAILWAY'.
MR. GLADSTONE CUTS THE FIRST SOD.

Amid general jubilations Mr. Gladstone yesterday afternoon performed the ceremony of cutting the first sod of the Wirral Railway at Hawarden Bridge in bois- terous weather. Special trains conveying distinguished persons arrived from Manchester, Chester, and Wrex- ham, a number of officials accompanying the trains. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone were accompanied by Sir Theo- dore Martin, Sir Edward and Lady Watkin, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Mr. Henry Gladstone. The Rev. Stephen and Mrs. Gladstone, Rev. Harry and Mrs. Drew, and others also journeyed from Elawarden to the Dee Bridge. The Premier's party were met by a crowd of visitors, who cheered lustily as Mr. Gladstone proceeded on to the golf ground.

div.head: NEW LIBERAL MAGISTRATES
div.p: NEW LIBERAL MAGISTRATES
FOR WARRINGTON.

The following gentlemen were by post on Tues- day morning asked by the Chancellor of the Duchy to allow their names to be placed on the Commis- sion of the Peace for the Borough of Warrington. Each has consented to accept the honour, and the new borough magistrates will therefore be : Mr. William Pierpoint, hair and sizing merchant, Latchford.
Councillor .J. H. Fleming, tanner, Springfield-st. • Councillor H. Roberts, builders' merchant, Bold- street.
Dr. T. Starkey Smith, 80ld-street.
Mr. Thomas liirchall;wire maker, Froghall-lane. Mr. John Wesley Hayward, wire roller, Lovely- lane.

The new magistrates are all well-known Liberals of the town. Mr. William Pierpoint is chairman of the executive of the Liberal Association, and during the last election, and for many years previously, he took a very active part in fur- thering the cause of political progress in War- rington and its neighbourhood. He was also for several years an active and useful member of the Town Council. Amongst other offices of a public, or semi-public nature, he fills the post of President of the Chamber of Commerce, and has held that of President of the Warrington Football Club, and still, we believe, takes a keen interest in football and other forms of athletics. Mr. Fleming is president of the Liberal Club, and is an ear- nest politician. He holds a seat in the Town Council as a representative of Town Hall ward, and is chairman of the School Attendance Committee.• lie carries on the business of a tanner, and he is an active member of the Chamber of Commerce. Mr. Henry Roberts, although the youngest of the new magistrates, has figured pro- minently as a public man for some years. He is a Town Councillor for Whitecross Ward, and is a member of several committees. Being a leading partner of the Warrington Slate Company, be is closely identified with the trade of the town. He is one of the most ardent and indefatigable sup- porters of the Liberal cause in Warrington, and holds the office of honorary secretary of the Liberal Association. Dr. F. Starkey Smith is a very well- known and a highly respected townsman of Warrington. Enjoying an extensive practice as a medical practitioner, he is not, though a Liberal, often seen at political gatherings. lie is, however, an active and a generous member of the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, and has long held office in connection with that congrega- tion. Mr. T. Birchall's name is also a familiar 0116 to Warringtonians. He has for very many years been to the fore in local politics as an advanced Liberal, but apart from this he has done much pub- lic service in the town in various ways. He is the president Ithe Warrington Co-opera- tive Society,and has hethat position continuously for 22 or 23 years. - The esteem in which he is held by the members of that Society is evidenced by the fact that he is annually and unanimously re-elected to the presidency, lie holds a responsible position at the Whitecross Works. Mr. J. Wesley Hay- ward is the least known of the six new magistrates. Like Mr. Birchall, he bolds a position under the Whitecross Company. He has done and is doing excellent work in connection with the Wesleyan body, of which he is a member. He owes his ap- pointment mainly to the desire of the Liberal Government to give working-men a part in the ad- ministration of justice.

It may be mentioned in this connection that Frank H. Roberts, C.C., who resides in Windermere, was placed .in the Commission of the Peace for the county of Westmoreland some weeks ago. Mr. Roberts was for several years chairman of the Executive of the Warrington Liberal Association.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. J. CROSFIELD.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. J. CROSFIELD.

The marriage of Mr. John Joseph Crosfield, second son of Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., of Walton Lea, Warrington, was celebrated at Christ Church, Lan- caster Gate, London, on Tuesday afternoon last. The bride was Miss Alice Lilian Stack, daughter of Mr. Oliver Stokes Stack, of 30 Lans- downe Crescent, London, W., formerly of Rock Ferry, near Birkenheasl, and late Inspector-General of Mounted Police at Bengal. A considerable num- ber of invited guests were present at the ceremony. The bridegroom was accompanied by his brother, Mr. Arthur Crosfield. As the guests assembled the organist played " The Festal March," by Smart. The bride was conducted to the choir steps by her father, and there met by the bridegroom. She wore a dress of ivory satin duchesse with clusters of orange blossoms on the corsage and sleeves, and tude veil, covering a tiara of orange blossoms, and carried a bouquet of beautiful white flowers. Her train was held by two pages, Masters Hedley Stack and Jan Dixon. She was followed by six bridesmaids—Miss Flora Moody, Miss Constance Crosfield, Miss Aileen Crosfield, Miss Rose Stack, Miss Alice Stack, and Miss Maud Stack—who were arrayed in cream ben- galine with empire sashes of broche, with tiaras of small Japanese chrysanthemums, and tulle veils. Each bridesmaid wore a bangle with the monogram of the bride and bridegroom in pearls, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a banging bouquet of large Japanese 3 ellow chrysanthemums. The clegyman who conducted the service was the Rev. M. It. Neligan. The service was a full choral one, and on the Deus Misereatur being chanted at the close of the ceremony, the united couple passed a few minutes in silent prayer, at the altar rails, after which a few words were addressed to them by the clergyman. They then repaired to the vestry and signed the register, the signatures being witnessed by A. Stack, E. M. Stack, and John Crosfield. Mendelesohn's "Wedding March" was struck up on the organ as the couple left the church. The bridal party and guests then proceeded to the residence of the bride's father, where a reception was held. In the course of the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Cros- field took their departure for Clifton, whence they proceeded to Devonshire. At Messrs. Crosfield's soap works, at Bank Quay, the happy event was becomingly celebrated, the majority of the work- men having holiday ; and bunting plentifully dis- tributed about the works imparted to them quite a festive aspect. Small cannon were discharged at half past two, the time at which the ceremony was fixed to take place, and in the evening there, were displays of fireworks, both at the works and at Walton Lea. It may be mentioned that the bridegroom received as a present from the workmen at the soap works, a complimentarily inscribed handsome electro-plated tea and coffee tray, to which we referred last week. The employes of Messrs. Crosfield were to have celebrated the marriage by a knife and fork tea and a concert at Bank Quay Mission Room, but these have been deferred in order to admit of Mr. J. J. Crosfield,the promoter of the treat, being present.

div.head: --*-- WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: --*-- WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
_ THURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. - __

LETTERS FROM A FEVER INFECTED HOUSE.—EIIen Barber, a young woman, sued Mr. James West, of 15, Legh-street, Warrington, for 18s. 6d. in consequence of a breach of engagement as domestic servant. The plain- tiff said that she was engaged to go as domestic servant to the defendant's house, on September Ist., at a %age of 4s. 6d. a week. But before she had entered upon her duties she received a letter advising her not to go and cancelling the engagement on the ground that as she was unacquainted with the management of children it would be unadvisable for her to enter upon her duties. The defendant said he wrote to the defendant not to come because there were three fever cases in his house. The plaintiff out into court three letters which she had received from the detendant, but his Honour remarked and it was a wrong thing to put these letters into court seeing that they had come from a house in which there were fever cases. He added that he must, however, be guided by the evidence and would give a verdict for the plaintiff for the amount claimed in lieu of notice. CLAIM FOR DAMAGE TO A TRAZ—Eustace J. Shepherd, 1 Hut, Acton Grange, an engine fitter, was tried by John Young, an ammunition fitter, for a sum of 50s. for damage done to a trap through the defendant's negli- gence.—Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Forshaw (Davies and Forshaw) for the defendant.— Evidence was given that on Sunday, September 4th. the defendant came to the plaintiff and asked him for the loan of his trap in order to go to Bigneld, Runcorn, with his wife and a Mr. and Mrs. Jones. On receiving an undertaking that there would be only four passengers he allowed Shepherd the loan of it. The plaintiff harnessed a pony to the trap and drove it round to the defendant's house. He saw the defendant and his wife and Mr. Jones and his wife go off. It was then alleged by the plaintiff that the defendant allowed two men to enter I the trap, and immediately they got on the step the shafts broke, and the trap was very much injured. The re- pairs cost 50s. After the accident the defendant came to the plaintiff, and told him to have the vehicle repair- ed. On the presentation of the bill he refused to pay the amount incurred. Three witnesses were called, who stated that, on hearing a crash in the road outside of the house in which they resided, they went outside and saw four men in the road, two of whom were covered with dirt. The defence was that the trap tilted up
through Mrs. Shepherd altering her position. The other men in the road were declared to be cyclists. The judgment was in favour of the defendant, without costs.

A. PLEA FOR LENIENCY.—At the last sitting of the Court a verdict was recorded in favour of Mr. Jenkins against Mr. Dooley in regard to a bicycle accident. On Thursday Mr. Jenkins (Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth) appeared and informed his Honour that the costs of the case amounted to £8 2s. 6d., and as the defendant was only a poor man, in receipt of El per week, he asked that he be allowed to pay off the amount in instalments. Mr. Browne objected to this application. The plaintiff was very indignant about the matter, because the defendant's wife had been going about the village slandering him. Further, before the 'ace came on for hearing, the plaintiff agreed to take 30s. in discharge of the claim, this amount only being half of the damage done to the machine. The defendant refused to pay the amount, mid thus incurred the sum in question. Mr. Jenkins said that the defendant was only a labourer, managing a farm, and in receipt of £1 wages per week. He had the rent to meet in the first week of the new year, and it was a very large sum—£2B. Ihe defendant had to meet the whole amount, as he was six months in arrears. His Honour said he would depart from his usual course in this instance. He would allow the defendant to pay half of the sum due in a month, and the balance at the rate of £2 a month.
LATEST NE WS.
THE OLDHAMI lURDER.

Mellor, who is charged with the murder of his wife at Oldham, continues to sleep and eat well, and seems in- different to his position. Yesterday a constable near his cell remarked" This is a sad case," and the prisoner, who overheard it, replied sharply, "I don't know that it is. All of us have got to die once ; thee and all."

FORTHCOMING GIOVE-FIGHTS IN AMERICA. THE CORBETT AND MITCHELL MEETING. New ORLEANS, FRIDAY.-It is announced that the Olympic Club here has arranged another series of boxing contests to take place during the second week in February next year. The pugilists will include Corbett and Mitchell, heavy-weights; Fitzsimmons and Hall (Australian), middle-weights; and Jack M'Auliffe and Dick Burge (the latter of England), light-weights.

div.head: WRECK AT BLACKPOOL.
div.p: THE WRECK AT BLACKPOOL.
SALE OF THE HULL AND EFFECTS.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. Marsden o ffered for sale the wreck of the Sirene at Blackpool. There was a large attendance of brokers from Liverpool. The sails, haw- sers, &c., were sold at the pence station. rhf, ship's anchor fetched £5 10s. and the anchor chain £l7 10s., the ship chronometer £l2 10s., and the bidding for the hull commenced at £2O and was disposed of fs..r £B2 to a Livet pool buyer.

div.head: MORE FLOODS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: MORE FLOODS IN CHESHIRE.
THE POTATO CROP IN PERIL. '

It is stated from Great Saughall that a heavy down- pour has once more flooded fields and roads. Pedestrians have to wade through water in many places. The stationmaster at Saughall has engaged a cart to convey the passengers to and from the trains over the deep flood. Many acres of corn are still standing out, and as the potato fields are submerged it is feared a large percentage of the crop will be spoiled by disease.

div.head: LAMBETH 'MURDERS.
div.p: THE LAMBETH 'MURDERS.
THE PRISONER FOUND GUILTY.

Thomas Neill was again placed in the dock at the Old Bailey, London, yesterday, charged with the Lambeth murders. Mr. Justice Hawkins commenced summing up. The jury retired at a quarter to two o'clock, and on returning found the prisoner guilty. After the jury had returned their verdict, Neill was asked whether he wished to say anything why the sentence of death should not be passed, but he merely shook his head, net utter- ing a word. Mr. Justice Hawkins, assuming the black cap, said the murder was of unparalleled atrocity, so diabolical in character that he dare,not trust himself to speak of its details. The law knew but one penalty, and that was death. The sentence was then passed in the usual manner, and prisoner left the dank without assist- ance. Neill is said to have expressed himself yesterday morning on entering the court as being hopeful of acquittal.

div.head: LA.TE MR. W. H. GI A.DSTONE.
div.p: THE LA.TE MR. W. H. GI A.DSTONE.

A WARRINGTON TABLET FOR HAWARDEN. A very handsome tablet, to be erected in 'Anwar- den Church, to the memory of the late Mr. iv. IL Gladstone, a son of the Prime Minister, has been tastefully and skilfully executed, by Messrs. Williams and Clay, of Warrington, to the designs of Messrs. Douglas and Fordham, architects, of Chester. The tablet is of considerable size and is composed for the most part of solid alabaster richly moulded. The upper part of the sunk penal con- tains an ornamental Tudor cross, chastely fashioned in alabaster, and bearing the monogram i h 8 in gold letters, and also representations of the Tudor rose. The background of the cross is formed of a mosaic of rich red Italian griotte marble. Beneath the cross is the following inscription : " William Henry Gladstone, born June 3rd, 1840, uniting the singleheartedness of childhood, to the full develop- ment of his mental powers and to high accomplish- ment, he closed in perfect peace a life of love and service to God and man, on July 4th, 1891." Beneath this inscription are the words " Placed by his father and mother." The tablet was despatched to llawarden on Wednesday afternoon, and on Thursday it was erected in the church.

div.head: LOCAL CASES AT CHESHIRE SESSIONS.
div.p: LOCAL CASES AT CHESHIRE SESSIONS.

The Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the County of Chester were opened at the Sessions House, Knutsford, on Monday. His Honour, Sir Horatio Lloyd, presided in the large court, and Mr. Chitties Lister in the smaller one. The:following local cases were heard : THEFT AT RUNCORN.

William Jones and John Perry, af Warrington, the former a bootmaker, and the latter a labourer, were charged with breaking and entering the shop of Thomas Whinyates, Runcorn, and stealing slippers, knives, a basket, &c., on the 14th September.—The man Perry pleaded not guilty, and Jones guilty. Perry was accord- ingly tried. Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and prisoner was undefended.—Mr. Whinyates had two boot shops in Runcorn, one in Church-st. and the other in High-st. The Church-st. shop was a lock-up one, and it was securely fastened on the night of the 13th inst., and a brother of Mr. Whinyates proved to finding the loss of the goods named in the charge. The man had been discharged because of doing unpas- sable work.—P.S. Cheeney, of the Warrington police force, proved visiting the prisoners in a common lodging-house. They swore they had no property in the house, although the basket (produced) and slippers were found by him. He arrested them, and P.C. Gregory came from Runcorn to take them there. On the way Jones admitted hiding four pairs of boots in a cornfield. That was in the hearing of Perry. The boots were sub- sequently found where Jones said he had hidden them. In reply to the prisoner, P.S. Cheeney said he hai known ' him for ten years.—Prisoner : You never saw me doing any robbery P—P.S. Cheeney : No.—Prisoner : You might have seen roe a little bit inebriated. (Laughter.) —The Chairman said it would require the deep consi- deration of the jury as to whether Perry was guilty or not, as he seemed merely to have been the tool of the other man.—The Chairman : Just try to keep off drink Perry ;it will get you into trouble. As to Jones he had committed a most impudent offence, and there were two previous convictions against him. He was sorry to see an old man in his position.—Jones was committed to gaol for four months. THEFT OF A MACKINTOSH. Arthur Harris and Arthur Walsh were charged with stealing a waterproof coat on the 31st August, the pro- perty of Mr. Jacob McGill, of Lymm, als, a melton cloth overcoat. Mr. Lloyd prosecuted. Walsh pleaded not guilty, and Harris guilty.—Miss McGill, Mr. Thornicroft, Mr. Burrows, and also Police-sergeants Wynne and Griffiths, gave evidence.—Walsh said he did not steal the coat.—The jury found the prisoners guilty, and they were bound over to appear for judgment when called upon in their own recognizances of £lO each.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A meeting of this Council will be held on Tues- day next for winding up the business of the muni- cipal year. Amongst the subjects on the minutes of the Committees are the following:—
TRII SANITARY COMMITTEE'S ACCOUNTS.

The Sanitary Committee has passed the following resolutions :—That the several Sub-Committees of this Committee be instructed to examine all accounts for work done or goods supplied in their respective depart- ments, and to certify the accounts to this Committee for payment ; and that each Sub-Committee report at the end of each quarter upon the amount of accounts al- lowe I in their respective departments. and the estimated cost of works and goods ordered for which accounts may not have been received.
THE PROPOSED DIVISION OF SANITARY COMMITTEE.

The Sanitary Committee has ;e7;i;e7i.`"tl);:i"&"iown Clerk prepare the draft duties of the two Committee's • into which the Council have resolved that it is desirable to divide the duties and responsibilities of this Commit- tee."

div.head: 'MB REGISTRATION OF PLUMBERS.
div.p: 'MB REGISTRATION OF PLUMBERS.

The Sanitary Committee have resolved "that, for the purposes of public health, all plumbers practising in the borough be registered by this Committee, and that certir- flcstes be given to suck plumbers as, in the opinion of this Committee,are properly qualified to perform plumb- ing work."

div.head: THE" BLOWING " OF CARCASES.
div.p: THE" BLOWING " OF CARCASES.
The Sanitary Committee will propose that the Town Clerk be instructed to prepare byelaws to prohibit the blowing of carcases of animals slaughtered for human food.
THE PROPOSED DIVERSION OF THE RIVER.

The minutes of the Paving and -6-OmmitTe contain the following resolution :—" That the Chair- man and deputy-chairman be appointed to consider and report on the plan now submitted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, for the construction of a dam across the river, opposite the end of River-road, and that they invite the Chairman and deputy-chairman of the Rivers Committee to join with them in the matter°

TII E BURGESSES OF BEWSEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— My term of office as one of your representatives in the Town Council having been completed, I have again been asked by a large representative body of burgesses. quite irrespective of party politics, to again become the Candidate for this Ward. I have great pleasure in consenting, relying upon the hope that my past services in the Council have met with your approval. If I am favoured with a renewal of your confidence, you may depend upon my constant attention to your interests. It is a matter of deep concern to me, that the town is at present suffering from a terrible epidemic, and I much regret that at the commencement of the outbreak no temporary accommodation was provided for the immediate removal and Isolation of the patients, lam strongly of opinion that the work of the Sanitary Committee is too onerous to be efficiently carried out by one Committee. I will therefore support the formation of a Health Committee as a relief to the Sanitary Committee in the discharge of responsible duties, which ought to be shared by a larger number of the Council. I confidently leave myself in your hands, feeling assured that you will place me at the head of the poll on the day of election. am Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, SAMUEL J. BEA3IAN.

WIDNES MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF FARNWORTH WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, At the request of a number of influential burgesses of the Ward, I beg to offer myself as a candidate for the represent- , ation of the ward in the Council. I have resided all my life in the Ward, and have served you to the best of my ability on the Local Board for a number of years. I strongly object to the introduction of politics into municipal affairs, and therefore I appear before you as an Independent Candidate and not as the nominee of any political party. If yen should honour me by returning me as one of yonr Members to the Council, I shall endeavour to do my duty in the future as I have done in the past, without fear, favour, or bias. am, ladies and gentlemen, Your obedient servant. FRANCIS HEYE S. Appleton, Oct. 14th, 1892,

THE SHOP ASSISTANTS HALF HOLIDAY has been granted since Marcia 24th by a large majority of tradesmen. but it-is remarkable that it is still refused by a few who could well afford to close on Thursdays at one o'clock. We hereby strongly appeal to the public of Warrington and distriet to decline to purchase after one o'clock.

_ WIDNES MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF SIMMS CROSS WARD. LADDIS AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been requested to become a Candidata at the ensu- ing Municipal Election, I have decided to accede to the same on INDEPENDENT LINES. AS a native of the good old town, it is my highest ambition to become a member of its first Council. As a member of the Local Board, I trust my conduct will have met with your approval. As anon-party man, but as one who has always tried to do his duty irrespective of PARTY or POLITICS, I appeal to you for your vote and confidence, assuring you nothing shall be wanting on my part to further the interests of our Borough, and of balms CROSS WARD in particular. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, GEORGE INGRAM NEIL. Simms Cross, October 7th, 1892.

WIDNES BOROUGH ELECTION. VOTE FOR BROWN, SMITH, and TIM MIS, THE INDEPENDENT CANDIDATES. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST BANK WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been honoured by an invitation from a large and influential number of the Burgesses in the aoove Ward to become Independent Candidates at the forthcoming Munici- pal Election, we have great pleasure in doing so, believing that the introduction of Politics is opposed to the best inte- rests of the Ratepayers. If elected, we pledge ourselves to support measures at Sani- tary Improvement, such as street making and lighting. abatement of Nuisances, and the general cleanliness of the town. The Ratepayers' property shall have our best attention, and we will endeavour to keep the Gas and Water Undertakings up to Weir present high standard of efficiency, and the Hos- pitals in thorough working order,BELIEVING EFFICIENCY TO BE TRUE ECONOMY. Fellow-ratepayers, as the Candidates of your cho'oe, we leave ourselves in your hands, confidently believing you will support us on the day of election. We are, Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servants, BENJ. BROWN, THOMAS SMITH. HENRY SUTTON TIMMIS.

BOROUGH OF WIDNES ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF SIMM'S CROSS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, We ars about to return into your hands the trust you have reposed in us as your representatives on the Widnes Local Board. We have felt honoured in being chosen by our fellow townsmen to:serve them in such a capacity, and claim to have discharged our trust conscientiously, and are per- suaded that all our actions which have been performed under your moat intelligent notice, have met with your approval; a-fact which gives us much encouragement in responding to the hearty invitation, extended to us by the Ratepayers of the ward to come forward as candidates for Election to the Municipal Council to be formed on November lat. As re presentatives of large interehts in the town, we are deeply and earnestly concerned in all matters affecting its welfare, and are gratified with the thought that the new Council will become possessed of a valuable corporate estate, in the Gas and Water undertakings,which have beau fostered and developed tender our care, and they are now about the most efficient and profitable in the United Kingdom. The roads, too, have been placed in a very fair state of efficiency, and very many of the streets which were a dis- grace to us have been sewered, made and lighted, at a reasonable cost to the property owners, whereby good value has been obtained, and, whilst we are in favour of continuing this policy in the immediate future, we pledge ourselves— that, if elected, a vigilant eye shall be kept on the spending departments of the Council, and will especially watch the Jae/ ests of this important Ward by doing all in our power to further any project which in our judgment shall advance the comfort and welfare of the inhabitants. We are, ladies and gentlemen, Your faithful and obedient servants, JOSHUA MID WOOD. SAMUEL OWENS. SAMUEL SADLER.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN. You are now called upon to elect Members for the Sckool Board, to represent you for the next three years. We beg to recommend to your favourable notice the follow- ing Candidates C. E. BARLOW, ESQ., H. WADE DEACON, ESQ., J.P., REV. G. H. GARRATT, 8.D., MAJOR WAREING. Three of these gentlemen have been on the Board for some years, and you are fully informed as to the eourse they have pursued in Educational Matters. The new candidate—the Rev. G. H. Garrett—is one who is intimately acquainted with the successful management of Elementary Schools, and will I bring to the Board much experience In Educational Matters. I All the Candidates are in favour of making the Board Schools as efficient as possible, and, whilst keeping in view Progressive Education, will exercise the greatest economy I compatible with the objects in view. They are in favour of Religious Teaching in your Schools ; will assist the Voluntary Schools of the town as far as the Education Acts permit; and by giving the Denominational Schools fair and just treatment, tend to preserve them, and thus keep down your Rates. THEREFORE VOTE FOR BARLOW, DEACON, GARRETT, AND WAREING. We are Ladies and Gentlemen, on behalf of the United Church Councils of Farnworth, S. Ambrose. and Widnes, A. THORPE. Chairman. STUART DEACON, Hon. Treasurer. JOHN C. CRAWFORD, Hon. Secretary.
